processed_clauses.metadata_title: ACT No. IV OF 1969
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
ACT No. IV OF 1969
[8th March, 1969]
An Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to customs
WHEREAS it is expedient to consolidate and amend the law relating to the levy and collection of customs-duties and to provide for other allied matters;
It is hereby enacted as follows: -

Customs Act 1969: This is the foundational parent statute enacted to consolidate and amend the laws governing customs in Bangladesh.
The Act serves as the supreme legal authority for the regulation of customs procedures and the governance of trade-related matters.
Customs Duty: The Act establishes the legal framework for the levy and collection of customs duties on goods.
The scope of the Act includes all matters connected to the administration of duties and other allied customs processes.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER I - PRELIMINARY
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER I
PRELIMINARY

Customs Act 1969: This refers to the primary statute governing customs procedures, duties, and enforcement in Bangladesh. The Preliminary chapter serves as the introduction to the legal framework established by this Act.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Short title, extent and commencement
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1. Short title, extent and commencement.- (1) This Act may be called the Customs Act, 1969.
(2) It extends to the whole of 1[Bangladesh].
(3) It shall come into force on such date2 as the 3[Government] may, by notification in the official Gazette, appoint.

Customs Act 1969: This is the official short title given to the legislation.
The application of this Act extends across the entire territory of Bangladesh.
The Act is designed to become effective on a date determined and publicly announced by the Government through an official gazette notification.
Government: The Government is granted the legal authority to determine and announce the specific commencement date for the enforcement of the Act through an official gazette notification.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Definitions

Agent: An agent is defined as any person, such as a shipping, clearing, forwarding, or cargo agent, who is licensed under section 207 or permitted to transact business under section 208 of this Act.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: This is the defined Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 196 of the Act for handling customs, excise, and VAT matters.
Officer of Customs: An appropriate officer is defined as an officer of customs tasked with specific functions assigned by or under this Act. The term officer of customs generally refers to any individual appointed under section 3.
Bangladesh customs-waters: This defines the maritime jurisdiction of the Act as the sea area extending twelve nautical miles from the appropriate baseline on the Bangladesh coast.
Bill of Entry: A bill of entry is a document delivered under section 79, which now includes electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
Bill of Export: A bill of export is a document delivered under section 131, which includes electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
National Board of Revenue: The Board refers to the National Board of Revenue, which is the entity constituted under the National Board of Revenue Order 1972.
Coastal Goods: Coastal goods are defined as items transported by vessel between ports in Bangladesh, excluding any imported goods for which customs duty remains unpaid.
Container: A container is a durable, enclosed receptacle of at least one cubic meter, specifically designed for the repeated carriage of goods across multiple transport modes without intermediate reloading.
Controlling Authority: This refers to the owner, legal occupier, or any person holding legal control over a customs-airport, customs-port, customs-inland container depot, or customs-station.
Conveyance: A conveyance is defined as any means of transport used to carry goods or passengers, including vessels, aircraft, vehicles, or animals.
Customs Airport: A customs-airport is any airport declared as such under section 9 of the Act.
Customs-area: A customs-area includes the limits of a customs-station as specified under section 10, encompassing locations where imported or export-bound goods are stored pending customs clearance.
Customs Computerised Entry Processing Sy: Defined as the Customs computer system, this is an automated processing system established by the National Board of Revenue to facilitate the purposes of this Act.
Customs-inland container depot: This is any location declared as a customs-inland container depot under section 9 of the Act.
Customs Port: A customs-port is any place declared under section 9 to be a port for the landing and shipment of goods.
Customs Station: A customs-station refers collectively to any customs-port, customs-airport, or land customs-station.
Export Manifest: An export manifest is a document delivered under section 53, including electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
Goods: Goods are defined broadly to include all movable property, specifically including conveyances, stores, materials, baggage, currency, negotiable instruments, and electronic data.
Import Manifest: An import manifest is a document delivered under sections 43 and 44, including electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
Land Customs Station: A land customs-station is any place, including inland river ports, declared as such under section 9.
Master of the Vessel: The master is the person, excluding pilots or harbour masters, who has command or charge of a vessel.
Person: For the purposes of this Act, a person includes companies, partnerships, associations, firms, or any body of persons.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: An entity appointed under section 25A to conduct pre-shipment inspections, including its representatives.
Prescribed: The term prescribed signifies that requirements or details are set out by rules or official orders made under this Act.
Registered User: A registered user is any individual or entity authorized and registered to access the Customs computer system for the purposes of the Act.
Rules: Rules refer to the regulations and operational procedures established under the authority of this Act.
Smuggling: Smuggling involves the illegal import or export of restricted goods, evasion of customs duties/taxes, or use of unauthorized routes, and includes any attempts, abetment, or concealment of such activities.
Special Bonded Warehouse: This is a private warehouse licensed under section 13 for hundred percent export-oriented industries, designated by the National Board of Revenue for specific exemptions.
Warehouse: A warehouse is defined as any place appointed under section 12 or licensed under section 13 of the Act.
Warehousing Station: A warehousing station is a location officially declared as such under section 11.
Wharf: A wharf is a place within a customs-port, approved under section 10(b), designated for the loading and unloading of goods.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER II - APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS OF CUSTOMS AND THEIR POWERS
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER II
APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS OF CUSTOMS AND THEIR POWERS

Customs Act 1969: This chapter of the Customs Act 1969 provides the legal foundation for the appointment of customs officers and delineates the scope of their official powers and functions.
Officer of Customs: The legislation establishes the framework for designating various classes and categories of customs officers who are authorized to carry out the enforcement of customs law.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Appointment of officers of Customs

National Board of Revenue: The Board is authorized under the Customs Act 1969 to appoint customs officers by notification in the official Gazette for specified areas or functions.
Customs Act 1969: This statute provides the legal framework and authority for the appointment of various customs officials to manage customs areas and functions.
Chief Commissioner of Customs: This is an official designation appointed by the Board to carry out customs functions as specified in the official gazette.
Commissioner of Customs: This is an official designation appointed by the Board to carry out customs functions as specified in the official gazette.
This is an official designation appointed by the Board to carry out customs functions related to bonded warehouses.
This is an official designation appointed by the Board to carry out customs functions related to valuation and internal audit.
Commissioner (Appeals): This is an official designation appointed by the Board to carry out customs functions as specified in the official gazette.
Director General: The Board may appoint officials to this role to oversee various specialized divisions such as customs intelligence, training, and duty exemption, as defined by the Act.
Additional Commissioner of Customs: This rank is appointed by the Board to perform customs duties within the organizational hierarchy established by the Act.
Joint Commissioner of Customs: This rank is appointed by the Board to perform customs duties within the organizational hierarchy established by the Act.
Deputy Commissioner of Customs: This rank is appointed by the Board to perform customs duties within the organizational hierarchy established by the Act.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This rank is appointed by the Board to perform customs duties within the organizational hierarchy established by the Act.
Revenue Officer: This official is appointed by the Board to assist in customs administration and revenue collection functions.
Officer of Customs: The Act grants the Board the power to appoint individuals to any other designation as an officer of customs to fulfill the objectives of the law.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Powers and duties of officers of customs
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
4. Powers and duties of officers of customs.- An officer of customs appointed under section 3 shall exercise such powers and discharge such duties as are conferred or imposed on him by or under this Act; and he shall also be competent to exercise all powers and discharge all duties conferred or imposed upon any officer subordinate to him:
Provided that, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or the rules, the Board may, by general or special order, impose such limitations or conditions on the exercise of such powers and discharge of such duties as it thinks fit.

Officer of Customs: These officers are empowered to exercise the powers and discharge the duties explicitly conferred upon them by the Customs Act 1969. They are also authorized to exercise the powers and duties assigned to any official subordinate to them.
National Board of Revenue: The Board maintains the authority to impose limitations or conditions on the powers and duties of customs officers through the issuance of general or special orders, regardless of provisions in the Customs Act 1969 or any subordinate rules.
Customs Act 1969: This is the foundational statute that grants powers and imposes duties upon customs officers and establishes the framework under which these officials operate.
Rules: These represent the subordinate legislation which, alongside the Customs Act 1969, is subject to the overriding authority of the National Board of Revenue when it issues orders restricting or conditioning the performance of customs officers.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Delegation of Powers

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue holds the authority to delegate its powers by issuing a notification in the official Gazette. This delegation is subject to such limitations or conditions as the Board may specify in the notification.
Additional Commissioner of Customs: The National Board of Revenue may empower an Additional Commissioner of Customs to exercise specific powers assigned to a Commissioner of Customs under section 3 of the Customs Act 1969.
Commissioner of Customs: Certain powers reserved for the Commissioner of Customs may be delegated to other customs officials, specifically the Additional Commissioner of Customs and the Joint Commissioner of Customs, subject to the conditions specified in the delegation notification.
Joint Commissioner of Customs: A Joint Commissioner of Customs may be empowered to exercise the powers of an Additional Commissioner of Customs or specific powers of a Commissioner of Customs as designated by the Board.
Deputy Commissioner of Customs: A Deputy Commissioner of Customs may be empowered to exercise the powers and functions of a Joint Commissioner of Customs or an Additional Commissioner of Customs.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: An Assistant Commissioner of Customs may be empowered to exercise any of the powers officially delegated to a Deputy Commissioner of Customs.
Officer of Customs: Other officers of customs may be granted the powers normally vested in an Assistant Commissioner of Customs through the official notification process defined by the Board.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Entrustment of functions of the customs officers to certain other officers
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 6. Entrustment of functions of the customs officers to certain other officers.- The Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, entrust, either conditionally or unconditionally, any functions of any officer of customs under this Act to any officer of the 8[Government].

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to delegate the functions of customs officers to other government officers through a notification in the official Gazette.
The delegation of functions by the National Board of Revenue can be made either conditionally or unconditionally.
Officer of Customs: The functions of an officer of customs, as defined by the Customs Act 1969, may be entrusted to other officers serving the government.
Government: The officers of the government may be assigned to perform the functions of customs officers when authorized by the National Board of Revenue.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Assistance to the officers of customs
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 9[7. Assistance to the officers of customs.- All officers and staffs of government and semi-government organizations, law enforcement agencies, security forces, autonomous bodies, statutory bodies, financial institutions, educational institutions, private organizations, local government and non- government organizations shall assist the officers of customs in the discharge of their functions under this Act.]

Officer of Customs: Officers of customs are granted the authority to receive assistance from a wide range of public and private sector entities to effectively perform their duties and functions under the Customs Act 1969.
Customs Act 1969: This statute establishes the legal mandate for customs officers to perform their functions and imposes a formal requirement for various governmental, autonomous, and private bodies to provide assistance to these officers in the course of their duties.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Exemption from service on jury or inquest or as assessors
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 8. Exemption from service on jury or inquest or as assessors.- Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, no officer of the Board or 3[Commissioner of Customs] and no other officer of customs whom the Board or 3[Commissioner of Customs] deems it necessary to exempt on grounds of public, duty shall be compelled to serve on 4[an inquest].

Officer of Customs: Officers of customs or officers of the National Board of Revenue may be exempted from mandatory service on jury or inquest duties. This exemption is granted when the National Board of Revenue or the Commissioner of Customs deems such relief necessary for the effective performance of public duty.
National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue possesses the authority to grant exemptions to customs personnel from serving on juries or inquests. This power is exercised to ensure that public duties are prioritized over external legal service obligations.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is empowered to exempt officers under their jurisdiction from mandatory service on juries or inquests. This discretionary authority is exercised on the grounds of public duty.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER III - DECLARATION OF PORTS, AIRPORTS, LAND CUSTOMS-STATIONS, ETC.
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER III
DECLARATION OF PORTS, AIRPORTS, LAND
CUSTOMS-STATIONS, ETC.

Customs Station: This chapter provides the legislative framework for the formal declaration and establishment of ports, airports, and land customs stations under the Customs Act.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Declaration of customs-ports, customs-airports, etc

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to issue notifications in the official Gazette to designate customs-ports, customs-airports, land customs-stations, customs-inland container depots, and transit routes for the movement of goods.
The National Board of Revenue has the authority to define which places are considered custom-houses and to establish their territorial limits for the purposes of the Customs Act.
Customs Port: The National Board of Revenue may designate specific ports that serve as the exclusive locations for unloading imported goods and loading goods for export.
Customs Airport: The National Board of Revenue may designate specific airports that serve as the exclusive locations for unloading imported goods and loading goods for export.
Land Customs Station: Specific locations may be declared as land customs-stations for the clearance of goods that are imported or exported via land or inland waterways.
Customs-inland container depot: Specific locations may be declared as customs-inland container depots for the clearance of goods that are imported or exported via land or inland waterways.
Customs House: The National Board of Revenue has the authority to define the locations that function as custom-houses and specify the legal limits of their jurisdiction.
Coastal Trade: The National Board of Revenue may declare specific places to be ports authorized to conduct coastal trade with designated customs-ports within the country.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to approve landing places and specify limits of customs-stations
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
10. Power to approve landing places and specify limits of customs-stations.- The Board may, by notification in the official Gazette-
(a) specify the limits of any customs-station; and
(b) approve proper places in any customs-station for the loading and unloading of goods or any class of goods.

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to issue notifications in the official Gazette to exercise control over customs-stations and their operational areas.
Customs Station: The National Board of Revenue has the authority to specify the geographic limits of any customs-station.
The Board may approve specific locations within a customs-station that are designated for the legal loading and unloading of various goods.
Goods: The movement of goods, including specific classes of goods, must be conducted at designated approved places within a customs-station for loading and unloading purposes.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to declare warehousing stations
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 11. Power to declare warehousing stations.- The Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare places to be warehousing stations at which alone public warehouses may be appointed and private warehouses may be licensed.

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to designate specific geographical locations as warehousing stations through an official gazette notification.
Warehousing Station: A warehousing station is a formally declared location where public warehouses may be appointed and private warehouses may be licensed, serving as the exclusive zone for these operations.
Public Warehouse: Public warehouses can only be appointed within those locations that have been officially declared as warehousing stations by the National Board of Revenue.
Private Warehouse: Private warehouses may only be licensed to operate within the specific geographical areas designated as warehousing stations.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to appoint public warehouses
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 12. Power to appoint public warehouses.- At any warehousing station, the 1[Commissioner of Customs (Bond) or any other Commissioner of Customs authorised by the Board] may, from time to time, appoint public warehouses wherein dutiable goods may be deposited without payment of customs-duty.

Public Warehouse: The Commissioner of Customs (Bond) or other authorized Commissioners are empowered to designate locations as public warehouses at any warehousing station.
Public warehouses are authorized facilities where dutiable goods can be stored without the immediate requirement to pay customs duties.
Commissioner of Customs: This official is specifically granted the authority to appoint public warehouses at any warehousing station to facilitate the storage of goods under bond.
Warehousing Station: These are designated locations where the appointment of public warehouses is legally permitted under the provisions of the Act.
National Board of Revenue: The Board holds the supervisory power to authorize specific Commissioners of Customs to exercise the function of appointing public warehouses.
Customs Duty: Goods deposited in a public warehouse are exempted from the immediate payment of customs duty until they are removed or otherwise cleared according to law.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Licensing of private warehouses
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
2["13. Licensing of private warehouses.- (1) Subject to sub-section (2), at any warehousing station, the Commissioner of Customs (Bond) or any other Commissioner of Customs authorized by the Board may, license private warehouses wherein dutiable goods imported by or on behalf of the licensee, or any other imported goods in respect of which facilities for deposit in a public warehouse are not available, may be deposited.

Private Warehouse: The Commissioner of Customs (Bond) or other authorized Commissioner may license private warehouses at any warehousing station. These facilities are used for depositing dutiable goods imported by the licensee or other imported goods where public warehouse facilities are unavailable.
Commissioner of Customs: This official is authorized to grant, suspend, or cancel licenses for private warehouses subject to conditions imposed by the National Board of Revenue.
National Board of Revenue: The Board holds the authority to empower specific Commissioners to license private warehouses. It also has the power to issue notifications in the official Gazette to impose conditions, limitations, or restrictions on the licensing, the type of goods warehoused, and import entitlements.
Licensee: A licensee of a private warehouse may have their license suspended or cancelled for contravening the Customs Act, violating rules, or breaching license conditions. In cases of potential cancellation, the licensee must be issued a show cause notice and provided a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
Show Cause Notice: A show cause notice must be served to a licensee thirty days prior to the cancellation of their private warehouse license, ensuring the party is granted a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal framework under which private warehouse licenses are granted, regulated, and subject to disciplinary actions such as suspension or cancellation.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Stations for officers of customs to board and land
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 14. Stations for officers of customs to board and land.- The 1[Commissioner of Customs] may, from time to time, appoint, in or near any customs-ports, stations or limits at or within which vessels arriving at or departing from such port shall bring to for the boarding or landing of officers of customs, and may, unless separate provisions therefor have been made under the Ports Act, 1908 (XV of 1908) direct at what particular place in any such vessels, not brought into port by pilots, shall anchor or moor.

Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is empowered to appoint specific stations or limits in or near customs-ports where vessels must stop for the boarding or landing of customs officers.

The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to direct where vessels that are not brought into port by pilots shall anchor or moor, provided such directions do not conflict with provisions made under the Ports Act 1908.
Customs Port: Customs-ports serve as the locations where the Commissioner of Customs may establish designated stations for the boarding and landing of customs officers.
Vessel: Vessels arriving at or departing from a customs-port are required to bring to at designated stations to facilitate the boarding or landing of officers of customs.
Vessels not brought into port by a pilot are subject to the direction of the Commissioner of Customs regarding their specific anchoring or mooring locations.
Officer of Customs: Officers of customs are authorized to board or land from vessels at designated stations established for this purpose.
Ports Act 1908: The Ports Act 1908 provides the legal framework under which separate provisions regarding the anchoring or mooring of vessels may be established, taking precedence over general directions given by the Commissioner of Customs.
Pilot: The involvement of a pilot in bringing a vessel into port determines whether the Commissioner of Customs may issue specific directions regarding the vessel's anchoring or mooring location.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER IV - PROHIBITION AND RESTRICTION OF IMPORTATION AND EXPORTATION
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER IV
PROHIBITION AND RESTRICTION OF
IMPORTATION AND EXPORTATION

Customs Act 1969: This chapter establishes the foundational legal framework under the Act for governing and regulating the prohibition and restriction of the movement of goods into and out of the country.
Importation: The Act provides the government with the authority to impose prohibitions or restrictions on the entry of goods into the country.
Export: The Act provides the government with the authority to impose prohibitions or restrictions on the departure of goods from the country.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Prohibitions

Goods: The importation of certain specified categories of goods into Bangladesh by air, land, or sea is prohibited.
The Government reserves the right to issue a written order to exempt specific classes of goods from these import prohibitions subject to conditions, limitations, or restrictions.
Penal Code 1860: This Act provides the legal definition of a counterfeit trademark used for determining prohibited imported goods.
Trademarks Act 2009: This Act provides the legal definition of a false trade description used to identify prohibited imported goods.
Patents and Designs Act 1911: This Act governs the existence of copyrights in designs; goods infringing on such designs are prohibited from import unless authorized by the registered proprietor.
Copyright Act 2000: The import of goods produced outside Bangladesh that infringe on rights protected under this Act or involve the unauthorized use of integrated circuit layout designs for commercial purposes is prohibited.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to prohibit or restrict importation and exportation of goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 16. Power to prohibit or restrict importation and exportation of goods.- The 2[Government] may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, prohibit or restrict the bringing into or taking out of 3[Bangladesh] of any goods of specified description by air, sea or land.

Government: The Government is empowered to issue notifications in the official Gazette to prohibit or restrict the import or export of specific types of goods.
Importation: The Government has the legal authority to restrict or prohibit the bringing of specific goods into Bangladesh by air, sea, or land.
Export: The Government has the legal authority to restrict or prohibit the taking of specific goods out of Bangladesh by air, sea, or land.
Goods: The Government may regulate the movement of goods into or out of the country by issuing notifications that specify descriptions of goods subject to prohibition or restriction.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Detention and confiscation of goods imported in breach of section 15 or section 16
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 10["17. Detention and confiscation of goods imported in breach of section 15 or section 16. - Where any goods are imported into or attempted to be exported out of Bangladesh in violation of the provisions of the section 15 or of a notification under section 16, such goods shall, without prejudice to any other penalty to which the offender may be liable under this Act, or any other law, be liable to be detained and confiscated and shall be disposed of in such a manner as may be prescribed."]

Imported Goods: Goods imported or attempted to be exported in violation of section 15 or section 16 of the Customs Act 1969 are subject to detention and confiscation.
Confiscated goods must be disposed of according to the procedures prescribed by law, regardless of any other penalties applicable to the offender.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal basis for detaining and confiscating goods that are imported or exported in breach of specific statutory provisions or notifications.
Confiscation of Goods: The power to confiscate goods serves as a legal consequence for violations of trade regulations, functioning independently of other penalties or liabilities an offender may face under the law.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER V - LEVY OF, EXEMPTION FROM, AND REPAYMENT OF, CUSTOMS-DUTIES
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER V
LEVY OF, EXEMPTION FROM, AND REPAYMENT OF,
CUSTOMS-DUTIES

Customs Duty: This chapter governs the legal framework for the assessment and collection of customs duties.
It outlines the provisions under which specific goods or transactions may be granted exemptions or qualify for the repayment of paid duties.
Customs Exemption: This chapter establishes the legislative basis for providing exemptions from the payment of customs duties on imported or exported goods.
Drawback of Customs Duties: The chapter provides the statutory authority for the repayment of customs duties, commonly referred to as drawback, under specified legal conditions.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Goods dutiable
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
6[18. Goods dutiable.- (1) Except as hereinafter provided, customs- duties shall be levied at such rates as are prescribed in the First Schedule 7[* *] or under any other law for the time being in force on-
(a) goods imported into, or exported from, Bangladesh;
(b) goods brought from any foreign country to any customs-station, and without payment of duty there, transhipped or transported for, or thence carried to, and imported at, any other customs- station; and
(c) goods brought in bond from one customs-station to another 1[:
Provided that no customs duty under this Act or other tax leviable by a customs officer under any other law for the time being in force shall be levied or collected in respect thereof, if-
(a) in value of the goods in any one consignment do not exceed one thousand taka; and
(b) the total amount of such duty and tax does not exceed taka one thousand.]
2[(2) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, levy, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions as it may deem fit to impose, a regulatory duty on all or any of the goods specified in the First Schedule at the rate not exceeding the highest rate of customs duty 3[* *] specified in the said Schedule.]
3["Explanation :- The rate of regulatory duty on any such goods may be higher than that of the customs duty leviable on that goods as prescribed in the said Schedule, provided such regulatory duty does not exceed the highest rate of customs duty of that Schedule."]
(3) The regulatory duty levied under sub-section (2) shall be in addition to any duty imposed under sub-section (1) or under any other law for the time being in force.
(4) Any notification issued under sub-section (2) shall, if not earlier rescinded, stand rescinded on the expiry of the financial year in which it was issued.]

Customs Duty: Customs duty is levied on goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh, as well as goods transhipped, transported, or moved in bond between customs stations, at rates prescribed in the First Schedule or other applicable laws.
Customs duty and other taxes are not leviable if the total value of a consignment and the total duty amount do not exceed the specified threshold amounts.
First Schedule: The First Schedule contains the rates for customs duties and serves as the reference for determining regulatory duty limits.
Regulatory Duty: The Government may levy a regulatory duty on goods specified in the First Schedule via notification in the official Gazette, subject to specific conditions, limitations, or restrictions.
Regulatory duty is collected in addition to customs duties and any other applicable taxes, and its rate is capped at the highest rate of customs duty specified in the First Schedule.
Any notification imposing a regulatory duty automatically expires at the end of the financial year in which it was issued, unless it is rescinded earlier.
Government: The Government is empowered to impose regulatory duties on goods through official Gazette notifications, subject to conditions and limitations deemed fit.
Goods: This provision governs the dutiability of various categories of goods, including those imported, exported, transhipped, or transported under bond between customs stations.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Imposition of countervailing duty
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
5[18A. Imposition of countervailing duty.- (1) Where any country or territory pays, bestows, directly or indirectly, any subsidy upon the manufacture or production therein or the exportation therefrom of any goods including any subsidy on transportation of such goods, then, upon the importation of any such goods into Bangladesh, whether the same is imported directly from the country of manufacture, production or otherwise, and whether it is imported in the same condition as when exported from the country of manufacture or production or has been changed in condition by manufacture, production or otherwise, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, impose a countervailing duty not exceeding the amount of such subsidy.
Explanation.- For the purposes of this section, subsidy shall be deemed to exist, if-
(a) there is financial contribution by a Government, or any public body within the territory of the exporting or producing country, that is, where-
(i) a Government practice involves a direct transfer of funds (including grants, loans and equity infusion) or potential direct transfer of funds or liability or both;
(ii) Government revenue that is otherwise due is forgone or not collected (including fiscal incentives);
(iii) a Government provides goods or services other than general infrastructure or purchases goods;
(iv) a Government makes payments to funding mechanism, or entrusts or directs a private body to carry out one or more of the type of functions specified in clauses (i), (ii) or (iii) which would normally be vested in the Government and the practice, in no real sense, differs from practices normally followed by Governments; or
(b) a Government grants or maintains any form of income or price support, which operates directly or indirectly to increase export of any goods from, or to reduce import of any goods to its territory, and a benefit is thereby conferred.
(2) The Government may, pending the determination of the amount of subsidy, in accordance with the provisions of this section and the rules made thereunder impose a countervailing duty under this sub-section not exceeding the amount of such subsidy as provisionally estimated by it and if such countervailing duty exceeds the subsidy as so determined,-
(a) the Government shall, having regard to such determination and as soon as may be after such determination reduce such countervailing duty; and
(b) refund shall be made of so much of such countervailing duty which has been collected as is in excess of the countervailing duty as so reduced.
(3) Subject to any rules made by the Government, by notification in the official Gazette, the countervailing duty under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall not be levied unless it is determined that-
(a) the subsidy relates to export performance;
(b) the subsidy relates to the use of domestic raw materials over imported raw materials in the exported goods; or
(c) the subsidy has been conferred on a limited number of persons engaged in manufacturing, producing or exporting the goods unless such a subsidy is for-
(i) research activities conducted by or on behalf of persons engaged in the manufacture, production or export; or
(ii) assistance to disadvantaged regions within the territory of the exporting country; or
(iii) assistance to promote adaptation of existing facilities to new environmental requirements.
(4) If the Government, is of the opinion that the injury to the domestic industry which is difficult to repair, is caused by massive imports in relatively short period, of the goods benefiting from subsidies paid or bestowed and where in order to preclude the recurrence of such injury, it is necessary to levy countervailing duty retrospectively, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, impose countervailing duty from a date prior to the date of imposition of countervailing duty under sub-section (2) but not beyond ninety days from the date of notification under that sub-section and notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, such duty shall be payable from the date as specified in the notification issued under this sub- section.
(5) The countervailing duty chargeable under this section shall be in addition to any other duty imposed under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.
(6) The countervailing duty imposed under this section shall unless revoked earlier, cease to have effect on the expiry of five years from the date of such imposition:
Provided that if the Government, in a review, is of the opinion that the cessation of such duty is likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of subsidization and injury, it may, from time to time, extend the period of such imposition for a further period of five years and such further period shall commence from the date of order of such extension:
Provided further that where a review initiated before the expiry of the aforesaid period of five years has not come to a conclusion before such expiry, the countervailing duty may continue to remain in force pending outcome of such a review for a further period not exceeding one year.
(7) The amount of any subsidy referred to in sub-section (1) or sub- section (2) shall, from time to time, be ascertained and determined by the Government, after such inquiry as it may consider necessary and the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for the identification of such goods and for the assessment and collection of any countervailing duty imposed upon the importation thereof under this section.
(8) No proceeding for imposition of countervailing duty under this section shall commence unless the Bangladesh Tariff Commission, on receipt of written application by or on behalf of a domestic industry, informs the Government that there is prima-facie evidence of injury which caused by direct or indirect subsidy on any particular imported goods.]

Countervailing Duty: The Government is authorized to impose a countervailing duty on imported goods that have benefited from foreign subsidies to manufacture, produce, or export them. This duty is levied in addition to any other duties payable under the Customs Act or other laws.

The Government may impose a provisional countervailing duty pending a final determination of the subsidy amount, with provisions for reduction and refund if the collected duty exceeds the final determined amount.

The duty remains in effect for five years from the date of imposition unless revoked earlier, with potential extensions if a review indicates that ending the duty would lead to the recurrence of subsidized injury.
Subsidy: A subsidy is defined as a financial contribution by a government or public body, including direct transfer of funds, forgone revenue, provision of goods and services, or support to specific entities that confers a benefit.
It also includes any form of income or price support that operates to increase exports or reduce imports for a territory. The Government determines the subsidy amount through necessary inquiries.
Government: The Government holds the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to impose, adjust, or retrospectively apply countervailing duties.
It is responsible for determining the amount of subsidies, conducting reviews, and establishing rules for the assessment and collection of countervailing duties.
Local Industry: The domestic industry may seek the initiation of countervailing duty proceedings by submitting a written application to the Bangladesh Tariff Commission.
Protection is provided to the domestic industry against injury caused by massive imports of subsidized goods or cases where subsidies confer benefits on a limited number of persons.
Bangladesh Tariff Commission: The Bangladesh Tariff Commission serves as the primary body to receive applications from the domestic industry regarding subsidized imports and must inform the Government if there is prima-facie evidence of injury to warrant the commencement of formal proceedings.
Imported Goods: Imported goods benefiting from subsidies, whether in their original state or having undergone changes through manufacture or production, are subject to countervailing duty upon entry into Bangladesh.
The duty applies even if the goods are not imported directly from the country where the subsidy originated.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Imposition of anti-dumping duty
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
118B. Imposition of anti-dumping duty.- (1) Where any goods are exported from any country or territory (hereinafter in this section referred to as the exporting country or territory) to Bangladesh at less than the normal value, then, upon the importation of such goods into Bangladesh, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, impose an anti-dumping duty not exceeding the margin of dumping in relation to such goods.
Explanation.- For the purposes of this section,-
(a) "margin of dumping", in relation to any goods, means the difference between its export price and its normal value;
(b) "export price", in relation to any goods, means the price of the goods exported from the exporting country or territory and in cases where there is no export price or where the export price is unreliable because of association or a compensatory arrangement between the exporter and the importer of a third party, the export price may be constructed on the basis of the price at which the imported goods are first resold to an independent buyer, or not resold in the condition as imported, on such reasonable basis as may be determined in accordance with the rules made under sub-section (6);
(c) "normal value", in relation to any goods, means-
(i) the comparable price, in the ordinary course of trade, for the like goods when meant for consumption in the exporting country or territory as determined in accordance with the rules made under sub-section (6); or
(ii) when there are no sales of the like goods in the ordinary course of trade in the domestic market of the exporting country or territory, or, when because of the particular market situation or low volume of the sales in the domestic market of the exporting country or territory, such sales do not permit a proper comparison the normal value shall be either-
(a) comparable representative price of the like goods when exported from the exporting country or territory or an appropriate third country as determined in accordance with the rules made under sub-section (6); or
(b) the cost of production of the said goods in the country of origin along with reasonable addition for administrative, selling and general costs and for profits, as determined in accordance with the rules made under sub-section (6):
Provided that in the case of import of the goods from a country other than the country of origin and where the goods have been merely transhipped through the country of export or such goods are not produced in the country of export, the normal value shall be determined with reference to the price in country of origin.
(2) The Government may, pending the determination of the normal value and the margin of dumping in relation to any goods, in accordance with the provisions of this section and the rules made thereunder, impose on the importation of such goods into Bangladesh an anti-dumping duty on the basis of a provisional estimate of such value and margin and if such anti-dumping duty exceeds the margin as so determined-
(a) the Government shall, having regard to such determination and as soon as may be after such determination, reduce such anti- dumping duty; and
(b) refund shall be made of so much of the anti-dumping duty which has been collected as is in excess of anti-dumping duty as so reduced.
(3) If the Government, in respect of the dumped goods under inquiry, is of the opinion that-
(i) there is a history of dumping which caused injury or that the importer was, or should have been, aware that the exporter practices dumping and that such dumping cause injury; and
(ii) the injury is caused by massive dumping of goods imported in a relative short time which in light of the timing and the volume of imported goods dumped and other circumstances, is likely to seriously undermine the remedial effect of the anti-dumping duty liable to be levied, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, levy anti-dumping duty retrospectively from a date prior to the date of imposition of anti-dumping duty under sub-section (2) but not beyond ninety days from the date of notification under that sub-section and notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, such duty shall be payable at such rate and from such date as may be specified in the notification.
(4) The anti-dumping duty chargeable under this section shall be in addition to any other duty imposed under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.
(5) The anti-dumping duty imposed under this section shall, unless revoked earlier, cease to have effect on the expiry of five years from the date of such imposition:
Provided that if the Government, in a view, is of the opinion that the cessation of such duty is likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury, it may, from time to time, extend the period of such imposition for a further period of five years and such further period shall commence from the date of order of such extension:
Provided further that where a review initiated before the expiry of the aforesaid period of five years has not come to a conclusion before such expiry, the anti-dumping duty may continue to remain in force pending outcome of such a review for a further period not exceeding one year.
(6) The margin of dumping as referred to in sub-section (1) or sub- section (2) shall, from time to time, be ascertained and determined by the Government after such inquiry as it may consider necessary and the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for the purposes of this section and without prejudice to the generality of the forgoing, such rules may provide for the manner in which goods liable for anti-dumping duty under this section may be identified and for the manner in which the export price and the normal value of and the margin of dumping in relation to such goods may be determined and for the assessment and collection of such anti-dumping duty.
(7) No proceeding for imposition of anti-dumping duty under this section shall commence unless the Bangladesh Tariff Commission, on receipt of written application by or on behalf of a domestic industry, informs the Government that there is prima-facie evidence of injury which is caused by dumping on any particular imported goods.]

Anti-Dumping Duty: The Government is empowered to impose an anti-dumping duty on goods imported into Bangladesh at prices below their normal value, provided the duty does not exceed the calculated dumping margin.
Anti-dumping duty acts as a supplementary levy in addition to any other duties or taxes applicable under existing laws and is typically subject to a five-year term unless extended or revoked.

The Government may levy anti-dumping duties retrospectively in cases where massive dumping occurs within a short period and causes injury, subject to specific time limits and evidentiary requirements.
Dumping Margin: The margin of dumping is defined as the difference between the normal value of goods and their export price, serving as the ceiling for the anti-dumping duty that can be imposed.
The Government is responsible for ascertaining and determining the margin of dumping through necessary inquiries and may establish rules to regulate this determination process.
Export Price: Export price represents the price of goods exported from a country to Bangladesh, which may be constructed based on resale prices to independent buyers when direct price information is unreliable due to arrangements between the exporter and importer.
Normal Value: Normal value refers to the comparable price of like goods sold for consumption in the exporting country, or alternatively, the cost of production in the country of origin plus reasonable costs and profits if domestic market data is unavailable.

In instances where goods are transhipped through a third country rather than being exported directly from the country of origin, the normal value is determined with reference to prices in the country of origin.
Government: The Government has the authority to issue official notifications for the imposition, extension, or retrospective application of anti-dumping duties and to frame rules for the assessment and collection of such levies.
Provisional Assessment of Customs Duty: Pending final determination of the normal value and dumping margin, the Government may impose a provisional anti-dumping duty, which is subject to adjustment and refund if it exceeds the finally determined margin.
Bangladesh Tariff Commission: The Bangladesh Tariff Commission serves as the gateway for initiating anti-dumping proceedings by verifying and reporting to the Government whether there is prima-facie evidence of injury caused to local industry by dumping.
Local Industry: Domestic industry may initiate anti-dumping investigations by submitting a written application to the Bangladesh Tariff Commission to demonstrate that imported goods are causing injury due to dumping practices.
Rules: The Government may make rules to prescribe the procedures for identifying dumped goods, calculating export prices and normal values, determining dumping margins, and managing the assessment and collection of anti-dumping duties.

processed_clauses.clause_title: No imposition under section 18A or 18B in certain cases

Countervailing Duty: No goods shall be subjected to both countervailing duty and anti-dumping duty to compensate for the same situation of export subsidization. The Government is restricted from levying these duties when goods are exempt from or refunded duties and taxes in the country of origin. The Government may suspend the levy of this duty upon receiving a satisfactory voluntary undertaking from the exporting country or territory to eliminate or limit subsidies.

For imports from World Trade Organization member countries or nations with most favoured nation agreements, this duty cannot be imposed unless an investigation determines that the import causes or threatens to cause material injury to a domestic industry or hinders the establishment of such an industry.
Anti-Dumping Duty: No goods shall be subjected to both countervailing duty and anti-dumping duty to compensate for the same situation of dumping. The Government is restricted from levying these duties when goods are exempt from or refunded duties and taxes in the country of origin. The Government may suspend the levy of this duty upon receiving a satisfactory voluntary undertaking from an exporter to revise prices or cease exports to the area at dumped prices.

For imports from World Trade Organization member countries or nations with most favoured nation agreements, this duty cannot be imposed unless an investigation determines that the import causes or threatens to cause material injury to a domestic industry or hinders the establishment of such an industry.
Government: The Government has the authority to investigate and determine whether imports cause material injury to domestic industries, and it may issue notifications in the official Gazette to establish rules for these investigations and related matters. It is empowered to accept voluntary undertakings from exporters or foreign governments to eliminate injurious effects, thereby preventing the imposition of countervailing or anti-dumping duties.
World Trade Organization: Imports from member countries of the World Trade Organization are subject to specific protective conditions before countervailing or anti-dumping duties can be imposed.
Local Industry: The imposition of countervailing or anti-dumping duties is conditional upon the findings of an investigation that imports are causing or threatening to cause material injury to a domestic industry or are materially retarding the establishment of such an industry.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Appeal against imposition of countervailing or anti-dumping duty
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
118D. Appeal against imposition of countervailing or anti-dumping duty.- (1) An appeal against the order of determination or review thereof regarding the existence, degree and effect of any subsidy or dumping in relation to import of any goods shall lie to the Customs, Excise and মূল্য সংযোজন কর Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 196.
(2) Every appeal under this section shall be filed within ninety days of the date of order under appeal:
Provided that the Appellate Tribunal may entertain any appeal after the expiry of the said period of ninety days, if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal in time.
(3) The Appellate Tribunal may, after giving the parties to the appeal, an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit, confirming, modifying or annulling the order appealed against.
(4) Every appeal under sub-section (1) shall be heard by a special Bench constituted by the President of the Appellate Tribunal for hearing such appeals and such Bench shall consist of the President and not less than two members and shall include one technical member and one judicial member.

Countervailing Duty: An appeal against an order determining the existence, degree, or effect of a subsidy in relation to the import of goods may be filed with the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal.
Anti-Dumping Duty: An appeal against an order determining the existence, degree, or effect of dumping in relation to the import of goods may be filed with the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: The tribunal serves as the appellate authority for orders concerning countervailing or anti-dumping duties.
The tribunal may hear appeals filed after the standard ninety-day period if it is satisfied that the delay was due to sufficient cause.
The tribunal has the authority to confirm, modify, or annul the orders appealed against after providing the parties an opportunity to be heard.
President of the Appellate Tribunal: The President is responsible for constituting a special bench for the purpose of hearing appeals related to countervailing and anti-dumping duties.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Imposition of safeguard duty
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
2[18E. Imposition of safeguard duty.—(1) If the Government after conducting such enquiry as it deems fit, is satisfied that any article is being imported into Bangladesh in such increased quantities and under such conditions that such importation may cause or threaten to cause serious injury to domestic industry, it may, by notification in the official Gazette, impose a safeguard duty on that article:
Provided that the Government, may, by notification in the official Gazette, exempt any goods from the whole or any part of safeguard duty leviable thereon, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions as it thinks fit to impose.
(2) The Government may, pending the determination under sub-section (1) of the injury or threat thereof, impose a provisional safeguard duty on the basis of a preliminary determination in the prescribed manner that increased imports have caused or threatened to cause serious injury to a domestic industry:
Provided that where, on final determination, the Government is of the opinion that increased imports have not caused or threatened to cause serious injury to a domestic industry, it shall refund the duty so collected:
Provided further that the provisional safeguard duty shall not remain in force for more than two hundred days from the date on which it was imposed.
(3) The duty chargeable under this section shall be in addition to any other duty imposed under this Act or under any other law for the time being in force.
(4) The duty imposed under this section shall, unless revoked earlier, cease to have effect on the expiry of four years from the date of such imposition:
Provided that if the Government is of the opinion that the domestic industry has taken measures to adjust to such injury or threat thereof and it is necessary that the safeguard duty should continue to be imposed, it may extend the period of such imposition:
Provided further that in no case the safeguard duty shall continue to be imposed beyond a period of ten years from the date on which such duty was first imposed.
(5) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for the purposes of this section, and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing, such rules may provide for the manner in which articles liable for safeguard duty may be identified and for the manner in which the causes of serious injury or causes of threat of serious injury in relation to such articles may be determined and for the assessment and collection of such safeguard duty.
(6) For the purposes of this section, —
(a) "domestic industry" means the producers—
(i) as a whole of the like article or a directly competitive article in Bangladesh; or
(ii) whose collective output of the like article or a directly competitive article in Bangladesh constitutes a major share of the total production of the said article in Bangladesh;
(b) "serious injury" means an injury causing significant overall impairment in the position of a domestic industry;
(c) "threat of serious injury" means a clear and imminent danger of serious injury.]

Safeguard Duty: The Government may impose a safeguard duty on imported articles if it determines, after inquiry, that increased importation threatens or causes serious injury to domestic industry.
This duty is in addition to any other duties imposed under the Customs Act 1969 or other laws.
The Government has the power to exempt goods from this duty, impose the duty provisionally, or extend the duration of the duty under specific conditions within established time limits.
Imported Goods: These are the articles subject to potential safeguard duty when their importation levels or conditions are found to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic industry.
Serious Injury: This term is defined as an injury that causes significant overall impairment to the position of a domestic industry.
Threat of Serious Injury: This term refers to a clear and imminent danger that a domestic industry will suffer serious injury due to increased imports.
Local Industry: This entity is defined as the collective producers of like or directly competitive articles in Bangladesh whose output constitutes a major share of total domestic production.
The Government evaluates the status of this entity to determine if import levels necessitate the imposition of safeguard duty to prevent or mitigate injury.
Provisional Safeguard Duty: The Government may impose this duty pending a final determination of injury or threat of injury to domestic industry.
If a final determination concludes that no such injury exists, the Government is required to refund the duty collected.
This provisional duty cannot remain in force for more than a specified number of days from the date of its imposition.
Rules: The Government is empowered to issue rules to facilitate the identification of articles liable for safeguard duty, the determination of injury, and the assessment and collection of such duty.

processed_clauses.clause_title: General power to exempt from customs-duties
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
19. General power to exempt from customs-duties.- 1[(1)] 2[If the Government is satisfied, after consultation with the Board, that it is necessary in the public interest to do so, it may, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions, if any, as it thinks fit to impose,] by notification in the official Gazette, exempt any goods imported into, or exported from, 3[Bangladesh] or into or from any specified port or station or area therein, from the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon 4[:
Provided that if, in a financial year, exemption under this sub-section is given in respect of any goods the rate of duty cannot be changed more than once in that year so as to increase that rate.]
5[(2) An exemption granted under sub-section (1) shall be effective from the date mentioned in the notification issued under that sub-section.]

Government: The Government is empowered, in the public interest and after consulting with the National Board of Revenue, to exempt imported or exported goods from the whole or any part of customs duties.
The Government may impose specific conditions, limitations, or restrictions when granting these exemptions through an official gazette notification.
National Board of Revenue: The Government must consult with the National Board of Revenue before exercising its authority to grant exemptions from customs duties.
Customs Duty: Exemptions from customs duties can be granted for goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh, or specific ports, stations, or areas within the country.
When an exemption is granted, the rate of duty for those goods cannot be increased more than once during the same financial year.
Imported Goods: These goods may be granted full or partial exemption from customs duties by the Government via official gazette notification.
Export Goods: These goods may be granted full or partial exemption from customs duties by the Government via official gazette notification.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Government's power to grant exemption from duty in exceptional circumstances
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 20. 6[Government's power] to grant exemption from duty in exceptional circumstances.- 7[If the 8[Government] is satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest to do so, it may, under circumstances of exceptional nature,] subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions, if any, as it thinks fit to impose, by a special order in each case recording such circumstances, exempt any goods from payment of the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon.

Government: The Government is empowered to grant exemptions from customs duties in exceptional circumstances when it deems such action to be in the public interest.
When granting such an exemption, the Government must record the exceptional circumstances in a special order for each individual case.
Customs Exemption: Exemptions may be granted for the whole or any part of the customs duties chargeable on goods.
The Government may impose conditions, limitations, or restrictions as it deems appropriate when granting an exemption.
Goods: Any goods may be eligible for a full or partial exemption from customs duties provided the Government satisfies the necessary legal conditions for such an exception.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to deliver certain goods without payment of duty and to repay duty on certain goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
21. Power to deliver certain goods without payment of duty and to repay duty on certain goods.- Subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions, as it thinks fit to impose, the Board 11[or any other authority authorised by the Board in writing in this behalf] may, in such general cases as may be prescribed by rules or in particular cases by special order, authorise-
(a) the delivery without payment of the customs-duties chargeable thereon of goods which are imported only temporarily with a view to subsequent exportation;
(b) the delivery without payment of the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon of imported goods of such classes or description, as it may prescribe, intended to be used in the production, manufacture, processing, repair or refitting in 10[Bangladesh] of goods of such classes or descriptions as it may prescribe; and
(c) the repayment in whole or in part of the customs-duties paid on the importation of any goods of such classes or descriptions as it may prescribe, which have been used in the production, manufacture, processing, repair or fitting in 1[Bangladesh] of goods of such classes or descriptions as it may prescribe, provided such repayment shall not be made in respect of the class or description of goods for which drawback can be claimed under section 37.

National Board of Revenue: The Board, or any authority it designates in writing, is empowered to grant exemptions from customs duties under specific conditions or restrictions.
The Board holds the authority to establish general cases for duty exemption or repayment through official rules, or to issue special orders for particular cases.
Imported Goods: The Board may authorize the delivery of goods imported temporarily for subsequent export without requiring payment of customs duties.
The Board may permit the delivery of certain imported goods intended for use in production, manufacture, processing, repair, or refitting within Bangladesh without full payment of duties.

Customs duties paid on imported goods utilized in the production, manufacture, processing, repair, or refitting of other goods within Bangladesh may be repaid in whole or in part, provided the goods are not eligible for drawback under section 37.
Customs Duty: The law provides mechanisms for the temporary waiver of duty payment for specific classes of goods and the potential repayment of duties already paid under defined conditions.
Customs Duty Drawback: Repayment of duties for goods used in domestic production is restricted if those goods are already eligible to claim a drawback under the provisions of section 37.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Re-importation of goods produced or manufactured in [Bangladesh]
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
22. Re-importation of goods produced or manufactured in 1[Bangladesh].- If goods produced or manufactured in and exported from 1[Bangladesh] are subsequently imported into 1[Bangladesh], such goods shall be liable to customs-duty and be subject to all the conditions and restrictions, if any, to which goods of the like kind and value not so produced or manufactured are liable on the importation thereof:
Provided if such goods have been imported within two years of their exportation 12[***] and have not undergone any processing since their exportation, the appropriate officer not below the rank of an 2[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] may admit the goods -
1[(a) where at the time of exportation of such goods, drawback was allowed, on payment of the amount of such drawback;
(b) where such goods were exported from any bonded warehouse, without payment of -
(i) the duties and taxes chargeable on the imported materials, if any, used in the manufacture of such goods ; or
(ii) the duties and taxes chargeable on the indigenous raw materials, if any, used in the manufacture or such goods; or
(iii) the duties and taxes, if any, chargeable on such indigenous goods;
on payment of customs-duty equal to the aggregate amount of all such duties and taxes calculated at the rates prevailing at the time and place of importation of goods; or]
2[(c) in any other case, without payment of customs-duty.]

Imported Goods: Goods originally produced or manufactured in and exported from Bangladesh that are later re-imported are generally subject to the same customs duties, conditions, and restrictions as similar imported goods.
Specific provisions allow for the exemption or conditional payment of duties upon re-importation if the goods return within a defined timeframe and have undergone no further processing.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: An officer of this rank or higher is authorized to review and admit re-imported goods under the specified relief conditions provided in this section.
Customs Duty Drawback: If drawback was granted at the time of the original exportation, re-importation of the goods requires the repayment of that drawback amount to clear the goods.
Bonded Warehouse: Goods exported from a bonded warehouse must satisfy specific duty and tax payment requirements related to the materials used in their manufacture or their indigenous status upon re-importation, calculated at current rates.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Goods, derelict, wreck, etc
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 23. Goods, derelict, wreck, etc.- All goods, derelict, jetsam, flotsam and wreck, brought or coming into 1[Bangladesh], shall be dealt with as if they were imported into 1[Bangladesh].

Goods: All goods, including derelict, jetsam, flotsam, and wreck, that are brought or come into Bangladesh are treated legally as if they were imported goods.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Provisions and stores may be exported free of duty
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 24. Provisions and stores may be exported free of duty.- Goods produced or manufactured in 1[Bangladesh] and required as provisions and stores on any conveyance proceeding to any foreign port, airport or station may be exported free of customs-duty, 2[and Value Added Tax (মূল্য সংযোজন কর)] in such quantities as the appropriate officer may determine having regard to the size of the conveyance, the number of passengers and crew and the length of the voyage or journey on which the conveyance is about to depart.

Stores and Provisions: Goods produced or manufactured in Bangladesh that are intended for use as stores and provisions on a conveyance heading to a foreign destination may be exported without the payment of customs duty or Value Added Tax.

The quantity of such goods allowed for duty-free export is determined by the appropriate customs officer based on factors such as the size of the conveyance, the number of crew and passengers, and the expected duration of the journey.
Customs Duty: Goods qualifying as stores and provisions for a conveyance departing to a foreign port or station are exempt from the payment of customs duty.
Value Added Tax: The export of stores and provisions for use on a conveyance proceeding to a foreign port or station is exempt from the levy of Value Added Tax.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is empowered to determine the permissible quantity of stores and provisions that may be exported duty-free, taking into account the specific requirements of the conveyance and its upcoming journey.
Conveyance: A conveyance departing for a foreign port, airport, or station may carry stores and provisions that are exempt from customs duty and Value Added Tax, subject to quantity limits set by the appropriate officer.

(a) the value of any goods shall include the freight, insurance, commission and all other cost, charges and expenses incidental to the sale and delivery at the place of importation or exportation; and
(b) the Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, fix the freight for the transportation of any goods or class of goods by aircraft that are delivered or could have been delivered at a Customs airport to the buyer.]

Customs Duty: Customs duty is levied on goods based on their value, which is determined according to the actual price paid or payable under fully competitive international trade conditions.
The Government may fix tariff values or minimum values for any goods chargeable with customs duty ad valorem, though if the declared value is higher, it serves as the basis for duty calculation.
Value: The value of goods for assessment purposes includes all costs such as freight, insurance, commissions, and other incidental charges related to sale and delivery at the place of importation or exportation.
Bill of Entry: The time of importation is defined as the date on which a bill of entry is delivered under the relevant legal provisions.
The bill of entry serves as the official document for determining the place and time of importation for valuation purposes.
Bill of Export: The time of exportation is determined by the delivery of a bill of export or, in cases where no such bill is required, the time when goods arrive at the customs port, airport, or station for export.
The place of exportation is the customs location where the bill of export is formally submitted.
Exchange Rate: The exchange rate for computing the value of goods is calculated based on the average rate prevailing during a specific thirty-day window prior to the submission of the bill of entry or bill of export.
The rate of exchange is fixed by the National Board of Revenue or an authorized officer, and is defined as the rate for converting Bangladesh currency to foreign currency or vice versa.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is empowered to fix the exchange rate for valuation purposes and to notify fixed freight charges for goods transported by aircraft to customs airports.
Foreign Currency Regulation Act 1947: This Act provides the legal definitions for foreign currency and Bangladesh currency as used in the context of customs valuation.
Government: The Government holds the authority to fix tariff values or minimum values for goods through official gazette notifications and to determine official exchange rates.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Pre-shipment inspection agencies and assessment on the basis of their certificates
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
4[25A. Pre-shipment inspection agencies and assessment on the basis of their certificates.-
5[(1) For the purposes of this Act, the Government may, by notification in the official gazette -
(a) appoint pre-shipment inspection agencies and audit agencies, and
(b) determine the scope and manner of certification, and also the scope and manner of audit, and any matter related to such certification and audit.]
13["(2) The Government may, by notification in the official gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by a pre-shipment inspection agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment, unless otherwise prescribed."]
(3) For the purposes of this section, "price" means value of the goods determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25.";]

Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: The Government may appoint these agencies through an official notification to verify and certify the quality, quantity, price, description, and customs classification of goods.
When verified and certified by these agencies in the prescribed manner, the information provided serves as the basis for customs assessment, subject to any exceptions prescribed by the Government.
Audit Agency: The Government is empowered to appoint these agencies via notification in the official gazette to perform audit functions related to customs procedures.
Value: For the purpose of pre-shipment inspection, the term price is defined as the value of the goods as determined under the specific provisions of section 25 of the Customs Act.
Customs Assessment: The assessment of goods may be based on the certifications provided by authorized pre-shipment inspection agencies regarding the nature and value of the imported items.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Mandatory pre-shipment Inspection
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[25B. Mandatory pre-shipment Inspection.- It is mandatory for the importers to have their importable goods inspected by a pre-shipment inspection agency before or at the time of shipment of those goods on board a vessel, aircraft or other conveyance:
Provided that the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, exempt any class of goods or any goods imported by any class of importers or any goods imported through a customs port or a customs station or any area within such port or station from the mandatory pre-shipment inspection.

Importer: Importers are mandatorily required to have their importable goods undergo pre-shipment inspection before or during the loading of goods onto a vessel, aircraft, or other conveyance.
Pre-shipment Inspection: This process is a mandatory requirement for importable goods prior to their shipment into the country.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: These agencies are the authorized entities responsible for conducting the mandatory inspection of importable goods before or at the time of shipment.
Government: The Government is empowered to grant exemptions from the mandatory pre-shipment inspection requirement for specific classes of goods, classes of importers, or goods imported through designated customs stations or ports via official Gazette notification.
Customs Port: The Government has the authority to exempt specific goods or classes of importers from mandatory pre-shipment inspection requirements when goods are imported through a customs port.
Customs Station: The Government may exempt goods imported through a customs station from the mandatory pre-shipment inspection requirement through an official notification.
Conveyance: This term refers to vessels, aircraft, or other means of transport used for the shipment of importable goods, which are subject to the pre-shipment inspection mandate.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Pre-shipment inspection service charge
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 25C.
