Pre-shipment inspection service charge.- The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, impose pre-shipment inspection service charge on imported goods required to be inspected by pre-shipment inspection agencies at a rate not exceeding one percent of the value of such goods and this charge shall be collected as if it were a customs duty leviable under section 18(1).];

Government: The Government is empowered to impose a pre-shipment inspection service charge on imported goods that are subject to mandatory inspection by authorized agencies.
Pre-shipment Inspection Service Charge: This charge is applied to imported goods subject to inspection, with a capped rate based on a percentage of the value of the goods.
The charge is legally treated and collected as if it were a customs duty under the Act.
Imported Goods: These goods may be subject to a pre-shipment inspection service charge if they are required to undergo inspection by a pre-shipment inspection agency.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: These agencies are authorized to perform inspections on imported goods, which triggers the imposition of the pre-shipment inspection service charge.
Customs Duty: The pre-shipment inspection service charge is legally classified for collection purposes as a customs duty leviable under the specific section of the Customs Act.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Requisition to produce documents
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
2[26. Requisition to produce documents.- (1) Where-
(a) an officer of Customs has reasons to believe that goods have been unlawfully imported, exported, under valued or overvalued, entered, removed, or otherwise unlawfully dealt with by any person contrary to this Act or that any person attempts to import, export, under or overvalue, enter, remove or otherwise deal with any goods; or
(b) goods have been seized under this Act, an officer of Customs not below the rank of an Assistant Commissioner may, by notice in writing, require that person or any person whom the officer suspects to be or to have been the owner, importer or exporter of those goods, or agent thereof, as the case may be, as and when required, to produce and deliver to the officer or to any other specified Customs officer all books of account, invoice books, or other books, records or documents in which any entry or memorandum appears or may be supposed to appear in respect of the purchase, importation, exportation, cost, or value of, or payment for, the goods and any other goods so imported or exported or otherwise dealt with within a period of three years preceding the date of the notice.
(2) In addition to the requirements of sub-section (1) of this section, an officer of Customs not below the rank of an Assistant Commissioner may require the owner or importer or exporter of those goods, or agent thereof, as the case may be, as and 3[when necessary], to-
(a) produce for the inspection of the officer or any specified Customs officer, and allow the officer to make copies of or extracts from, any of the documents, books, or records referred to in sub-section (1), 4[* *]
4[(aa) transmit or send, by electronic or other means, the information contained in those documents, books or records, and]
(b) answer any question concerning those documents, books, or records.

Officer of Customs: An officer of Customs is authorized to requisition documents when they have reason to believe that goods have been unlawfully handled or when goods have been seized under the Customs Act 1969.

An officer of Customs, not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs, may issue a written notice requiring any person suspected of involvement to produce and deliver relevant records for goods dealt with in the preceding three years.

An officer of Customs not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs may compel the production of records for inspection, request the transmission of information electronically, or require answers to questions regarding such documentation.
Goods: The provisions apply to goods believed to be unlawfully imported, exported, undervalued, overvalued, or otherwise dealt with in violation of the law.
Person: Any person suspected of being the owner, importer, exporter, or agent of goods under investigation may be required to produce books of account, invoices, and other records regarding the purchase, value, or payment for such goods.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer rank holds the specific legal authority to issue written notices for the production and delivery of documents and records during customs investigations.
Customs Documents: Required documents include books of account, invoice books, and any other records containing entries or memoranda concerning the purchase, importation, exportation, cost, or value of goods.
Customs Information Access: The authority includes the right to inspect, copy, or extract information from records, as well as the right to receive transmitted information via electronic or other means and to demand answers regarding the content of such records.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Further powers in relation to documents

Joint Commissioner of Customs: The Joint Commissioner of Customs is empowered to issue written notices requiring any person, including government or bank officials, to produce documents or records for customs inspection. They are further authorized to compel persons to appear before them to answer questions regarding goods, transactions, or relevant records during an investigation or audit.
Officer of Customs: An officer of Customs not below the rank of Joint Commissioner has the authority to examine documents or records produced under notice. Additionally, they are permitted to make copies of or take extracts from any such documents or records provided for inspection.
Person: Any individual, including officers employed by government departments, corporations, local authorities, or banks, is legally obligated to comply with a written notice to produce documents or records for inspection. Such individuals may also be required to appear before the Joint Commissioner of Customs to provide testimony regarding goods or transactions subject to a customs investigation.
Customs Documentation and Records: Documents and records deemed necessary for a customs investigation or audit must be produced for inspection upon request by a qualified Customs official. These materials are subject to being copied or extracted by the customs officer to facilitate official oversight.
Customs Investigation and Audit: The Joint Commissioner of Customs possesses broad authority to request information and documentation when deemed relevant to an investigation or audit conducted under the Customs Act 1969.

processed_clauses.clause_title: A Customs officer may take possession of and retain documents and records
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
26B. A Customs officer may take possession of and retain documents and records.- (1) A Customs officer may take possession of and retain any document or record presented in connection with any entry or required to be produced under this Act.
(2) Where the Customs officer takes possession of a document or record under sub-section (1) of this section, the said officer shall, at the request of the person otherwise entitled to the document or record, provide that person with a copy of the document certified by him or on his behalf under the seal of the Customs as a true copy.
(3) Every copy so certified shall be admissible as evidence in all Courts as if it were the original.

Customs Officer: A Customs officer is granted the authority to take possession of and retain any documents or records presented during the entry process or required to be produced under the Customs Act.
When a Customs officer retains such documents, they are required to provide a certified copy to the person entitled to the original if requested.
Customs Documentation and Records: These items may be seized and retained by customs authorities during the course of official proceedings.
Certified copies of retained documents, when issued under the official customs seal, are considered legally admissible as evidence in all courts with the same weight as the original documents.
Person: A person who is entitled to a document or record taken into possession by a customs officer has the right to request and receive a certified true copy of that document.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Copying of documents obtained during search
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
26C. Copying of documents obtained during search.- (1) Where an officer of Customs or an authorized person carries out any lawful search, inspection, audit, or examination under this Act, and has reasonable cause to believe that documents coming into his possession during such search, inspection, audit, or examination are evidence of the commission of an offence under this Act, he may remove the documents for the purpose of making copies.
(2) The documents or records so removed must, as soon as practicable after copies thereof have been made, be returned to the person otherwise entitled to them.

Customs Documents: Officers of Customs or authorized persons have the authority to remove documents obtained during a lawful search, inspection, audit, or examination if they possess reasonable cause to believe such documents constitute evidence of a customs offence.
Any documents or records removed for the purpose of making copies must be returned to the person entitled to them as soon as is practicable after the reproduction process is complete.
Customs Offence: The power to remove and copy documents is strictly linked to the discovery of evidence indicating that an offence has been committed under the Customs Act 1969.
Officer of Customs: An officer of Customs is granted the authority to remove and copy documents gathered during official investigative processes when such documents are deemed necessary as evidence.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Retention of documents and goods obtained during search
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
26D. Retention of documents and goods obtained during search.- Where an officer of Customs or an authorized person carries out any lawful search, inspection, audit, or examination under this Act, and has reasonable cause to believe that any document or goods coming into his possession during such search, inspection, audit, or examination are evidence of the commission of an offence under this Act, or are intended to be used for the purpose of committing any offence under this Act, the officer or his authorized person may take possession of and retain the documents or goods, as the case may be.
(2) Where an officer of Customs or his authorized person takes possession of a document under sub-section (1) of this section, he shall, at the request of the person otherwise entitled to the document, provide that person with a copy of the document certified by or on behalf of the Custom officer under the seal of the Customs as a true copy.
(3) Every copy so certified shall be admissible in evidence in Courts as if it were the original.]

Officer of Customs: Officers are authorized to take possession of and retain documents or goods seized during a search, inspection, audit, or examination if they have reasonable cause to believe such items constitute evidence of a customs offence or are intended to be used in the commission of one.
When an officer seizes a document, they are required to provide a certified copy to the person entitled to it upon request, with such copies being admissible in court as originals.
Customs Records Retention: This provision allows for the legal seizure and holding of goods and documentation encountered during official customs checks when such items are linked to the commission of an offence under the Customs Act.
Customs Seizure and Evidence: Documents seized by customs officers can be copied and certified under official seal, and these certified copies hold the same legal status and admissibility as the original documents in court proceedings.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Abatement of duty on damaged, deteriorated, lost, or destroyed goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[27. Abatement of duty on damaged, deteriorated, lost, or destroyed goods.- 14(1)Where, at the time of first examination, of any imported goods, it is shown by the owner in writing to the satisfaction of an officer not below the rank of an 2[Assistant Commissioner of Customs]-
(a) that the goods had been damaged or had deteriorated at any time before or during their landing; or
(b) that the goods 3[* *] had been damaged, at any time after landing but before such examination, by accident and not due to any wilful act, negligence or default of the importer or his agents;
the value of such goods shall, on a written application made by the owner of the goods, be appraised by an appropriate officer of Customs, and the owner shall be allowed abatement of duty in proportion to the diminution in value of the gods as so appraised.
(2) Where it is shown, in writing by the owner of any imported goods to the satisfaction of the 4[Commissioner of Customs] that the goods have been 5[damaged, deteriorated, lost or destroyed] by an accident or force majeure, after importation but before clearance thereof for home consumption, the Commissioner may, on an application made by the owner, furnishing all particulars necessary to establish the fact of such 6[damage, deterioration, loss or destruction], remit or repay any duty chargeable or paid on such goods.
Explanation.-For the purpose of this sub-section "force majeure" means an act of god.]
7[(3) Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the 4[Commissioner of Customs] that any warehoused goods had been damaged at any time before clearance for home-consumption by an accident or force majeure, the 4[Commissioner of Customs] may, on an application from the owner of the goods furnishing all particulars necessary to establish the fact of such damage, allow the value of such goods to be appraised by an appropriate officer of customs and the owner of the goods shall be allowed abatement of duty in proportion to the diminution in value of the goods as so appraised.]

Imported Goods: If imported goods are damaged or deteriorated before or during landing, the owner may apply to have the goods' value reappraised to allow for a proportionate abatement of duty.
Damage occurring after landing but before examination may also qualify for duty abatement if the owner proves it was caused by accident and not through negligence or wilful default.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer is authorized to verify the owner's written claim regarding damage or deterioration of imported goods occurring before or during the initial examination.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is responsible for appraising the value of goods that have been damaged or deteriorated to determine the appropriate amount of duty abatement.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to remit or repay duty on imported goods that were damaged, deteriorated, lost, or destroyed due to accident or force majeure after importation but before clearance for home consumption.
The Commissioner also oversees the duty abatement process for warehoused goods that suffer damage due to accident or force majeure before being cleared for home consumption.
Warehoused Goods: If warehoused goods are damaged by accident or force majeure prior to clearance for home consumption, the owner may apply for a reappraisal of the goods' value to receive a proportionate abatement of duty.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to test and denature imported spirit
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 28. Power to test and denature imported spirit.- When by any law for the time being in force a duty lower than that prescribed by 8[this Act], is imposed on denatured spirit, any such spirit imported into 9[Bangladesh] may, subject to rules, be tested and if necessary adequately denatured by officers of customs, at the expense of the person importing the same, before the customs-duty is charged thereon.

Imported Goods: This clause specifically applies to denatured spirit that is imported into Bangladesh.
Such goods may be subjected to testing and further denaturation by customs officials to ensure they comply with applicable standards before they are assessed for customs duty.
Officer of Customs: These officials are empowered to test and, if necessary, perform additional denaturation on imported spirit that is subject to a lower rate of duty under other laws.
The cost of these procedures is to be borne by the person importing the goods.
Customs Duty: The assessment and charging of this duty on imported spirit may be deferred until after the goods have been tested or properly denatured by customs authorities.
Person: Any person importing denatured spirit is responsible for covering all expenses incurred by customs officials during the testing and denaturation process.
Rules: The authority granted to test and denature imported spirit must be exercised in accordance with these rules.
Customs Act 1969: The Act serves as the legal foundation for the regulation and taxation of imported spirit, including instances where alternative duty rates from other laws apply.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Restriction on amendment of bill of entry or bill of export
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 29. Restriction on amendment of bill of entry or bill of export.- Except as provided in section 88, no amendment of a bill of entry or bill of export relating to goods assessed for duty on the declared value, quantity or description thereof shall be allowed after such goods have been removed from the customs-area.

Bill of Entry: Amendments to a bill of entry are generally prohibited once the associated goods have been cleared and removed from the customs-area, provided those goods were assessed based on their declared value, quantity, or description.
An exception to this restriction on amendments exists as provided under the specific provisions of the Customs Act.
Bill of Export: Amendments to a bill of export are restricted after goods assessed for duty on declared value, quantity, or description have been removed from the customs-area.
Any amendment to such a document is only permissible if it falls within the specific exceptions prescribed by the law.
Customs-area: The removal of goods from the customs-area marks the critical point in time after which amendments to the bill of entry or bill of export for goods assessed on declared criteria are no longer permitted.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Date for determination of rate of duty, value and exchange rate for imported goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1["30. Date for determination of rate of duty, value and exchange rate for imported goods- The rate of duty, 8[value and exchange rate applicable to any imported goods, shall be the rate of duty, value and exchange rate] in force, -
(a) in the case of goods cleared for home consumption under section 79, on the date a bill of entry is presented under that section and a bill of entry number is allocated thereto;
(b) in the case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption under section 104, on the date 15[a bill of entry was presented under section 79 and the bill of entry number was allocated thereto]; and
(c) in the case of any other goods, on the date of payment of duty:
Provided that if a bill of entry is presented in anticipation of arrival of a conveyance by which the goods are imported, the relevant date for the purpose of this section shall be the date on which the manifest of the conveyance is delivered after its arrival."]

Imported Goods: The applicable rate of duty, value, and exchange rate for imported goods are determined based on specific trigger points within the customs process.
These metrics are fixed depending on whether the goods are cleared for home consumption directly or from a warehouse, or if they fall under other miscellaneous categories.
Bill of Entry: For goods cleared for home consumption, the relevant date for determining duty and value is the date the bill of entry is presented and assigned a number.
When goods are cleared from a warehouse for home consumption, the governing date remains tied to the date the bill of entry was originally presented and allocated a number.
Duty Payment: For any imported goods not covered by specific home consumption or warehouse clearance provisions, the applicable date for rate and value determination is the date the duty is paid.
Manifest: If a bill of entry is presented early, in anticipation of the arrival of a conveyance, the relevant date for duty and value determination is adjusted to the date on which the conveyance manifest is delivered.
Conveyance: The arrival and subsequent delivery of the manifest for a conveyance provide the foundational timing for determining applicable duty and exchange rates when entry documentation is filed in advance.
Warehouse: For goods cleared for home consumption from a warehouse, the legal date for determining duty and value rates remains anchored to the initial filing of the entry documentation.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Value and effective rate of duty
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 2[30A. Value and effective rate of duty.- Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any court, for the purposes of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under section 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duty that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale of goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof.]

Customs Act 1969: This section clarifies that notwithstanding any other laws or court decisions, the determination of value and applicable duty rates remains governed by specific sections of the Act, including those covering valuation and the imposition of duties.
Value: The value applicable to goods for the purposes of the customs law shall be determined in accordance with the valuation procedures defined in the Act.
Customs Duty Rate: The effective rate of duty includes both the standard duties imposed under the specified sections of the Act and any additional amounts payable due to the withdrawal of duty exemptions or concessions, regardless of whether a sales contract or letter of credit was established prior to the change.
Goods: The value and rate of duty apply to all goods imported or exported, with the legal framework ensuring that duty liabilities are calculated based on the conditions prescribed by the Act at the relevant time of assessment.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Date for determination of export duty
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
3[31. Date for determination of export duty.- The rate of duty applicable to, and the rate of exchange for computation of the value of, any goods exported shall be the rate of duty or, as the case may be, the rate of exchange prevailing on the date of the delivery of the bill of export under section 131:
Provided that where the export of any goods is permitted without a bill of export or in anticipation of the delivery of such a bill, the rate of duty applicable to, and the rate of exchange for the computation of the value of, such goods shall be the rate of duty or, as the case may be, the rate of exchange applicable on the date on which loading of the goods on the outgoing conveyance commences.]

Export Duty: The applicable rate of duty for goods intended for export is determined based on the date of delivery of the bill of export.

In cases where export is permitted without a bill of export or prior to its delivery, the applicable rate of duty is determined based on the date when the loading of the goods onto the conveyance begins.
Exchange Rate: The exchange rate used to calculate the value of exported goods is determined by the rate prevailing on the date the bill of export is submitted.
For exports allowed without a formal bill of export, the exchange rate is determined based on the date when the loading of goods onto the outgoing conveyance commences.
Bill of Export: This document serves as the primary instrument for determining the date of applicability for duty rates and exchange rates for export goods.
When goods are exported without the prior delivery of this document, the legal date for determining fiscal rates shifts to the time loading onto the conveyance begins.
Conveyance: The date on which the loading of goods commences on an outgoing vessel or vehicle determines the applicable duty and exchange rates when a bill of export is not submitted before loading.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Untrue statement, error, etc
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
32. Untrue statement, error, etc.- (1) If any person, in connection with any matter of customs,-
(a) make or signs or causes to be made or signed, or delivers or causes to be delivered to an officer of customs any declaration, notice, certificate or other document whatsoever, or
(b) makes any statement in answer to any question put to him by an officer of customs which he is required by or under this Act to answer, 4[or]
5[(c)transmits any statement, document, information or record through electronic device or produces soft copy thereof,]
and such document or statement is untrue in any material particular, he shall be guilty of an offence under this section.
(2) Where, by reason of any such document or statement as aforesaid or by reason of some collusion, any duty or charge has not been levied or has been short-levied or has been erroneously refunded, the person liable to pay any amount on that account shall be served with a notice 16[**] requiring him to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified in the notice.
(3) Where, by reason of any inadvertence, error or misconstruction, any duty or charge 1[amounting to not less than one thousand taka] has not been levied or has been short-levied or has been erroneously refunded, the person liable to pay any amount on that account shall be served with a notice within 2[three years] of the relevant date requiring him to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified in the notice.
(4) The appropriate officer, after considering the representation, if any, of such person as is refereed to in sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) shall determine the amount of duty payable by him which shall in no case exceed the amount specified in the notice, and such person shall pay the amount so determined3[:
Provided that where the amount so determined is less than one thousand taka, the person concerned shall not be required to make the payment.]
(5) For the purposes of this section, the expression "relevant date" means-
(a) in any case where duty is not levied, the duty on which an order for the clearance of goods is made;
(b) in a case where duty is provisionally assessed under section 81, the date of adjustment of duty after its final assessment;
(c) in a case where duty has been erroneously refunded, the date of its refund;
(d) in any other case, the date of payment of duty or charge.

Customs Offence: It is an offence to make, sign, or deliver any untrue document to an officer of customs, or to provide an untrue statement in response to a mandatory inquiry, or to transmit such information via electronic means.
Show Cause Notice: A show cause notice is issued to a person when duty or charges have not been levied, have been short-levied, or have been erroneously refunded due to untrue statements or collusion.
In cases of inadvertence, error, or misconstruction, a show cause notice for recovery of duties or charges must be served within a specific time period from the relevant date.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is responsible for considering representations from the person concerned and determining the final amount of duty payable, which cannot exceed the amount originally specified in the notice.
Relevant Date: The relevant date serves as the statutory anchor for time-bound actions and is defined differently based on whether duty was not levied, provisionally assessed, erroneously refunded, or paid through other means.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Refund to be claimed within [six months]
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
33. Refund to be claimed within 4[six months].- (1) No refund of any customs-duties or charges claimed to have been paid or over-paid through inadvertence, 17[error or misconstruction or in any other way] shall be allowed, unless such claim is made within 4[six months] of the date of payment:
18[“Provided that where the amount so claimed is less than one thousand taka, refund shall not be allowed.”]
(2) In the case of provisional payment made under section 81, the said period of 4[six months] shall be reckoned from the date of the adjustment of duty after its final assessment.

Refund of Customs Duty: A claim for a refund of customs duties or charges paid by inadvertence, error, or misconstruction must be submitted within a prescribed statutory period from the date of payment to be considered valid.
Refunds are disallowed for any claim amount that falls below a specified minimum threshold value.
For duties paid on a provisional basis, the time limit for filing a refund claim is calculated starting from the date the final assessment is adjusted.
Provisional Assessment of Customs Duty: When goods are subject to a provisional assessment, the period for claiming a refund begins only once the final duty adjustment has been completed.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to give credit for, and keep account-current of, duties and charges
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 34. Power to give credit for, and keep account-current of, duties and charges.- An officer of customs, not below the rank of 5[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] may, in the case of any mercantile firm or public body, if he so thinks fit, instead of requiring payment of customs-duties or charges as and when they become due, keep with such firm or body an account-current of such duties and charges, which account shall be settled at intervals of not exceeding one month, and such firm or body shall make a deposit or furnish a security sufficient in the opinion of that officer to cover the amount which may at any time be payable by it in respect of such duties or charges.

Assistant Commissioner of Customs: Officers at or above this rank are empowered to allow mercantile firms or public bodies to maintain a current account for the payment of customs duties and charges, provided they deem it appropriate.
Current Account for Customs Charges: This mechanism allows firms or public bodies to defer the immediate payment of customs duties and charges by keeping an account-current that is settled at monthly intervals.
The use of this account is contingent upon the entity providing a deposit or security deemed sufficient by the customs officer to cover all potential outstanding liabilities.
Security Bond: Entities wishing to maintain a current account for customs duties must furnish a deposit or security sufficient to cover the total amount of duties and charges that may be payable at any given time.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER VI - DRAWBACK
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER VI
DRAWBACK

Customs Drawback: This chapter sets out the foundational framework for the repayment of customs duties paid upon the import of goods that are subsequently exported or used in a manner qualifying for drawback under the Customs Act 1969.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Drawback of the export on imported goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
35. Drawback of the export on imported goods.- Subject to the subsequent provisions of this Chapter and the rules, when any goods, capable of being easily identified, which have been imported into 1[Bangladesh] and upon which customs-duties have been paid on importation, are exported to any place outside 1[Bangladesh] or as provisions or stores for use on board a conveyance proceeding to any foreign territory, 2[such duties, not exceeding seven-eights thereof] shall be repaid as drawback, subject to the following conditions, namely:-
(1) the goods are identified to the satisfaction of an officer of customs not below the rank of 3[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] at the customs-station, to be the same as had been imported, and
(2) the goods are entered for export within two years of the date of their importation, as shown by the records of the custom-house or if such time is extended by the Board or the 4[Commissioner of Customs] for sufficient cause within such extended time:
Provided that the 4[Commissioner of Customs] shall not extend the time beyond three years of the importation of such goods.
Explanation.- For the purposes of this section, the goods shall be deemed to have been entered for export on the date on which the bill of export is delivered to the appropriate officer under section 131.

Customs Duty Drawback: A portion of customs duties paid on imported goods may be repaid as a drawback when those goods are subsequently exported to a place outside Bangladesh.
The amount of the drawback repayment is limited to a maximum of seven-eighths of the duties originally paid upon importation.
Imported Goods: To qualify for a drawback, goods must be capable of being easily identified and must have had customs duties paid upon their original importation into Bangladesh.
Export: Goods qualify for drawback if they are exported to a foreign destination or are supplied as stores or provisions for a conveyance traveling to a foreign territory.
The exportation must occur within two years of the original importation date, though this period may be extended by authorized customs officials for sufficient cause.
The limit for any extension of the export deadline is set at three years from the date of the original importation.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer is tasked with verifying the identity of the goods to ensure they are the same items that were originally imported.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner has the authority to extend the two-year deadline for entering goods for export upon sufficient cause, provided the total time does not exceed three years.
Bill of Export: For the purposes of determining compliance with time limits, goods are considered to have been entered for export on the date the bill of export is delivered to the appropriate officer.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Drawback on goods taken into use between importation and exportation
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 36. Drawback on goods taken into use between importation and exportation.- Notwithstanding anything contended in section 35, the repayment of duty as drawback in respect of goods which have been taken into use between their importation and subsequent exportation shall be made in accordance with the provisions of the rules made in that behalf.

Customs Drawback: The repayment of customs duty as a drawback for goods that have been used between their initial importation and subsequent exportation must be handled according to specific governing rules.
This provision acts as an exception to general drawback regulations, mandating that the rules set for such used goods take precedence over other standard procedures.
Rules: These rules serve as the authoritative framework for determining the repayment process and conditions for drawback on goods that were utilized during the interval between import and export.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Drawback on goods used in the manufacture of goods which are exported
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 37. Drawback on goods used in the manufacture of goods which are exported.- Where it appears to the Board that in respect of goods of any class or description manufactured in 1[Bangladesh] and exported to any place outside 1[Bangladesh], a drawback of customs-duties should be allowed on any imported goods of a class or description used in the manufacture of such exported goods, the Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, direct that drawback shall be allowed in respect of such imported goods to such extent and subject to such condition as may be provided in the rules.

National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to determine if a customs duty drawback should be allowed for imported goods that were utilized in the manufacturing of items subsequently exported from the country.
The Board is empowered to issue notifications in the official Gazette to prescribe the extent of such drawbacks and specify the conditions under which they may be claimed.
Imported Goods: Imported goods used in the manufacturing process of products for export may be eligible for a drawback of customs duties if the Board determines such relief is warranted.
Export Goods: Goods manufactured in the country and exported to destinations outside the country serve as the basis for claiming duty drawbacks on the imported components used in their production.
Customs Duty Drawback: The granting of drawback on customs duties for imported materials used in exported goods is subject to regulations and conditions established by the Board through official notifications.
Rules: The procedural requirements, specific conditions, and the extent of the duty drawback are to be governed by rules formulated under the Act.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to declare what goods are identifiable and to prohibit drawback in case of specified foreign territory
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
38. Power to declare what goods are identifiable and to prohibit drawback in case of specified foreign territory.- (1) The Board may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, declare what goods shall, for the purposes of this Chapter, be deemed to be not capable of being easily identified.
(2) The 1[Government] may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, prohibit the payment of drawback upon the exportation of goods or any specified goods or class of goods to any specified foreign port or territory.

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to issue official notifications declaring which specific types of goods shall be treated as difficult or impossible to identify for the purposes of drawback claims.
Customs Drawback: The identification status of goods determined by the National Board of Revenue directly impacts the eligibility of goods for drawback claims under this Chapter.
The Government reserves the authority to prohibit the payment of drawback on the export of certain goods or classes of goods destined for specific foreign ports or territories.
Government: The Government has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to ban drawback payments for exports sent to particular foreign locations or territories.
Export: The Government may restrict or prohibit drawback benefits on goods being exported to specified foreign destinations.

processed_clauses.clause_title: When no drawback allowed
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
39. When no drawback allowed.- Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, no drawback shall be allowed-
(a) upon goods which are required to be included in export manifest and are not so included, or
(b) when the claim is for drawback amounting, in respect of any single shipment, to less than hundred 2[Taka], or
(c) unless the claim for drawback has been made and established at the time of export 3[or within six months from the date of export].

Customs Drawback: No drawback of duties shall be granted for goods that are required to be included in an export manifest but are not included.
A drawback claim is not allowed if the total amount for a single shipment is below a specified minimum threshold.
Drawback claims must be formally made and established at the time of export or within a defined period thereafter, otherwise the entitlement is forfeited.
Export Manifest: The inclusion of goods in an export manifest is a mandatory condition for the eligibility of any customs drawback.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Time of payment of drawback
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 40. Time of payment of drawback.- No such payment of drawback shall be made until the vessel carrying the goods has put out to sea or other conveyance has left 4[Bangladesh].

Duty Drawback: The payment of drawback is prohibited until the vessel or conveyance carrying the goods has departed from Bangladesh for an international destination. This ensures that the goods have truly exited the country before the claim is settled.
Vessel: A vessel transporting goods must have departed for sea before any related drawback payment can be legally made.
Conveyance: Any conveyance transporting goods must have officially left the territory of Bangladesh for the purpose of initiating or completing the eligibility for drawback payment.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Declaration by parties claiming drawback
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 41. Declaration by parties claiming drawback.- Every person, or his duly authorized agent, claiming drawback on any goods duly exported shall make and subscribe a declaration that such goods have been actually exported and have not relanded and are not intended to be relanded at any place in 4[Bangladesh] and that such person was at the time of entry outwards and export and continues to be entitled to drawback thereon.

Customs Drawback: A person or their authorized agent must provide a formal declaration when claiming drawback on goods that have been exported.
The declaration must confirm that the exported goods have not been relanded in Bangladesh and that there is no intention for them to be relanded.
Drawback Claimant: The person claiming drawback is required to certify that they were entitled to the drawback at the time of the goods' entry outwards and export, and continue to hold that entitlement.
Agent: A duly authorized agent may act on behalf of a person to make and subscribe the necessary declarations for claiming drawback.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER VII - ARRIVAL AND DEPARTURE OF CONVEYANCE
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER VII
ARRIVAL AND DEPARTURE OF CONVEYANCE

Conveyance Arrival and Departure: This chapter outlines the legal framework and regulatory requirements governing the arrival and departure of any conveyance used for the transport of goods or persons into or out of the country.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Arrival of conveyance

Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance entering Bangladesh from abroad is legally mandated to ensure the conveyance first arrives only at a designated customs station.

In cases of emergency, such as accidents or unavoidable circumstances forcing an arrival elsewhere, the person in charge must immediately report the arrival to the nearest customs officer or police station.

During emergency arrivals, the person in charge must produce relevant transport documents like the cargo book, manifest, or log-book upon request and must not permit the unloading of goods or the departure of passengers or crew without official consent.
The person in charge is obligated to comply with all directions provided by customs or police officers regarding the goods onboard during emergency situations.
Customs Station: A customs station is the mandatory first point of arrival for any conveyance entering Bangladesh from outside the country.
Officer of Customs: Customs officers have the authority to receive reports of emergency arrivals, inspect conveyance documents, and provide binding directions regarding the handling of goods, passengers, and crew.
Officer-in-charge of Police Station: In the event of an emergency landing at a location other than a customs station, the officer-in-charge of the police station may receive arrival reports and exercise oversight similar to a customs officer until further authority is established.
Passenger or Crew: Passengers and crew members are restricted from leaving the vicinity of a conveyance that has made an emergency landing at a non-customs location without the consent of a customs or police officer.
Departures from the conveyance are permitted without prior consent only when necessary for urgent reasons of health, safety, or the preservation of life and property.
Goods: Goods transported by a conveyance forced into an emergency landing at a non-customs location cannot be unloaded without authorization, and their handling is subject to the directives of the relevant customs or police authorities.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Delivery of import manifest in respect of a vessel
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
43. Delivery of import manifest in respect of a vessel.- (1) The Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, fix a place in any river or port beyond which no vessel arriving shall pass until an import manifest has been delivered to the pilot, 1[officer of customs, or other person duly authorised to receive the same, or as the case may be, until the manifest has been transmitted to the Customs computer system by a registered user].
(2) If in any river or port wherein a place has been fixed by the Board under this section, the master of any vessel arriving remains outside or below the place so fixed, such master shall, nevertheless, within twenty-four hours after the vessel anchors, deliver an import manifest to the pilot, officer of customs or other person duly authorised to receive the same.
(3) If any vessel arrives at any customs-port in which a place has not been so fixed, the master of such vessel shall, within twenty-four hours after such vessel has anchored within the limits of the port, deliver an import manifest to the pilot, officer of customs or other person authorised to receive the same 2[:
Provided that if any officer not below the rank of 19[Revenue Officer] is satisfied that the master of the vessel was prevented by circumstances beyond his control from delivering the import manifest within twenty-four hours after the vessel anchored outside or below the place fixed by the Board under sub-section (1), allow it to be delivered within a further period of twenty-four hours or immediately after the first lighter vessel takes berth, whichever is earlier.]
(4) Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, the appropriate officer may allow an import manifest to be delivered in anticipation of the arrival of a vessel.

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to fix geographical limits in rivers or ports beyond which an arriving vessel cannot proceed until the import manifest has been properly delivered or transmitted.
Import Manifest: The master of a vessel must deliver an import manifest to a designated officer or transmit it via the customs computer system within specified timeframes after the vessel anchors.
The appropriate officer may grant permission for an import manifest to be submitted in anticipation of the vessel's arrival.
Revenue officers have the authority to extend the submission deadline for an import manifest if the vessel master was prevented by uncontrollable circumstances from meeting the original requirement.
Vessel: Vessels arriving at a river or port must adhere to restrictions regarding movement past fixed points until the import manifest is delivered or transmitted.
Vessels are subject to specific reporting requirements and timelines for the delivery of documents based on their location relative to fixed customs points.
Master of the Vessel: The master of the vessel is legally responsible for delivering the import manifest to the appropriate authorities within twenty-four hours of anchoring at a port or a fixed location.
Officer of Customs: Officers of customs are authorized to receive the import manifest from the master of a vessel upon its arrival or anchorage.
Customs Computerised System: The customs computerised system serves as the digital channel for the transmission of the import manifest by a registered user.
Registered User: A registered user is responsible for transmitting the import manifest to the customs computerised system in compliance with legal requirements.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer of customs has the discretionary power to accept an import manifest before a vessel has actually arrived at the port.
Revenue Officer: Revenue officers are authorized to grant an extension for the delivery of an import manifest if the master of the vessel demonstrates that they were unable to comply with the deadline due to circumstances beyond their control.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Delivery of import manifest in respect of a conveyance other than a vessel
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 44. Delivery of import manifest in respect of a conveyance other than a vessel.- The person-in-charge of a conveyance other than a vessel shall, within twenty-four hours after arrival thereof at a land customs-station or customs- airport, as the case may be, deliver an import manifest to the appropriate officer 4[or if the person-in-charge is a registered user, he may transmit the manifest to the Customs computer system].

Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance that is not a vessel must deliver an import manifest to the appropriate officer within a specific timeframe after reaching a customs station or customs airport.
A registered user acting as the person in charge may fulfill their obligation by transmitting the manifest electronically to the customs computer system.
Land Customs Station: This location serves as a point of arrival where the person in charge of a non-vessel conveyance must submit an import manifest.
Customs Airport: This location serves as a point of arrival where the person in charge of a non-vessel conveyance must submit an import manifest.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is the designated recipient of the import manifest delivered by the person in charge of a conveyance upon its arrival.
Import Manifest: This document is required to be delivered by the person in charge of a conveyance to the appropriate officer or transmitted electronically via the customs computer system upon arrival at a customs station.
Registered User: A registered user has the authority to submit import manifests by transmitting them to the customs computer system rather than through manual delivery.
Customs Computerised System: This system is used by registered users to electronically transmit import manifests to fulfill customs arrival obligations.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Signature and contents of import manifest and amendment thereof
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
45. Signature and contents of import manifest and amendment thereof.- (1) Every manifest delivered under section 43 or section 44 shall be signed by the person-in-charge of the conveyance or his duly authorised agent and shall specify all goods imported in such conveyance showing separately all goods, if any, intended to be landed, transhipped, transited or taken on to another customs-station or to a destination outside 1[Bangladesh] and stores intended for consumption at the customs-station or in the outward voyage or journey, and shall be made out in such form and contain such further particulars as the Board may from time to time direct 2[:]
3[Provided that the manifest transmitted to the Customs computer system by a registered user shall be deemed to have been signed by him.]
(2) The appropriate officer shall permit the person-in-charge of a conveyance or his duly authorised agent to correct any obvious error in the import manifest or to supply any omission which in the opinion of such officer results from accident or inadvertence, by furnishing an amended or supplementary import manifest and shall levy thereon such fees as the Board from time to time directs.
4[(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (2), the Board may specify, by special Order, the manner, conditions, limitations or restrictions under which the appropriate officer shall permit the person-in-charge of a conveyance, or his duly authorised agent, to submit an amended or supplementary import manifest in special circumstances and shall levy thereon such fees as the Board may direct.]

Import Manifest: The import manifest must be signed by the person in charge of the conveyance or their authorized agent and must specify all goods imported, categorizing them by their intended status such as landed, transhipped, or destined for another station or country.
The manifest must include stores intended for consumption and be prepared in the form and with the particulars as directed by the National Board of Revenue.

The person in charge of a conveyance or their authorized agent may be permitted to correct obvious errors or omissions in an import manifest by submitting an amended or supplementary version, subject to fees directed by the National Board of Revenue.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance or their authorized agent is responsible for signing and delivering the import manifest and providing any necessary amendments or supplementary documentation to the appropriate officer.
Agent: A duly authorized agent may sign and deliver an import manifest or submit amendments and supplementary information on behalf of the person in charge of a conveyance.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to prescribe the form and particulars of the import manifest, determine the fees for amendments or supplements, and issue special orders regarding the conditions and limitations for submitting such amendments in special circumstances.
Registered User: An import manifest transmitted to the customs computer system by a registered user is legally deemed to have been signed by that user.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is empowered to allow corrections of obvious errors or omissions in the import manifest and to impose prescribed fees for the processing of amended or supplementary manifests.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Duty of person receiving import manifest
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 46. Duty of person receiving import manifest.- The person receiving an import manifest under section 43 or section 44 shall countersign the same and enter thereon such particulars as the 5[Commissioner of Customs] from time to time directs6[, and where the import manifest is transmitted electronically to the Customs computer system by a registered user, the import manifest shall be deemed to have been countersigned by the person authorised to receive such transmission and that person shall comply with the direction of that Commissioner, if any, in this regard].

Import Manifest: The person receiving an import manifest is required to countersign it and include specific particulars as directed by the Commissioner of Customs.
When transmitted electronically to the customs computer system by a registered user, the manifest is legally deemed to be countersigned by the authorized receiving party.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to specify the particulars that must be entered onto an import manifest and to issue directions regarding compliance with electronic transmissions.
Registered User: A registered user is authorized to transmit an import manifest electronically to the customs computer system, which satisfies the requirement for countersignature by the designated recipient.
Customs Computerised System: The customs computerised system serves as the official platform for the electronic transmission and processing of import manifests.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Bulk not to be broken until manifest, etc., delivered and vessel entered inwards
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 47. Bulk not to be broken until manifest, etc., delivered and vessel entered inwards.- No vessel arriving in any customs-port shall be allowed to break bulk, until an import manifest has been delivered as hereinbefore provided or until a copy of such manifest, together with an application for entry of such vessel inwards, has been presented by the master to the appropriate officer and an order has been given thereon for such entry.

Vessel: A vessel arriving at a customs-port is prohibited from breaking bulk until specific documentation and entry requirements are satisfied.
Customs Port: This location serves as the jurisdictional point where vessels must comply with manifest delivery and inward entry procedures before commencing cargo discharge.
Import Manifest: The delivery of an import manifest is a mandatory legal prerequisite that must be satisfied before a vessel is authorized to break bulk.
Master of the Vessel: The master is responsible for presenting the import manifest and a formal application for inward entry to the appropriate officer to obtain authorization for breaking bulk.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is responsible for receiving the manifest and application for inward entry from the vessel master and granting the necessary order to proceed.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to require production of documents and ask questions
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
48. Power to require production of documents and ask questions.- (1) When an import manifest is presented, the person-in-charge of a conveyance or his duly authorised agent, if required so to do by the appropriate officer, shall deliver to the officer the bill of lading or the bill of freight or a copy thereof for every part of cargo or goods laden or board, journey log-book and any port clearance, docket or other paper granted in respect of such conveyance at the place from which it is stated to have come, and shall answer all such questions relating to the conveyance, goods, crew7[, passengers] and voyage or journey as are put to him by such officer.
(2) The appropriate officer may, if any requisition or question made or put by him under this section is not complied with or answered, refuse to grant permission to a vessel to break bulk and to other conveyance to land the imported goods, as the case may be.

Import Manifest: The presentation of an import manifest triggers the authority of customs officers to request specific documents and information from the person in charge of a conveyance.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance or their authorized agent is legally obligated to produce transport documents and answer questions regarding the cargo, crew, passengers, and journey upon request by an appropriate officer of customs.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer of customs has the authority to demand production of shipping documents and to pose questions to the person in charge of a conveyance.
The officer is empowered to refuse permission for a vessel to break bulk or for other conveyances to land imported goods if their requisitions for documents or answers to questions are not satisfied.
Bill of Lading: The person in charge of a conveyance must deliver the bill of lading or a copy thereof for the cargo upon the request of an appropriate officer of customs.
Port Clearance: The person in charge of a conveyance must produce port clearance and other related papers issued at the point of origin when required by an appropriate officer of customs.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Special pass for breaking bulk
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 49. Special pass for breaking bulk.- Notwithstanding anything contained in section 47 and subject to rules, the appropriate officer may grant, prior to receipt of the import manifest and the entry inwards of a vessel, a special pass permeating bulk to be broken.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is authorized to issue a special pass allowing for the breaking of bulk prior to the vessel's official entry inwards and the receipt of the import manifest.
Import Manifest: The submission of the import manifest is a standard requirement that may be bypassed under specific conditions for the purpose of granting a special pass for breaking bulk.
Vessel: A special pass for breaking bulk may be granted for a vessel before the formal completion of the entry inwards process.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Order for entry outwards or loading of goods to be obtained before export goods are loaded
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
50. Order for entry outwards or loading of goods to be obtained before export goods are loaded.- (1) No goods other than passengers baggage and mail bags shall be loaded on a conveyance until-
(a) in the case of a vessel, a written application for entry of such vessel outwards, subscribed by the master of such vessel has been made to the appropriate officer and an order has been given thereon for such entry; and
(b) in the case of any other conveyance, a written application for authority to load the goods subscribed by the person-in-charge of the conveyance has been made to the appropriate officer and an order has been given thereon authorising the loading.
(2) Every application made under this section shall specify the particulars as prescribed by the Board.

Export Goods: No goods, excluding passenger baggage and mail bags, may be loaded onto a conveyance for export until specific regulatory requirements for entry or loading authorization have been satisfied.
Vessel: A vessel is subject to a mandatory entry outward process, requiring the master to submit a written application to the appropriate officer and obtain an order for entry before any export goods can be loaded.
Vessel Master: The master of a vessel is responsible for submitting a formal written application for entry outwards to the appropriate officer to facilitate the legal loading of export goods.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is the authority responsible for receiving written applications and issuing the necessary orders for the entry of vessels or authorization for the loading of other conveyances.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: For conveyances other than vessels, the person in charge must submit a written application for loading authorization to the appropriate officer to ensure legal compliance before loading goods.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to prescribe the specific particulars that must be included in applications for vessel entry or conveyance loading authorization under this section.

processed_clauses.clause_title: No vessel to depart without port-clearance
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
51. No vessel to depart without port-clearance.- (1) No vessel, whether laden or in ballast, shall depart from any customs-port until a port-clearance has been granted by the appropriate officer.
(2) No pilot shall take charge of any vessel proceeding to sea, unless the master of such vessel produces a port-clearance.

Vessel: No vessel, whether carrying cargo or in ballast, is permitted to leave a customs port without first obtaining formal port clearance.
Customs Port: A customs port serves as the location from which vessels must obtain official clearance before their departure.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate customs officer is the authority responsible for granting the necessary port clearance to a vessel.
Pilot: A pilot is prohibited from taking charge of a vessel heading out to sea unless the master of that vessel presents a valid port clearance.
Master: The master of a vessel is required to produce a port clearance before a pilot can take charge of the vessel for its departure to sea.
Port Clearance: Port clearance acts as the mandatory legal authorization that must be granted by an appropriate customs officer and produced by the vessel master before a vessel can lawfully depart from a port.

processed_clauses.clause_title: No conveyance other than vessel to leave without permission
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 52. No conveyance other than vessel to leave without permission.- No conveyance other than a vessel shall depart from a land customs-station or customs-airport until a written permission to that effect has been granted by the appropriate officer.

Conveyance: Any conveyance, excluding a vessel, is prohibited from leaving a land customs station or customs airport without first obtaining written permission from the appropriate customs officer.
Customs Station: Departures of conveyances other than vessels from land customs stations are subject to mandatory written authorization from customs authorities.
Customs Airport: Departures of conveyances other than vessels from customs airports are subject to mandatory written authorization from customs authorities.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is responsible for granting the formal written permission required before a non-vessel conveyance may depart from a land customs station or customs airport.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Application for port-clearance of vessels
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
53. Application for port-clearance of vessels.- (1) Every application for port-clearance Shall be made by the master of a vessel at least twenty-four hours before the intended departure of the vessel:
Provided that the 1[Commissioner of Customs] or an officer authorised by him in this behalf may for special reasons to be recorded allow a shorter period for the delivery of the said application2[:]
3[Provided further that when the master is a registered user, he may make the application under this sub-section by transmitting it to the Customs computer system, and an application so transmitted shall be deemed to have been duly signed by him.]
(2) The master shall, at the time of applying for port-clearance,-
(a) deliver to the appropriate officer an export manifest in duplicate in such form as may from time to time be prescribed by the Board signed by such master specifying all goods to be exported in the vessel and showing separately all goods and stores entered in the import manifest, and not landed or consumed on board or transhipped;
(b) deliver to the appropriate officer such bills of export or other documents as such officer acting under the general instructions of the 1[Commissioner of Customs] requires; and
(c) answer such questions respecting the departure and destination of the vessel as are put to him by the appropriate officer2[:
Provided that if the master is a registered user, he may transmit to the Customs computer system the export manifest and other documents specified at clauses (b) and (c) and the documents so transmitted shall be deemed to have been signed by him for the purposes of this section.]
(3) The provisions of section 45, relating to the amendment of import manifest shall, mutatis mutandis, apply also to export manifest delivered under this section or under section 54.

Port Clearance: The master of a vessel is required to submit an application for port clearance at least twenty-four hours before the vessel's intended departure. The Commissioner of Customs or an authorized officer may permit a shorter application period under special recorded circumstances.
Master: The master is responsible for applying for port clearance, delivering necessary documentation such as the export manifest and bills of export, and answering inquiries regarding the vessel's departure and destination. When acting as a registered user, the master may fulfill these requirements by transmitting documents to the customs computer system.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to approve a reduced timeframe for port clearance applications and provides general instructions for the documentation required during the clearance process.
Export Manifest: The master must deliver an export manifest in duplicate, which specifies all goods to be exported and details items carried over from the import manifest that remain on board. The document must follow the prescribed form and be signed by the master, or transmitted electronically if the master is a registered user.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer receives the export manifest, bills of export, and other required documents, and has the authority to examine the master regarding the vessel's departure and destination.
Registered User: A master who is a registered user may submit applications, export manifests, and other required documents via the customs computer system, with such transmissions legally deemed as signed by the master.
Customs Computerised Entry Processing Sy: The customs computer system serves as the digital platform for registered users to transmit export manifests and other clearance documents, substituting for physical document submission.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Conveyances other than vessels to deliver documents and answer question before departure
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
54. Conveyances other than vessels to deliver documents and answer question before departure.- The person-in-charge of a conveyance other than a vessel or his duly authorised agent shall-
(a) deliver to the appropriate officer an export manifest in duplicate in such form as may from time to time be prescribed by the Board signed by such person-in-charge or the agent specifying all goods or stores entered in the import manifest, and not landed or transhipped or consumed on board the conveyance;
(b) deliver to the appropriate officer such bills of export or other documents as such officer acting under the general instructions of the 1[Commissioner of Customs] requires; and
(c) answer such questions respecting the departure and destination of the conveyance as are put to him by the appropriate officer.

Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance, other than a vessel, or their authorized agent is legally obligated to perform specific procedural tasks before the departure of the conveyance.

They must provide the appropriate officer with an export manifest in the prescribed form, submit necessary bills of export or other required documentation, and respond to inquiries regarding the conveyance's departure and destination.
Agent: An agent may act on behalf of the person in charge of a conveyance to fulfill legal requirements for document delivery and manifest submission before departure.
Export Manifest: The person in charge of a conveyance must deliver an export manifest in duplicate to the appropriate officer.
This document must be signed and detail all goods or stores that were included in the import manifest but were not landed, transhipped, or consumed during the transit.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is the designated authority to receive the export manifest, bills of export, and other required documents from the person in charge of the conveyance.
They are also authorized to question the person in charge regarding the conveyance's departure and destination.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to prescribe the form for the export manifest that must be submitted by the person in charge of the conveyance.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs provides the general instructions under which the appropriate officer requires the submission of specific bills of export and additional documentation.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to refuse port-clearance to vessels or permission for departure to other conveyance

Port Clearance: The appropriate officer of customs has the authority to refuse port clearance to a vessel or permission for departure to other conveyances until all relevant legal requirements and payments are satisfied.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to demand security, guarantees, or deposits to ensure the payment of dues, taxes, and penalties before granting departure permission to a conveyance.
The officer may require the unloading of goods exported in violation of the law or, if unloading is impractical, demand an undertaking and security for bringing the goods back to Bangladesh.
Conveyance: Departure permission for any conveyance may be withheld until all port dues, charges, and penalties applicable to the conveyance or its person-in-charge have been settled.
Vessel: Port clearance for a vessel may be withheld until all applicable port dues, penalties, and taxes related to the vessel, its master, or its cargo have been paid or secured.
Agent: An agent may provide a written declaration assuming liability for specific penalties and furnish security, thereby becoming responsible for such discharge.
An agent may provide a written declaration assuming responsibility for claims regarding damage or short delivery of imported goods, becoming legally bound to discharge those claims.
Person in Charge: The person-in-charge of a conveyance is responsible for the payment of all dues, taxes, and penalties related to the conveyance or its cargo before departure is permitted.
Export Goods: If export goods are loaded without paying required taxes or duties, or in violation of law, they must be unloaded or the agent must provide an undertaking and security to bring the goods back to Bangladesh.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 56. Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure.- When the appropriate officer is satisfied that the provisions of this Chapter relating to the departure of conveyances have been duly complied with, he shall grant a port- clearance to the master of the vessel or a written permission for departure to the person-in-charge of any other conveyance and shall return at the same time to such master or person-in-charge one copy of the manifest duly countersigned by the appropriate officer.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The officer is responsible for verifying that all legal requirements concerning the departure of a conveyance have been satisfied before authorizing its departure.
Port Clearance: This document is granted to the master of a vessel by the appropriate officer once all departure requirements are met.
Departure Permission: This written authorization is issued to the person-in-charge of a conveyance, other than a vessel, upon the fulfillment of all necessary departure formalities.
Master of the Vessel: The master must receive port clearance and a countersigned copy of the manifest from the appropriate officer before the vessel is permitted to depart.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: This person must obtain written permission for departure from the appropriate officer, along with a countersigned copy of the manifest, after ensuring all regulatory compliance for departure.
Manifest: A copy of the manifest must be countersigned by the appropriate officer and returned to the master or person-in-charge of the conveyance upon the granting of departure permission.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure on security of agent
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 57. Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure on security of agent.- Notwithstanding anything contained in section 55 or section 56 and subject to rules, the appropriate officer may grant a port-clearance in respect of a vessel or permission for departure in respect of any other conveyance, if the agent furnishes such security as such officer deems sufficient for duly delivering within ten days from the date of such grant, the export manifest and other documents specified in section 53 or section 54, as the case may be.

Port Clearance: The appropriate officer of customs may grant port clearance to a vessel despite standard requirements if the agent provides adequate security for the timely delivery of required export documents.
Departure Permission: The appropriate officer of customs may grant permission for the departure of a conveyance, other than a vessel, provided the agent furnishes sufficient security to ensure the later submission of mandatory export manifests and associated documents.
Agent: The agent is responsible for providing financial security as deemed sufficient by the appropriate officer of customs to secure the delivery of export documents within a specified period following the grant of clearance or departure permission.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to exercise discretion in accepting security from an agent to facilitate the clearance of vessels or the departure of conveyances.
Export Manifest: Agents must ensure the delivery of the export manifest within ten days from the date of receiving port clearance or departure permission.
Security Bond: A security bond or equivalent security must be furnished by the agent to guarantee the timely submission of required export documents to customs authorities.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to cancel port-clearance or permission for departure
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
58. Power to cancel port-clearance or permission for departure.- (1) For the purpose of securing compliance with any provision of this Act or the rules or any other law, the appropriate officer may at any time, while the vessel is within the limits of any port or any other conveyance is within the limits of any station or airport or within 1[Bangladesh] territory, demand the return of port- clearance or the written permission for departure, as the case may be.
(2) Any such demand may be made in writing or may be communicated to the person-in-charge of the conveyance by wireless, and if made in writing it may be served-
(a) by delivery to the person-in-charge or his agent personally; or
(b) by leaving it at the last known place of abode of such person or agent; or
(c) by leaving it on board the conveyance with the person appearing to be in charge or command thereof.
(3) Where a demand for the return of a port-clearance or of a permission for departure is made as aforesaid, the port-clearance or permission shall forthwith become void.

Port Clearance: The appropriate officer may demand the return of a port clearance for the purpose of securing compliance with the Customs Act or other relevant laws while a vessel is within port limits or Bangladesh territory.
A port clearance becomes immediately void once a valid demand for its return has been made by the appropriate officer.
Departure Permission: The appropriate officer is empowered to demand the return of written permission for departure from a conveyance while it is located within a customs station, airport, or Bangladeshi territory.
Once a formal demand for the return of a departure permission is issued, the document is legally rendered void.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is authorized to secure legal compliance by demanding the return of port clearance or departure permission from conveyances located within their jurisdiction.
The officer may issue these demands in writing or via wireless communication to the person in charge of the conveyance.
Conveyance: When located within the limits of a station, airport, or Bangladeshi territory, a conveyance is subject to the authority of customs officers regarding the cancellation of departure permissions.
Demands for the return of clearance documents may be served by leaving the notice on board the conveyance with the person currently in command.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance is the recipient of any demand for the return of clearance or departure permissions, which may be delivered personally, left at their last known residence, or communicated via wireless.
