Customs Offence Penalties: This clause defines a wide range of offences related to customs procedures, illicit imports, exports, and administrative failures, stipulating that penalties apply in addition to any other legal liabilities.
Penalties include confiscation of goods, monetary fines proportional to the duty or value of the goods, and imprisonment upon conviction by a Magistrate for more serious violations.
Specific provisions address unauthorized access to the Customs computerized entry processing system, data falsification, and misuse of unique identifiers by users.
Customs Computerised Entry Processing Sy: Unauthorized access, disclosure of information, or tampering with records within the computerized system are strictly prohibited and subject to severe penalties, including fines and imprisonment.
Registered users are explicitly penalized for misuse of unique identifiers, and any damage to the system or stored digital media is considered a criminal offence.
Vessel: Vessels must follow established maritime regulations, including anchoring at designated places and stopping for customs officials, with penalties for masters who fail to comply.
Vessels involved in the irregular unloading or transport of goods, or that attempt to depart without proper clearance, are liable to confiscation.
Goods: Goods imported, exported, or transported in contravention of customs laws, including smuggling, concealment, or misdeclaration on manifests or bills of entry, are subject to confiscation.
The person responsible for goods that are lost, deficient, or handled irregularly is liable for the duty payable and additional monetary penalties.
Conveyance: The person-in-charge of a conveyance is responsible for delivering manifests and complying with customs orders, with failure to do so resulting in financial penalties.
Conveyances may be confiscated if they are used to facilitate smuggling, irregular unloading, or departure without port clearance.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs holds authority to appoint stations for boarding or landing officers and to issue directions regarding the anchoring or mooring of vessels.
Officer of Customs: Obstruction of an officer of customs, including refusal to provide access for searches or failing to provide required accommodations, is a punishable offence.
Officers have the authority to place locks, marks, or seals on goods, and the unauthorized interference with these security measures is prohibited.
Magistrate: Conviction by a Magistrate is required for the imposition of imprisonment penalties related to serious customs offences, such as smuggling or tampering with customs computer systems.
Pre-shipment Inspection: Failure to undergo mandatory pre-shipment inspection for non-exempt goods renders the person responsible liable to pay service charges and significant financial penalties.
Manifest: The failure to deliver a manifest, or the submission of an inaccurate, false, or incomplete manifest by the person-in-charge of a conveyance, is a punishable offence.
Bill of Entry: Declarations made on a bill of entry must be truthful, as the concealment, mixing of goods, or misleading descriptions discovered during inspection lead to penalties and potential confiscation.
Agent: An agent or person who removes goods from the port area with the intention of defrauding the revenue is liable for heavy penalties, duty recovery, and potential imprisonment.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Extent of confiscation

Confiscation of Goods: The confiscation of goods under the Customs Act extends to include any package containing the goods and all other items found within such packages.
Confiscation of Vehicles: Any vehicle used for the removal of goods that are liable to confiscation is itself subject to confiscation under the law.
Confiscation of Vessels: The confiscation of a vessel under this Act encompasses all associated tackle, apparel, and furniture belonging to the vessel.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: An officer at or above the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs is authorized to order the provisional release of a seized conveyance pending the final adjudication of the confiscation case.
This officer is responsible for accepting personal undertakings or bank guarantees as conditions for releasing a seized conveyance.
Scheduled Bank: A scheduled bank provides the necessary guarantees for the provisional release of seized conveyances other than motor vehicles, as required by customs authorities.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER XVIII
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER XVIII
PREVENTION OF SMUGGLING-POWER OF SEARCH, SEIZURE AND ARREST- ADJUDICATION OF OFFENCES

Smuggling Prevention: This chapter sets out the foundational framework for preventing smuggling activities through legal and enforcement measures.
Search Warrant: The chapter establishes legal powers for conducting searches to support the prevention of smuggling.
Seizure of Goods: This section provides the legal authority for the seizure of goods involved in smuggling or related offences.
Adjudication of Customs Offences: The chapter outlines the procedures for the adjudication of offences and matters related to search, seizure, and arrest in customs cases.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to search on reasonable ground
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
158. Power to search on reasonable ground.- (1) The appropriate officer, if he has reason to believe that any person is carrying about himself goods liable to confiscation or any documents relating thereto, may search such person, if he has landed from or is on board or is about to board a vessel within the 3[Bangladesh] customs-waters, or if he has alighted from or is about to get into or is in any other conveyance arriving in or proceeding from 3[Bangladesh] or if he is entering or about to leave 3[Bangladesh] or if he is within the limits of any customs-area.
(2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1) the appropriate officer may search a person, if he has reason to believe that such person is carrying about himself smuggled Platinum, any radio active mineral, gold, silver, precious stones, manufactures of Platinum, any radio active mineral, gold, silver or precious stones, or currency, or any other goods or class of goods notified by the 4[Government] in the official Gazette, or any documents relating to any one or more of the aforementioned goods.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to search any person if there is a reasonable belief that the individual is carrying goods liable to confiscation or related documents.
The officer may conduct searches on persons located within customs-areas, in conveyances, or on vessels within Bangladesh customs-waters.
The officer has the authority to search persons suspected of carrying specific prohibited items like gold, silver, currency, or precious stones, or other goods notified by the Government.
Person: A person is subject to search by an appropriate officer if they are suspected of carrying goods liable to confiscation while present in customs-areas, or upon boarding or leaving vessels and conveyances.
Vessel: Vessels within the Bangladesh customs-waters serve as specific locations where an appropriate officer may exercise search powers over persons on board.
Conveyance: The appropriate officer is authorized to search persons arriving in or departing from Bangladesh who are in, alighting from, or entering into any conveyance.
Bangladesh customs-waters: This geographic area defines a zone where an appropriate officer may board and search vessels and the individuals located thereon.
Customs-area: The limits of a customs-area constitute a jurisdictional boundary within which the appropriate officer is granted the power to search persons.
Smuggled Goods: The search powers extend to persons suspected of carrying precious metals, minerals, stones, or currency, as well as any other goods specifically notified by the Government in the official Gazette.
Government: The Government has the authority to notify in the official Gazette specific classes of goods that, when carried by a person, provide grounds for a search by the appropriate officer.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Conferring certain Powers of Magistrate 1st Class on Customs officers
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 5[158A. Conferring certain Powers of Magistrate 1st Class on Customs officers.- For the purposes of entry search, seizure and arrest under this Act, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, confer the powers of a Magistrate of the First Class described in the Schedule III of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898) on an officer of customs not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner.]

Customs Officer: The Government is empowered to grant specific powers of a Magistrate of the First Class to officers of customs holding the rank of Assistant Commissioner or higher.
These conferred powers are limited to the purposes of conducting entry, search, seizure, and arrest as provided under the Customs Act 1969.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: This Act serves as the legal reference for the powers of a Magistrate of the First Class that can be conferred upon authorized customs officials under the customs law.
Government: The Government has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to formally grant magisterial powers to designated customs officials.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Persons to be searched may desire to be taken before gazetted officer of customs or Magistrate
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
159. Persons to be searched may desire to be taken before gazetted officer of customs or Magistrate.- (1) When any officer of customs is about to search any person under the provisions of section 158, the officer of customs shall inform such person about his right to be taken to a gazetted officer of customs or Magistrate, and if such person so desires take him without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted officer of customs or Magistrate before searching him, and may detain him until he can be so taken.
(2) The gazetted officer of customs or the Magistrate before whom such person is brought shall, if he sees no reasonable ground for search, forthwith discharge the person and record reasons for doing so, or else direct search to be made.
(3) Before making a search under section 158, the officer of customs shall call upon two or more persons to attend and witness the search and may issue an order in writing to them or any of them so to do, and the search shall be made in the presence of such persons and a list of all things seized in the course of such search shall be prepared by such officer or other person and signed by such witnesses.
(4) A female shall not be searched except by a female1[:
Provided that where practicable samples of such things with proper identification marks may be kept for the purpose of any legal proceeding or for any other purpose of this Act.]

Officer of Customs: Before conducting a search of any person, the officer of customs is legally required to inform the individual of their right to be taken before a gazetted officer or a Magistrate.
The officer of customs must follow specific procedures, including calling witnesses to attend the search and preparing a list of all items seized during the process.
The officer has the authority to detain an individual until they can be brought before a gazetted officer or Magistrate if the person requests such an appearance.
Gazetted Customs Officer: This officer acts as an independent authority to whom a person about to be searched by a customs official may request to be taken.

If a person is brought before them, the gazetted customs officer must decide whether reasonable grounds for the search exist and either discharge the person with recorded reasons or order that the search proceed.
Magistrate: A person who is subject to a customs search has the right to request to be taken before a Magistrate before the search is conducted.
The Magistrate has the power to evaluate the grounds for the search and can either discharge the individual or authorize the search to proceed.
Personal Search: The law mandates that a search of a person must be witnessed by two or more individuals, and a record of all seized items must be prepared and signed by these witnesses.
A search of a female must only be conducted by another female to ensure appropriate procedure is followed.
Seized Goods: When items are seized during a personal search, the officer must prepare a formal list, and samples of such items may be retained for legal proceedings or other purposes of the Customs Act 1969.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to screen or X-Ray bodies of suspected persons for detecting secreted goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
160. Power to screen or X-Ray bodies of suspected persons for detecting secreted goods.- (1) Where the appropriate officer has reason to believe that any person liable to search under section 158 has any goods liable to confiscation secreted inside his body, he may detain such person and produce him without unnecessary delay before an officer of customs not below the rank of an 2[Assistant Commissioner of Customs].
(2) The aforesaid officer, if he has reasonable grounds for believing that such person has any such goods secreted inside his body and that it is necessary to have the body of such person screened or X-Rayed, may make an order to that effect, or else discharge such person forthwith, except where he is held on any other grounds.
(3) Where the aforesaid officer orders such person to be screened or X-Rayed, the appropriate officer shall, as soon as practicable, take him to a radiologist possessing such qualifications as may be recognised by the 3[Government] for that purpose and such person shall allow the radiologist to screen or X-Ray his body.
(4) The radiologist shall screen or X-Ray the body of such person and forward his report thereon, together with any X-Ray pictures taken by him to the aforesaid officer without unnecessary delay.
(5) Where on the basis of a report from a radiologist or otherwise, the aforesaid officer is satisfied that any person has any goods liable to confiscation secreted inside his body , he may direct that suitable action for bringing such goods out of his body be taken on the advice and under the supervision of a registered medical practitioner and such person shall be bound to comply with such direction:
Provided that in the case of a female no such action shall be taken except on the advice and under the supervision of a female registered medical practitioner.
(6) Where any person is brought before an officer of customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] as aforesaid, he may direct that pending completion of all action under this section such person be detained.
(7) No person shall be subjected to screening or X-Ray if he confesses that goods liable to confiscation are secreted inside his body and of his own consent agrees to suitable steps being taken to bring out such goods.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is authorized to detain a suspected person if there is reason to believe they have secreted goods inside their body that are liable to confiscation.
The officer must promptly produce the detained person before an officer of at least the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs for further authorization of screening or X-ray procedures.
The officer is responsible for taking the suspect to a recognized radiologist for screening and must supervise or direct the removal of any secreted goods based on medical advice.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: A customs officer at or above the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs is authorized to review the case of a detained person and order a body screening or X-ray if reasonable grounds exist.
This officer is empowered to direct the detention of a suspect while the required medical actions or investigations are being completed.
Confiscated Goods: Goods suspected of being secreted inside a person's body and which are liable to confiscation are subject to detection through screening or X-ray procedures.
The law provides mechanisms for the recovery of such goods under medical supervision when their presence is confirmed.
Radiologist: A radiologist, possessing qualifications recognized by the Government, is the authorized professional tasked with performing body screenings or X-rays on suspects to detect secreted goods.
The radiologist is required to forward the screening report and any associated imagery to the relevant customs officer without delay.
Registered Medical Practitioner: Any action taken to remove secreted goods from a person's body must be performed under the advice and supervision of a registered medical practitioner.
In the case of a female suspect, the intervention must be supervised specifically by a female registered medical practitioner.
Government: The Government is responsible for recognizing the qualifications of the radiologists authorized to perform the medical procedures required for detecting secreted goods.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to arrest
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
161. Power to arrest.- (1) Any officer of customs authorised in this behalf who has reason to believe that any person has committed an offence under this Act may arrest such person.
(2) Any person duly empowered for the prevention of smuggling who has reason to believe that any person who has committed an offence of smuggling under this Act may arrest such person.
(3) Every person arrested under this Act shall be taken forthwith before the nearest officer of customs authorised by the 2[Commissioner of Customs] to deal with such cases, or, if there is no such officer of customs within a reasonable distance, to the officer-in-charge of the nearest police-station.
(4) The officer of customs or the officer-in-charge of a police-station before whom any person is taken under this section shall, if the offence be bailable, either admit him to bail to appear before the Magistrate having jurisdiction or have him taken in custody before such Magistrate.
(5) When any person is taken under sub-section (4) before an officer of customs as aforesaid, such officer shall proceed to inquire into the charge against such person.
(6) For the purpose of an inquiry under sub-section (5), the officer of customs may exercise the same powers and shall be subject to the same provisions, as an officer-in-charge of a police-station may exercise and is subject to under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), when investigating a cognizable offence:
Provided that, if the officer of customs is of opinion that there is sufficient evidence or reasonable ground of suspicion against the accused person, he shall if the offence be bailable, either admit him to bail to appear before a Magistrate having jurisdiction, or have him taken in custody before such Magistrate.
(7) If it appears to the officer of customs that there is no sufficient evidence or reasonable ground of suspicion against the accused person, he shall, release the accused person on his executing a bond, with or without sureties as the officer may direct, to appear, if and when so required, before the Magistrate having jurisdiction and shall make a full report of the case to his immediate superior.

Officer of Customs: An authorized officer of customs has the power to arrest any person if there is reason to believe that the person has committed an offence under the Customs Act.
Arrested persons must be brought before an authorized officer of customs or the nearest police station for further action.
When an arrested person is brought before an officer of customs, the officer must conduct an inquiry into the charges.
During such inquiries, the officer of customs may exercise powers similar to an officer-in-charge of a police station under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
If an offence is bailable, the officer may grant bail or produce the accused before the Magistrate, and if evidence is insufficient, the officer may release the accused upon the execution of a bond.
Smuggling Prevention: Persons duly empowered for the prevention of smuggling have the legal authority to arrest individuals they believe have committed an offence of smuggling under the Customs Act.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to designate specific officers to deal with cases involving persons arrested under the Customs Act.
Officer-in-charge of Police Station: In the absence of an authorized officer of customs within a reasonable distance, an arrested person must be taken to the officer-in-charge of the nearest police station.
The officer-in-charge of a police station has the authority to grant bail for bailable offences or produce the arrested person before a Magistrate.
Magistrate: Arrested persons may be produced before the Magistrate having jurisdiction to address the charges brought against them under the Customs Act.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: This Code governs the investigative powers and legal procedures that an officer of customs exercises when inquiring into charges against an arrested person.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to issue search warrant
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
162. Power to issue search warrant.- (1) Any Magistrate may, on application by a gazetted officer of customs stating the grounds of his belief that goods liable to confiscation or documents or things which in his opinion will be useful as evidence in any proceeding under this Act are secreted in any place within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such Magistrate, issue a warrant to search for such goods, documents or things.
(2) Such warrant shall be executed in the same way, and shall have the same effect, as a search-warrant issued under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898).

Magistrate: A Magistrate is empowered to issue a search warrant upon the application of a gazetted officer of customs who provides valid grounds for believing that seizable goods or relevant evidence are hidden within the Magistrate's jurisdiction.
Gazetted Customs Officer: A gazetted customs officer has the authority to apply for a search warrant by documenting the reasons for their belief that evidence or goods liable to confiscation are secreted at a specific location.
Search Warrant: A search warrant issued for customs purposes is executed using the same procedures and carries the same legal weight as a warrant issued under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 serves as the standard legal framework for the execution and legal effect of search warrants issued under the customs law.
Confiscated Goods: Goods liable to confiscation are among the items subject to search and seizure under a warrant issued by a Magistrate.
Documentary Evidence: Documents or other items that may serve as evidence in customs proceedings are subject to search and seizure under the authority of a judicial search warrant.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to search and arrest without warrant
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
163. Power to search and arrest without warrant.- (1) Whenever any officer or customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] or any other officer 2[* * * *] employed for the prevention of smuggling has reasonable grounds for believing that any goods liable to confiscation or any documents or things which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any proceeding under this Act are concealed or kept in any place and that there is a danger that they may be removed before a search can be effected under section 162, he may, after preparing a statement in writing of the grounds of his belief and of the goods, documents or things for which search is to be made, search or cause of search to be made for such goods, documents or things in that place.
(2) Any officer or person who makes a search or causes a search to be made under sub-section (1) shall leave a signed copy of the aforementioned statement in or about the place searched and shall, at the time the search is made or as soon as is practicable thereafter, deliver furthermore a signed copy of such statement to the occupier of the place at his last known address.
(3) All searches made under this section shall be carried out mutatis mutandis in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898).
(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing sub-sections and subject to previous authorization by an officer of customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs], any officer of customs or any person duly empowered as such may, with respect to an offence 3[of smuggling]-
(a) arrest without warrant any person concerned in such offence or against whom reasonable suspicion exists that he is about to be concerned in such offence;
(b) enter and search without warrant any premises to make an arrest under clause (a), or to seize an goods which are reasonable suspected to be intended for 4[smuggling] contrary to any prohibition or restriction for the time being in force, and all documents or things which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any proceeding under this Act; and
(c) for the purpose of arresting, detaining or taking into custody or preventing the escape of any person concerned or likely to be concerned in such offence, or for the purpose of seizing or preventing the removal of any goods in respect of which any such offence has occurred or is likely to occur, use or cause to be used such force to the extent of causing death as may be necessary.
(5) The provisions of sub-section (4) shall apply only to the areas within five miles of the land frontier of 1[Bangladesh], and within a five mile belt running along the sea coast of 1[Bangladesh].
(6) No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall be instituted, except with the previous sanction in writing of the 2[Government], against any person in respect of anything done or purporting to be done in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) or, in the areas specified in sub-section (3), by sub-section (4).

Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer is authorized to form beliefs regarding the concealment of goods or documents subject to search and to authorize officers to conduct searches or arrests without a warrant under specified conditions.
Smuggling: The prevention of smuggling is a primary function that empowers customs officers to carry out searches and arrests without a warrant in defined circumstances.
Specific enforcement powers, including the use of force and warrantless entry of premises, are granted to customs officers when dealing with offences related to smuggling.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: All searches conducted under this section must adhere to the procedural requirements established in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Officer of Customs: Officers are empowered to enter and search premises, seize goods suspected of smuggling, and arrest individuals involved in such offences without a warrant under specific conditions.
When necessary to execute duties such as arresting persons or seizing goods, these officers may use force, including lethal force, to prevent escape or the removal of illicit items.
Government: Legal proceedings cannot be instituted against any person acting under the powers granted in this section without the prior written sanction of the Government.
Customs Offence: Special enforcement provisions apply to offences related to smuggling, allowing for warrantless arrests, entry of premises, and the use of force within designated border and coastal zones.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to stop and search conveyances
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
164. Power to stop and search conveyances.- (1) Where the appropriate officer has reason to believe that within the territories of 1[Bangladesh] (including territorial waters) any conveyance has been, is being, or is about to be used in the smuggling of any goods or in the carriage of any smuggled goods, he may at any time stop any such conveyance or, in the case of an aircraft, competent it to land, and-
(a) rummage and search any part of the conveyance ;
(b) examine and search any goods thereon ; and
(c) break open the lock f any door, fixure or package for making search.
(2) Where in the circumstances referred to in sub-section (1)-
(a) it becomes necessary to stop any vessel or compel any aircraft to land, it shall be lawful for any vessel or aircraft in the service of the Government while flying her proper flag or bearing flag marks and any authority authorised in this behalf by the 3[Government] to summon such vessel to stop or the aircraft to land, by means of an international signal, code or other recognised means, and thereupon such vessel shall forthwith stop or such aircraft shall forthwith land, and it fails to do so, chase may be given there to by any vessel or aircraft as aforesaid and if after a gun is fired as a signal the vessel fails to stop or the aircraft fails to land, it may be fired upon;
(b) it becomes necessary to stop any conveyance other than a vessel or aircraft, the appropriate officer may use or cause to be used all lawful means for stopping it or preventing it escape including, if all other means fail, firing upon it.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to stop and search any conveyance if they have reason to believe it is being used for smuggling goods or transporting smuggled goods within Bangladesh.
They are authorized to search, examine, and break open any locks, fixtures, or packages within the conveyance to carry out these duties.
When dealing with conveyances other than vessels or aircraft, they may use all lawful means to stop or prevent the escape of the conveyance, including firing upon it as a last resort.
Conveyance: Any conveyance, including vessels and aircraft, suspected of involvement in smuggling or carrying smuggled goods is subject to being stopped, searched, or compelled to land by customs authorities.
Owners or operators are legally required to stop immediately when signaled by authorized government vessels or aircraft, or face the risk of being chased or fired upon if they fail to comply.
Smuggling: This act forms the basis for the enforcement powers granted to customs officers to intervene against vehicles or vessels suspected of facilitating the illegal movement of goods.
Smuggled Goods: The transport of such goods within Bangladesh grants customs officers the legal authority to intercept and search any conveyance found to be carrying or intending to carry them.
Government: The government is authorized to designate specific authorities to signal vessels or aircraft to stop or land, and may employ government vessels or aircraft to enforce these directives through international signaling or the use of force.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to examine persons
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
165. Power to examine persons.- (1) The appropriate officer may, during the course of an inquiry in connection with the smuggling of any goods,-
(a) require any person to produce or deliver any document or thing to such officer,
(b) examine any person acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case.
(2) The appropriate officer shall exercise the powers in sub-section (1) only in relation to a person who is readily available or present before him and shall be subject to the same provisions as an officer-in-charge of a police-station is subject to under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), when investigating a offence.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer has the authority to conduct inquiries related to the smuggling of goods.
During such inquiries, the officer may require individuals to produce documents or objects and examine those familiar with the facts of the case.

The officer must exercise these examination powers only on persons present or readily available to them, operating under the same legal constraints as an officer-in-charge of a police station when investigating an offence.
Smuggling: The appropriate officer is empowered to initiate an inquiry whenever there is a connection to the smuggling of goods.
Person: Persons involved in a customs inquiry may be required to produce documents or things to the appropriate officer or be examined regarding the facts of the case.
These investigative powers are applicable only to individuals who are readily available or present before the appropriate officer.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: The procedures and legal standards governing an appropriate officer's investigation are subject to the same provisions as those applied to an officer-in-charge of a police station under this code.
Officer-in-charge of Police Station: The legal conduct and powers of the appropriate officer during an examination are benchmarked against the standards required of an officer-in-charge of a police station when performing investigations under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to summon persons to give evidence and produce documents or things
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
166. Power to summon persons to give evidence and produce documents or things.- (1) Any gazetted officer of customs shall have power to summon any person whose attendance he considers necessary either to give evidence or to produce a document or any other thing in any inquiry which such officer is making in connection with the smuggling of any goods.
(2) A summon to produce documents or other things may be for the production of certain specified documents or things or for the production of all documents or things of a certain description in the possession or under the control of the person summoned.
(3) All persons so summoned shall be bound to attend either in person or by an authorised agent, as such officer may direct; and all persons so summoned shall be bound to state the truth upon any subject respecting which they are examined or make statement and produce such documents and other things as may be required :
Provided that the exemption under section 132 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908), shall be applicable to any requisition for attendance under this section.
(4) Every such inquiry as aforesaid shall be deemed to be judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 and section 228 of the 1[Penal Code], (Act XLV of 1860).

Gazetted Customs Officer: A Gazetted Customs Officer is empowered to summon any person whose attendance is necessary to provide evidence or produce documents and items related to smuggling inquiries.
The officer has the authority to direct whether a summoned person must appear in person or through an authorized agent.
Smuggling Prevention: The power to summon persons and evidence is granted specifically for inquiries conducted by customs authorities in relation to the smuggling of goods.
Person: A person summoned by a customs officer is legally obligated to attend, state the truth during examination, and produce the requested documents or things.
Summoned persons have the right to claim exemptions from personal attendance as provided under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908.
Code of Civil Procedure 1908: The provisions regarding exemptions from personal appearance in court as established in the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 apply to summons issued under this Act.
Penal Code 1860: Inquiries conducted by a customs officer under this power are legally classified as judicial proceedings for the purposes of applying relevant sections of the Penal Code 1860 concerning false evidence and intentional insult or interruption.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Persons escaping may be afterwards arrested
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 167. Persons escaping may be afterwards arrested.- If any person liable to be arrested under this Act is not arrested at the time of committing the offence for which he is so liable, or after arrest makes his escape, he may at any time afterwards be arrested and dealt with in accordance with the provisions of sub-sections (3) to (7) section 161 as if he had been arrested at the time of committing such offence.

Person: Any person liable to be arrested for a customs offence may be apprehended after the time of the offence if they were not arrested initially or if they escaped from custody. Once subsequently arrested, the individual must be processed according to the established legal procedures as if they had been arrested at the time the offence was originally committed.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Seizure of things liable to confiscation
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
168. Seizure of things liable to confiscation.- (1) The appropriate officer may seize any goods liable to confiscation under this Act, and where it is not practicable to seize any such goods, he may serve on the owner of the goods or any person holding them in his possession or charge an order that he shall not remove, part with, or otherwise deal with the goods except with the previous permission of such officer.
(2) Where any goods are seized under sub-section (1) and no show cause notice in respect thereof is given under section 180 within two months of the seizure of the goods, the goods shall be returned to the person from whose possession they were seized:
Provided that the aforesaid period of two months may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, be extended by the 1[Commissioner of Customs] by a period not exceeding two months.
(3) The appropriate officer may seize any documents or things which in his opinion will be useful as evidence in any proceedings under this Act.
(4) The person from whose custody any documents are seized under sub-section (3) shall be entitled to make copies thereof or take extracts therefrom in the presence of an officer of customs.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer of customs is empowered to seize goods that are liable to confiscation under this Act.
When physical seizure is not practicable, the appropriate officer may issue a restrictive order preventing the owner or possessor from dealing with the goods without prior permission.
The appropriate officer is authorized to seize any documents or things deemed useful as evidence in legal proceedings conducted under this Act.
Seizure of Goods: Goods liable to confiscation may be seized by customs authorities, or if physical seizure is not possible, restricted through a formal order.
If a show cause notice is not issued within a specified timeframe following the seizure of goods, the goods must be returned to the person from whom they were seized.
The period for issuing a show cause notice after a seizure may be extended by the Commissioner of Customs for a limited duration, provided the reasons for the extension are recorded in writing.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to extend the period for issuing a show cause notice after the seizure of goods for an additional period, contingent upon recording the reasons in writing.
Documentary Evidence: Documents or things may be seized by an appropriate officer if they are considered useful as evidence for customs proceedings.
Persons from whose custody documents are seized retain the right to create copies or take extracts from those documents in the presence of a customs officer.
Person: A person in possession or charge of goods may be served with an order restricting the movement or disposal of those goods when physical seizure by customs is not feasible.
A person from whom goods were seized is entitled to their return if a formal show cause notice is not issued within the legally prescribed period.
A person from whom documents are seized for evidence is permitted to copy or extract information from them while supervised by a customs officer.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Things seized how dealt with
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
169. Things seized how dealt with.- (1) All things seized on the ground that they are liable to confiscation under this Act shall, without unnecessary delay, be delivered into the care of the officer of customs authorised to receive the same.
(2) If there be no such officer at hand, at hand, all such things shall be carried to and deposited at the custom-house nearest to the place of seizure.
(3) If there be no custom-house within a convenient distance, such things shall be deposited at the nearest place appointed by the 2[Commissioner of Customs] for the deposit of things so seized.
(4) If the 2[Commissioner of Customs] or any other officer of customs authorised by him in this behalf considers that any things is perishable or liable to rapid deterioration, he shall immediately cause it to be sold in accordance with the provisions of section 201 and have the proceeds kept in deposit pending adjudication of the case:
3[Provided that where practicable samples of such things with proper identification marks may be kept for the purpose of any legal proceeding or for any other purpose of this Act.]
(5) If on such adjudication the thing so sold is found not to have been liable to such confiscation, the entire sale proceeds, after necessary deduction of duties, taxes or dues as provided in section 201, shall be handed over to the owner.

Seizure of Goods: All goods seized on the grounds of being liable for confiscation under the Customs Act must be delivered promptly to an authorized officer of customs.
When no authorized officer is available, seized goods must be deposited at the nearest custom-house or at a place specifically designated by the Commissioner of Customs.
Perishable and Hazardous Goods: If seized items are perishable or subject to rapid deterioration, the Commissioner of Customs or an authorized officer must arrange for their immediate sale.
The proceeds from the sale of such goods are held in deposit pending the final adjudication of the customs case, although samples may be retained for legal proceedings.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is empowered to appoint specific locations for the storage of seized goods when a custom-house is not within a convenient distance.
The Commissioner of Customs or an authorized delegate has the authority to order the immediate sale of perishable seized items.
Confiscation and Disposal of Goods: Following the adjudication of a case, if seized goods that were sold are determined not to have been liable for confiscation, the net sale proceeds must be returned to the owner after accounting for all applicable duties and taxes.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Procedure in respect of things seized on suspicion by the police
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
170. Procedure in respect of things seized on suspicion by the police.- (1) When any things liable to confiscation under this Act are seized by any police-officer on suspicion that they had been stolen, he may carry them to any police-station or Court at which a complaint connected with the stealing or receiving of such things has been made, or any inquiry connected with such stealing or receiving of such things has been made, or an inquiry connected with such stealing or receiving is in progress, and there detain such things until the dismissal of such complaint or the conclusion of such inquiry or of any trial thence resulting.
(2) In every such case the police-officer seizing the things shall send written notice of their seizure and detention to the nearest custom-house and immediately after the dismissal of the complaint or the conclusion of the inquiry or trial he shall cause such things to be conveyed to and deposited at, the nearest custom-house, to be there proceeded against according to law.

Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal authority for the seizure and confiscation of items that are deemed liable for such action under its provisions.
Police Officer: A police officer who seizes items on suspicion of theft must transport them to the relevant police station or court where the investigation or legal proceedings are being held.
The officer must detain the seized items until the related criminal complaint or inquiry is concluded and subsequently notify the nearest custom-house of the seizure.
Police Station: A police station serves as a temporary detention point for goods seized on suspicion of theft until the relevant legal proceedings or inquiries are completed.
Customs House: The nearest custom-house must receive formal written notice regarding any items seized by the police that are liable to customs confiscation.
Upon the conclusion of police inquiries or criminal trials, the seized items must be deposited at the custom-house for subsequent legal proceedings under customs law.

processed_clauses.clause_title: When seizure or arrest is made, reason in writing including inventory to be given
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[171. When seizure or arrest is made, reason in writing including inventory to be given.- When anything is seized or any person is arrested under this Act, the officer or any other person making such seizure or arrest shall, at the time of making the seizure or arrest, inform in writing the person so arrested or the person from whose possession the things are seized of the grounds of such seizure or arrest; and shall, in the case of seizure of anything, also deliver to the person from whose possession they have been seized an inventory relating thereto;
Provided that where it is not practicable to deliver such inventory at the time of seizure, it shall be delivered within a period of seven working days from the date of the seizure.]

Customs Seizure and Evidence: When an officer or person makes a seizure or arrest under the Customs Act 1969, they are legally required to provide written notification detailing the specific grounds for the action to the affected individual.
In instances of seizure, the official must provide an inventory of the seized items to the person from whom they were taken.
If it is not feasible to provide the inventory immediately, the law requires it to be delivered within a set number of working days from the date of the seizure.
Person: A person who is arrested or from whom goods are seized under this Act has the right to be informed in writing of the reasons for the action taken against them.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to detain packages containing certain publications imported in [Bangladesh]
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
172. Power to detain packages containing certain publications imported in 2[Bangladesh].- (1) Any officer of customs duly authorised by the 3[Commissioner of Customs] or any other officer authorised by the 4[Government] in this behalf may detain any package, brought whether by land, air or sea into 2[Bangladesh] which he suspects to contain-
5[(a) any newspaper or book as defined in the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 (XXIII of 1973), or]
(b) any document, containing any treasonable or seditious matter, that is to say, any matter, the publication of which is punishable under section 123A or section 124A, as the case may be, of the 6[Penal Code] (Act XLV of 1860), and shall forward such package to such officer as the 4[Government] may appoint in this behalf.
(2) Any officer detaining a package under sub-section (1) shall, where practicable, forthwith send by post to the addressee or consignee of such package notice of the fact of such detention.
(3) The 4[Government] shall cause the contents of such package to be examined, and if it appears to the 4[Government] that the package contains any such newspaper, book or other document, as aforesaid, it may pass such order as to the disposal of the package and its contents as it may deem proper, and, if it does not so appear, shall release the package and its contents unless the same be otherwise liable to seizure under any law for the time being in force:
Provided that any person interested in any package detained under the provisions of this section, may, within two months of the date of such detention, apply to the 4[Government] for release of the same, and the 4[Government] shall consider such application and pass such order thereon as it may deem to be proper:
Provided further that, if such application is rejected, the applicant may, within two months of the date of the order rejecting the application, apply to the 1[High Court Division] for release of the package or its contents on the ground that the package or the contents do not contain any such newspaper, book or other document.
(4) No order passed or action taken under this section shall be called in question in any court save as provided in the second proviso to sub-section (3).
Explanation.- In this section "document" includes any writing, painting, engraving, drawing or photograph or other visible representation.

Officer of Customs: Officers duly authorized by the Commissioner of Customs or the Government are empowered to detain packages imported into Bangladesh that are suspected to contain prohibited publications or seditious materials.
An officer who detains a package must, where practicable, provide notification of the detention to the addressee or consignee.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is authorized to grant the power to specific officers to detain packages suspected of containing prohibited materials.
Government: The Government is empowered to appoint specific officers to receive detained packages for further examination.
The Government has the authority to examine the contents of detained packages and pass orders regarding their disposal or release.
The Government acts as the deciding authority for applications regarding the release of detained packages, with decisions being subject to review by the High Court Division under specific conditions.
Detained Goods: Packages containing prohibited newspapers, books, or documents are subject to detention and subsequent inspection by the Government.

Any person with an interest in a detained package may apply to the Government for its release within a specified timeframe, or subsequently appeal to the High Court Division if the application is rejected.
Printing Presses and Publications (Decla: This Act provides the definitions for newspapers and books that may be subject to detention if imported into Bangladesh.
Penal Code 1860: Packages containing documents with treasonable or seditious matter, as defined by specific sections of the Penal Code 1860, are liable for detention and examination.
High Court Division: The High Court Division serves as the appellate authority for individuals seeking the release of detained packages after their initial application to the Government has been rejected.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Procedure for disposal by [High Court Division] of applications for release of packages so detained
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 173. Procedure for disposal by 1[High Court Division] of applications for release of packages so detained.- Every application under the second proviso to sub-section (3) of section 172 shall be heard and determined, in the manner provided by sections 99D to 99F of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), by a special bench of the 1[High Court Division] constituted in the manner provided by section 99C of that Code.

High Court Division: The High Court Division is empowered to hear and determine applications for the release of detained packages.
The procedure for these hearings must follow the specific judicial framework established by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, involving a special bench constituted under the same code.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: This act provides the procedural framework for hearing and determining applications regarding detained packages, specifically referencing sections 99D to 99F for adjudication and section 99C for the constitution of the special bench.
Detained Goods: Applications concerning the release of detained packages are subject to specific judicial review procedures handled by the High Court Division.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to require production of order permitting clearance of goods imported or exported by land
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
174. Power to require production of order permitting clearance of goods imported or exported by land.- The appropriate officer may require any person in charge of any goods which such officer has reason to believe to have been imported, or to be about to be exported by land from, or to, any foreign territory to produce the order made under section 83, permitting inward clearance of the goods or the order passing the bill of export made under section 131 permitting export of the goods:
Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to any imported goods passing from a foreign frontier to any inland customs-station by a route prescribed under clause (c) of section 9:
Provided further that the Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, direct that the provisions of this section shall not apply to any particular area adjoining foreign territory in relation to goods of any specified description or value.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is authorized to demand the production of specific clearance orders from any person in charge of goods believed to be imported or exported by land.
Person in Charge: A person in charge of goods being imported or exported by land must produce the required clearance orders upon the request of an appropriate officer of customs.
Imported Goods: Imported goods passing from a foreign frontier to an inland customs station via a prescribed route are exempted from the requirement to produce clearance orders.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to exempt specific areas or goods of a certain description or value from these clearance production requirements.
Customs Clearance: The officer may demand the production of the order permitting inward clearance under section 83 or the order passing the bill of export under section 131.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to prevent making or transmission of certain signals or messages
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 175. Power to prevent making or transmission of certain signals or messages.- If an officer of customs or police or any member of the armed forces of 2[Bangladesh] has reasonable grounds for suspecting that any signal or message connected with smuggling or intention or designs of smuggling any goods into or out of 2[Bangladesh] is being or is about to be made or transmitted from any conveyance, house or place, he may board or enter such conveyance, house or place, and take such steps as are reasonably necessary to stop or prevent the making or transmission of the signal or message.

Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to board any conveyance or enter any house or place upon reasonable suspicion that signals or messages related to smuggling are being transmitted.
The officer may take all steps reasonably necessary to stop or prevent the making or transmission of such signals or messages.
Police Officer: A police officer is authorized to enter any place, house, or conveyance if they have reasonable grounds to suspect that messages or signals concerning smuggling are being transmitted.
The officer has the power to take necessary action to effectively stop or prevent the unauthorized transmission of such signals.
Smuggling Prevention: The law grants authority to intercept communications, signals, or messages when there is reasonable suspicion they are connected to the smuggling of goods.
Preventative powers extend to entering conveyances, houses, or locations to halt activities related to the planning or execution of smuggling.
Conveyance: Any conveyance is subject to entry and inspection by authorized officers if there is suspicion that it is being used to transmit signals or messages related to smuggling.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to station officers in certain factories
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 176. Power to station officers in certain factories.- An officer of customs not below the rank of an 3[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] may, if he so deems fit, station an officer of customs in any factory or building used for commercial purposes and situated within five miles of the frontier of 2[Bangladesh] with the object of ensuring that the factory or building is not used in any way for the unlawful or irregular importation or exportation of goods and the officer so stationed shall have the power to inspect at all reasonable times the records of the factory or business carried on in the building and such other powers as may be prescribed by rules.

Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer holds the authority to decide if it is necessary to station a customs official in specific factories or commercial buildings located near the national border.
Customs Officer: Customs officers may be stationed in factories or buildings near the border to prevent the unlawful or irregular importation or exportation of goods.
Stationed customs officers are empowered to inspect business records at reasonable times and exercise other duties as defined by the rules.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Restriction or the possession of goods in certain areas
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
177. Restriction or the possession of goods in certain areas.- (1) This section shall apply to such areas adjacent to the frontier of 1[Bangladesh] as may, from time to time, be notified by the Board in the official Gazette.
2[(2) In any area to which this section for the time being applies, no person shall have in his possession or control any such goods or class of goods in excess of such quantity or value as may from time to time be notified by the Government in the official Gazette, except under a permit granted by the Government in respect of the particular goods or class of goods, or by an officer authorised by the Government.]

Goods: The possession or control of specific goods or classes of goods within designated frontier areas is restricted.
Possession of such goods in excess of a notified quantity or value is prohibited unless authorized by a permit issued by the Government or an authorized officer.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to designate specific areas adjacent to the frontier where these restrictions on goods apply.
Government: The Government is empowered to notify the maximum quantity or value of specific goods that may be held within restricted frontier areas.
The Government or its authorized officers maintain the authority to issue permits allowing for the possession of restricted goods in excess of the defined limits.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Punishment of persons accompanying a person possessing goods liable to confiscation
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 178. Punishment of persons accompanying a person possessing goods liable to confiscation.- If any two or more persons in company o found together and they or any of them, have goods liable to confiscation under this Act, every such person having knowledge of this fact is guilty of an offence and punishable in accordance with the provisions of this Act as if goods were found on such person.

Customs Offence: It is considered an offence for individuals to accompany someone who is in possession of goods liable to confiscation, provided that they are aware of the presence of such goods.
Persons found together with someone possessing goods liable to confiscation are treated as if they were in personal possession of those goods and are subject to the same penalties under the law.
Confiscated Goods: These are goods identified under the Customs Act that are subject to seizure and forfeiture when found in the possession of persons acting in concert.
Customs Offence Penalties: This clause provides the legal basis for punishing individuals who knowingly accompany a person carrying goods liable to confiscation, applying penalties equivalent to those for actual possession of the goods.

Adjudication of Customs Cases: This clause establishes the jurisdiction and powers of various officers of customs to adjudicate cases involving the confiscation of goods and the imposition of penalties. The legal authority of each officer is determined based on the monetary value of the goods involved in the case.
The National Board of Revenue holds the authority to modify the jurisdiction and powers of any customs officer or class of officers through a notification in the official Gazette.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is authorized to adjudicate cases involving the confiscation of goods or imposition of penalties where the value of the goods exceeds a specific threshold defined in the Act.
The Commissioner of Customs (Bond) is empowered to adjudicate cases involving the confiscation of goods or imposition of penalties where the value of the goods exceeds a specific monetary threshold.
Director General: The Director General (Duty Exemption and Drawback) is authorized to perform adjudications for cases involving the confiscation of goods or imposition of penalties where the value exceeds a specific statutory limit.
Additional Commissioner of Customs: The Additional Commissioner of Customs is granted the power to adjudicate customs cases where the value of the goods does not exceed a designated monetary threshold.
Joint Commissioner of Customs: The Joint Commissioner of Customs is empowered to adjudicate cases concerning the confiscation of goods or imposition of penalties up to a specified value limit.
Deputy Commissioner of Customs: The Deputy Commissioner of Customs is authorized to adjudicate cases involving the confiscation of goods or imposition of penalties up to a defined monetary value threshold.
They are also empowered to adjudicate cases relating to manifest clearance in custom-houses and customs-stations involving the imposition of penalties, regardless of the value of the goods.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: The Assistant Commissioner of Customs is authorized to adjudicate cases involving the confiscation of goods or imposition of penalties up to a specific monetary value.
They are also empowered to adjudicate cases relating to manifest clearance at custom-houses and customs-stations concerning the imposition of penalties, without any limit on the value of goods.
Revenue Officer: The Revenue Officer is empowered to adjudicate cases involving the confiscation of goods or imposition of penalties where the value of the goods does not exceed a specified statutory limit.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is empowered to fix jurisdiction and confer adjudication powers upon any officers of customs for cases not covered by the statutory table. Additionally, it may extend or reduce the powers of any customs officer through a notification in the official Gazette.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Issue of show-cause notice before confiscation of goods or imposition of penalty

Confiscation of Goods: This clause requires that a show-cause notice must be issued to the owner of the goods before any order for their confiscation is passed under the Customs Act 1969.
The requirement for a show-cause notice does not apply if the owner of the goods admits the offence in writing and consents to the order without the issuance of such a notice.
Customs Penalty: Before any penalty is imposed on a person under the Customs Act 1969, they must be formally notified in writing of the grounds for the proposed action.
The person facing a penalty must be given a reasonable opportunity to make a written representation and to be heard personally or through an authorized representative.
The requirement to issue a show-cause notice prior to imposing a penalty is waived if the person concerned admits the offence in writing and requests that the order be passed without such notice.
Show Cause Notice: A show-cause notice acts as a mandatory procedural safeguard that informs an individual of the grounds for a proposed confiscation or penalty action.
The notice provides the recipient with a reasonable opportunity to respond in writing and to be heard, ensuring due process before any final administrative order is issued.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is responsible for specifying the reasonable time frame within which the person affected by a proposed customs action must submit their written representation.
Agent: The person against whom a customs action is proposed has the legal right to be heard personally or through a duly authorized agent during the show-cause process.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Option to pay fine in lieu of confiscated goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
181. Option to pay fine in lieu of confiscated goods.- 2[(1)] Whenever an order for the confiscation of goods is passed under this Act, the officer passing the order may give the owner of the goods an option to pay in lieu of the confiscation of the goods such fine as the officer thinks fit.
Explanation.- Any fine in lieu of confiscation of goods imposed under this section shall be in addition to any duty and charges payable in respect of such goods, and of any penalty that might have been imposed in addition to the confiscation of goods.
3[(2) Nothing in this section shall apply to any goods the import of which is prohibited by or under any law.]

Confiscation and Disposal of Goods: When an order of confiscation is passed under the Customs Act, the authorized officer has the discretionary power to provide the owner of the goods the option to pay a fine in lieu of the physical confiscation of those goods.
The fine imposed as an alternative to confiscation is independent of and payable in addition to any customs duty, charges, or other penalties applicable to the goods.
Prohibited Goods: The option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation is strictly prohibited for any goods whose import is restricted or banned under the law.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Vesting of confiscated property in the [Government]
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 182. Vesting of confiscated property in the 4[Government].- When any goods are confiscated under this Act they shall forthwith vest in the 4[Government], and the officer who orders confiscation shall take and hold possession of the confiscated goods.

Government: Confiscated goods vest automatically and immediately in the Government upon the issuance of a confiscation order under the Act.
Confiscated Goods: Once goods are subject to an order of confiscation, they legally belong to the Government.
The customs officer who issues the confiscation order is responsible for taking and maintaining physical possession of the confiscated items.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal authority for the confiscation of goods and establishes the procedures for the transfer of ownership to the Government.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Levy of penalty for departure without authority or failure to bring-to
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
183. Levy of penalty for departure without authority or failure to bring-to.- (1) If any conveyance actually departs without a port clearance or permission in writing or, in the case of a vessel, after having failed to bring-to when required at any station appointed under section 14, the penalty to which the person-in-charge of such conveyance is liable may be adjudged by the appropriate officer of any customs-station, to which such conveyance proceeds, or in which it for the time being is.
(2) A certificate in respect of such departure or failure to bring-to when required, purporting to be signed by the appropriate officer of the customs-station from which the conveyance is stated to have so departed, shall be prima facie proof of the fact so stated.

Conveyance: A conveyance that departs without required port clearance or written permission, or a vessel that fails to bring-to as instructed at an appointed station, is subject to specific penalty provisions.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer at any customs station where the conveyance is found or proceeds has the authority to adjudge penalties against the person in charge for unauthorized departure or failure to bring-to.
A signed certificate issued by an officer at the customs station of departure serves as evidence regarding the occurrence of the unauthorized departure or failure to comply with instructions.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance is held liable for penalties if the conveyance departs without proper authorization or fails to follow lawful instructions to bring-to at a station.
Burden of Proof: A certificate issued by the appropriate customs officer confirming a violation acts as evidence for the facts stated therein regarding the conveyance's departure or failure to bring-to.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to try summarily
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 184. Power to try summarily.- Any Magistrate for the time being empowered to try in a summary way the offences specified in sub-section (1) of section 260 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 ( Act V of 1898) may , if he thinks fit, on application in this behalf by the prosecution, try an offence under this Act except when the value of goods involved in such offences exceeds 1[Taka five thousand] in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 262 and sections 263, 264 and 265 of the Code.

Magistrate: A Magistrate empowered to conduct summary trials under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 may try offences committed under the Customs Act 1969.
The power to try these offences summarily is subject to a monetary threshold concerning the value of the goods involved in the offence and requires an application from the prosecution.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: The Code provides the procedural framework for the summary trial of specified offences, which is applied to certain customs offences under the Customs Act 1969.
The summary trial of customs offences must be conducted in accordance with specific sections of this Code.
Customs Offence Summary Trial: Summary trials for customs offences are permissible for cases where the value of the goods involved does not exceed a specified monetary limit.
The trial process is initiated by an application from the prosecution and follows the procedures laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Goods: The authority of a Magistrate to conduct a summary trial for a customs offence is limited by the value of the goods involved in that specific offence.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Special power for Magistrates
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 185. Special power for Magistrates.- Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 ( Act V of 1898 ) and subject to the other provisions of this Act, any Magistrate of the first class specially empowered by the 2[Government] in this behalf may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding 3[five years] and of fine exceeding 4[ten thousand taka] for an offence under this Act.

Magistrate: A Magistrate of the first class who is specially empowered by the Government is granted the authority to impose sentences of imprisonment and fines exceeding statutory limits for offences committed under the Customs Act 1969.
This special power granted to the Magistrate operates notwithstanding the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, but remains subject to other provisions of the Customs Act 1969.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: The sentencing powers granted to a specially empowered Magistrate under the Customs Act 1969 are exercised notwithstanding the general limitations prescribed in this Code.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal framework for the prosecution of customs offences and empowers the Government to designate Magistrates with enhanced sentencing authority.
The exercise of special sentencing powers by a Magistrate remains subject to the provisions contained within this Act.
Government: The Government is empowered to specially authorize a Magistrate of the first class to exercise enhanced sentencing powers for offences committed under the Customs Act 1969.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Detention of goods pending payment of fine or penalty
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
186. Detention of goods pending payment of fine or penalty.- (1) When any fine or penalty has been imposed, or while imposition of any fine or penalty is under consideration, in respect of any goods, such goods shall not be remove by the owner until such fine or penalty has been paid.
(2) When any fine or penalty has been imposed in respect of any goods, the appropriate officer may detain any other goods belonging to the same owner pending payment of such fine or penalty.

Goods: Where a fine or penalty has been imposed or is under consideration in respect of specific goods, those goods may not be removed by the owner until the payment of the fine or penalty is satisfied.
Appropriate officers of customs are authorized to detain other goods belonging to the same owner as security for the payment of an outstanding fine or penalty imposed on any goods.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to detain goods belonging to an owner who has an unpaid fine or penalty in order to ensure the recovery of such amounts.
Customs Penalty: The law requires the satisfaction of fines or penalties as a condition for the release of goods involved in an offence and provides for the detention of other assets of the owner until such liabilities are discharged.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Burden of proof as to lawful authority, etc.
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 187. Burden of proof as to lawful authority, etc.- (1) When any person is alleged to have committed an offence under this Act and any question arises whether he did any act or was in possession of anything with lawful authority or under a permit, licence or other document prescribed by or under any law for the time being in force, the burden of proving that he had such authority, permit, licence or other document shall lie on him.

Burden of Proof: In cases involving alleged customs offences where the legality of an act or the possession of items is questioned, the onus is on the accused person to demonstrate that they held the required lawful authority, permit, license, or documentation.
Customs Offence: This clause applies to any person alleged to have committed an offence under the Customs Act 1969 where the legitimacy of their actions or possession of goods is in dispute.
Person: The person accused of a customs offence bears the legal obligation to prove they acted or possessed items under a valid permit, license, or other legal authority prescribed by the law.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Presumption as to documents in certain cases

Customs Documents: These are documents produced under the Customs Act 1969 or seized from the custody or control of any person that are subsequently tendered by the prosecution as evidence.
The court shall presume the contents of such documents to be true and verify signatures or handwriting unless the contrary is proven.
These documents are admissible as evidence even if they are not duly stamped, provided they meet other requirements for admissibility.
Magistrate: In legal proceedings involving evidence seized or produced under the Customs Act 1969, the Magistrate is empowered to make specific evidentiary presumptions regarding the authenticity and truth of such documents.
Customs Seizure and Evidence: The law establishes a framework for the treatment of evidence in customs cases, where documents obtained through production or seizure are subject to statutory presumptions in favor of the prosecution during judicial proceedings.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Notice of conviction to be displayed
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
189. Notice of conviction to be displayed.- (1) Upon the conviction of any person for the offence of smuggling, the 1[Government] may require him to exhibit in or outside, or both in and outside, his place of business, if any notices of such number, size and lettering, and placed in such positions and containing such particulars relating to the conviction as it may determine, and to keep them so exhibited continuously for a period not less than three months from the date of conviction; and if he fails to comply fully with the requirement he shall be deemed to have committed a further offence under this Act of the nature of the original offence for which he was convicted.
(2) If any person so convicted refuses or fails to comply fully with any such requirement, any officer authorised in that behalf by an order of the 1[Government] in writing may, without prejudice to any proceedings which may be brought in respect of any such refusal or failure, affix the notices in or outside, or both in or outside, the place of business of such person in accordance with the requirement of the 1[Government] in pursuance of sub-section (1).
(3) If, in any case the 1[Government] is satisfied that the exhibition of notices in accordance with the requirements of the provisions of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) will not effectively bring the conviction to the notice of persons dealing with the convicted person, the 1[Government] may, in lieu of, or in addition to any such requirement, require the convicted person to exhibit for such period, not being a period less than three months, on such stationery used in his business as may be specified in the requirement; and, if he fails to comply fully with the requirement, he shall be deemed to have committed a further offence under this Act of the nature of the original offence for which he was convicted.

Smuggling: A person convicted of smuggling may be legally required to publicly display notices of their conviction at their place of business for a mandatory minimum period.
Failure to comply with the display requirements for conviction notices constitutes a further offence of the same nature as the original smuggling offence.
Government: The Government is empowered to determine the specifications of conviction notices, including their size, lettering, number, and placement.

The Government may authorize officers to enter and affix such notices if the convicted person fails to comply with the requirement, and it may also mandate that notices be printed on business stationery if public display is deemed ineffective.
Person: A person convicted of a smuggling offence faces additional legal obligations, including the mandated display of their conviction to the public or their business contacts.
Failure to adhere to these display mandates results in the person being deemed to have committed a fresh offence equivalent to the original smuggling conviction.
Officer of Customs: An officer authorized by the Government may, in the event of a convicted person's refusal or failure, enter the person's place of business to affix the required conviction notices on their behalf.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to publish conviction
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 190. Power to publish conviction.- If the 1[Government] is satisfied that it is necessary so to do, the conviction and the particulars relating to the conviction of any person for the offence of smuggling may be published in the official Gazette.
