Government: The Government is empowered to publish the details of a person's conviction for smuggling in the official Gazette when it deems such publication necessary.
Smuggling Offences: The Government has the authority to release information regarding the conviction and specific particulars of any person found guilty of smuggling through the official Gazette.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Imprisonment may be of either description
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 191. Imprisonment may be of either description.- Imprisonment for any offence under this Act may, in the discretion of the Magistrate, be either simple or rigorous.

Customs Offence Penalties: The punishment for any offence committed under the Customs Act 1969 includes the possibility of imprisonment.
The Magistrate is granted the discretion to determine whether the term of imprisonment shall be served as simple or rigorous confinement.
Magistrate: The Magistrate is authorized to exercise judicial discretion in deciding the nature of imprisonment, specifically whether it is to be simple or rigorous, for any customs-related offence.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Duty of certain person to give information
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
192. Duty of certain person to give information.- (1) Any person who comes to know of the commission of any offence under this Act, or any attempt or likely attempt to commit any such offence, shall, as soon as my be, give information thereof in writing to the officer-in-charge of the nearest custom-house or customs-station, or if there is no such custom-house or customs-station, to the officer-in-charge of the nearest police-station.
(2) The officer-in-charge of a police-station who receives any information mentioned in sub-section (1) shall as soon as possible communicate it to the officer-in-charge of the nearest customs-house or customs-station.

Customs Offence Reporting Obligation: Any person who becomes aware of the commission or likely commission of a customs offence is required to provide written information to the nearest customs-house, customs-station, or police-station as soon as possible.
Customs House: This entity acts as a receiving point for mandatory reports concerning the commission of offences under the Customs Act.
Customs Station: This entity acts as a receiving point for mandatory reports concerning the commission of offences under the Customs Act.
Police Station: The officer-in-charge of a police station is designated as a receiving authority for customs offence information when a customs facility is not available. Upon receipt of such information, the officer-in-charge is mandated to relay it to the nearest customs facility.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: Chapter XVIII A
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
Chapter XVIII A
Alternative Dispute Resolution

Alternative Dispute Resolution: This chapter establishes a mechanism for Alternative Dispute Resolution within the customs legal framework to provide an alternative to traditional litigation processes.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Alternative Dispute Resolution
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 192 A. Alternative Dispute Resolution.- Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act regarding adjudication or disposal of any dispute as defined and mentioned in section 192C which may or may not be pending with concerned customs authority or customs and VAT appellate authorities, any importer or exporter or Pre-shipment Inspection Agency concerned in such disputes may apply to the concerned authorities for the resolution of the dispute through the Alternative Dispute Resolution (hereinafter ADR) process in the manner as laid down in the following sections and rules made hereunder and resort to ADR must precede the completion of the procedures under adjudication or appeal provisions of the Act.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: This mechanism provides a formal process for importers, exporters, and pre-shipment inspection agencies to resolve disputes with customs authorities.
Resorting to this process is a mandatory step that must occur before finalizing procedures under existing adjudication or appeal provisions defined in the Act.
Customs Act 1969: The Act establishes the legal framework for resolving disputes, including the initiation of the Alternative Dispute Resolution process.
It mandates that disputes defined under its provisions may be addressed through this alternative process notwithstanding existing adjudication or appeal procedures.
Importer: An importer involved in a dispute with customs authorities is eligible to apply for the resolution of their case through the Alternative Dispute Resolution process.
Exporter: An exporter involved in a dispute with customs authorities is eligible to apply for the resolution of their case through the Alternative Dispute Resolution process.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: Pre-shipment inspection agencies are entitled to utilize the Alternative Dispute Resolution process to settle disputes related to their activities.
Customs Authority: Customs authorities serve as the body to which applications for Alternative Dispute Resolution must be submitted for pending or non-pending disputes.
Customs and Value Added Tax Appellate Au: Disputes pending or related to these appellate authorities may be diverted to the Alternative Dispute Resolution process in accordance with the Act.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Commencement
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 192 B. Commencement.-The ADR process as mentioned in this chapter shall come into force on such date and in such custom house or Customs-station or Commissionerate as the Board may determined by notification in the official Gazette.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: The process for alternative dispute resolution is established to come into force at designated locations on a date determined by the National Board of Revenue.
Customs House: The Board may specify which custom houses shall implement the alternative dispute resolution process through an official notification.
Customs Station: The Board is empowered to determine by notification in the official Gazette the specific customs-stations where the alternative dispute resolution process will become operational.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to trigger the commencement of the alternative dispute resolution process at identified locations.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Definition and Scope of Disputes for ADR

Alternative Dispute Resolution: This mechanism is established to resolve disputes regarding customs levy, assessment, classification, collection, refund of duties, and the imposition of fines or penalties.
It provides a structured process for handling disagreements involving customs assessment and valuation that are pending before customs authorities, appellate authorities, or courts of law.
Customs Authority: These are the administrative bodies responsible for handling customs-related cases, including those subject to Alternative Dispute Resolution.
Customs Valuation: Disputes concerning the determination of value for assessment purposes fall under the scope of Alternative Dispute Resolution, subject to the relevant subsections of the Customs Act.
Bill of Entry: Disputes arising from the submission of this document or related Demand Notices and Show Cause Notices are eligible for Alternative Dispute Resolution, provided they do not involve excluded criminal or fraudulent categories.
Bill of Export: Disputes arising from the submission of this document or related Demand Notices and Show Cause Notices are eligible for Alternative Dispute Resolution, provided they do not involve excluded criminal or fraudulent categories.
Show Cause Notice: This instrument is recognized as a basis for disputes eligible for Alternative Dispute Resolution when issued in relation to import or export declarations.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: Pending disputes related to penalties imposed on these agencies are eligible for consideration under Alternative Dispute Resolution.
Prohibited Goods: Disputes involving the seizure and confiscation of these items are explicitly excluded from the scope of Alternative Dispute Resolution.
Smuggled Goods: Disputes involving the seizure and confiscation of these items are explicitly excluded from the scope of Alternative Dispute Resolution.
Bonded Warehouse: Disputes arising from violations of licensing or bond-related conditions are excluded from the scope of Alternative Dispute Resolution.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Type of ADR Mechanism and Duties of the Parties Concerned
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
192D. Type of ADR Mechanism and Duties of the Parties Concerned. - (1) ADR mechanism provided in this chapter is based on facilitation and a facilitator, appointed as per provisions of this chapter will act as a neutral between the disputing parties.
(2) For ADR under this chapter the selection or appointment, fees, duties and responsibilities of the facilitator will be as provided in the rules made for this purpose.
(3) The duties and responsibilities of the applicant importer or exporter [or Pre-shipment Inspection Agency] for ADR will be as provided in the rules.
(4) Selection of officer for representing customs authorities in the ADR negotiation and his duties and responsibilities will be as provided in the rules.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: The alternative dispute resolution mechanism is founded on the principle of facilitation and utilizes a neutral facilitator appointed according to the provisions of this chapter.
The appointment, fees, duties, and responsibilities of the facilitator in this process are to be determined by the relevant rules.
Importer: The duties and responsibilities of an applicant importer participating in the alternative dispute resolution process are governed by the applicable rules.
Exporter: The duties and responsibilities of an applicant exporter participating in the alternative dispute resolution process are governed by the applicable rules.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: The duties and responsibilities of a pre-shipment inspection agency when participating in the alternative dispute resolution process are governed by the applicable rules.
Customs Officer: The selection of a customs officer to represent the customs authorities in alternative dispute resolution negotiations, as well as their associated duties and responsibilities, shall be defined by the rules.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Application for ADR
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
192 E. Application for ADR.- For seeking Alternative Resolution of a dispute, referred to in section 192C, the concerned importer, or exporter [or Pre-shipment Inspection Agency], as the case may be, shall apply to the following authorities:
(a) for a dispute which was created and not already been adjudicated or settled before the commencement of the ADR System, the application is to be submitted in such form and manner as may be prescribed in the rules, to the concerned Customs Commissioner or Adjudicating officer or Appellate authorities, as the case may be;
(b) for a dispute which arises after the commencement of the ADR System, the application is to be made before seeking or trying for settlement of the said dispute under sections 179, 193 or 196 as the case may be, of this Act, to the concerned customs commissioner or Adjudicating officer, as the case may be, in the manner prescribed in the rules, within ten working days from the date of issue of the concerned show cause notice or assessment order, or demand notice, as the case may be.
(c) for an application on a matter suitable for ADR which is pending before the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, the concerned petitioner, if he so desires, may apply to the concerned Customs Commissioner for Alternative Resolution, after obtaining permission from the said court, and upon granting of such permission by the court the matter shall remain in abeyance for the duration of the ADR process:
Provided that, if the court disposes any such Writ Petition with directions to any of the above authorities to settle the matter through ADR, therefore the authority shall settle the case accordingly, if not otherwise barred by law.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: This clause provides the framework for applying for Alternative Dispute Resolution regarding customs disputes. It establishes specific requirements for parties to seek resolution before, during, or in relation to pending legal proceedings.
Importer: Importers are authorized to apply for Alternative Dispute Resolution to settle disputes under the procedures outlined in this section.
Exporter: Exporters are authorized to apply for Alternative Dispute Resolution to settle disputes under the procedures outlined in this section.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: Pre-shipment Inspection Agencies are authorized to apply for Alternative Dispute Resolution to settle disputes under the procedures outlined in this section.
Customs Act 1969: This section establishes the procedural rules for Alternative Dispute Resolution and references specific sections of the Act governing dispute adjudication and settlement.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is one of the designated authorities to whom an application for Alternative Dispute Resolution must be submitted.
Show Cause Notice: For disputes arising after the commencement of the Alternative Dispute Resolution system, an application must be filed within a specified timeframe following the issuance of a show cause notice, assessment order, or demand notice.
Rules: The application for Alternative Dispute Resolution must be submitted in the form and manner prescribed by the rules.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Processing and Disposal of Applications for ADR
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 192 F. Processing and Disposal of Applications for ADR.- Applications received from the aggrieved or disputant importer or exporter [or Pre-shipment Inspection Agency] for ADR within this chapter, is to be processed and disposed of, according to the rules.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: The application and disposal process for Alternative Dispute Resolution is governed by the established rules.
Aggrieved parties, including importers, exporters, and Pre-shipment Inspection Agencies, are eligible to submit applications for this process.
Importer: An importer may submit an application for Alternative Dispute Resolution if they are aggrieved or involved in a dispute.
Exporter: An exporter may submit an application for Alternative Dispute Resolution if they are aggrieved or involved in a dispute.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: A Pre-shipment Inspection Agency has the standing to submit an application for Alternative Dispute Resolution if they are an aggrieved party in a dispute.
Rules: The processing and disposal of applications for Alternative Dispute Resolution must be conducted in accordance with the relevant rules.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Duration of Negotiation and Resolution
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
192 G. Duration of Negotiation and Resolution.- (1)Whether pending or new dispute if the application submitted for ADR relates to the same Customs House or Station, all formalities mentioned in this chapter including the negotiation and agreement or disagreement or resolution, as the case may be, of the dispute, are to be completed in a period of maximum thirty working days from the date of submission of the application.
(2) For a pending dispute for which application is submitted to the Commissioner Appeal or Customs and VAT Appellate Tribunal or any Court, the duration for the above purposes will be sixty working days from the date of submission of the application.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: The process of dispute resolution through application must be completed within a specified timeframe of working days from the date the application is submitted.
For disputes originating at the same Custom House or Station, a maximum duration of thirty working days is allotted for completing all formalities including negotiation, agreement, or resolution.

For disputes that are already pending before the Commissioner (Appeals), the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, or a Civil Court, an extended duration of sixty working days is provided for completing the resolution process.
Customs House: When an application for dispute resolution relates to a specific Custom House or Station, the time limits for completing the negotiation and resolution process are strictly enforced.
Commissioner (Appeals): If a dispute is pending before this authority, a longer period of sixty working days is granted for the resolution process to be completed following the submission of an application.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: For disputes pending before this tribunal, the legal framework provides a sixty-day working period for the resolution process upon the submission of an application.
Civil Court: In cases where a dispute is pending before a Civil Court, the duration for completing the Alternative Dispute Resolution process is set at sixty working days from the application submission date.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Decision of the ADR
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
192H. Decision of the ADR.- (1) A dispute may be resolved by an [agreement, including commitment to pay the duty and taxes or refund the same, as the case may be, in the agreed time limit], and may be concluded either wholly or in part where both the parties to the dispute accept the points for determination of the facts or laws applicable to the facts in the dispute, and agree on a settlement.
(2) Where an agreement is concluded, either wholly or in part, between the applicant importer or exporter [or Pre-shipment Inspection Agency] and the customs commissioner's representative, the facilitator shall record, in writing, the details of the agreement in the manner as prescribed by rules and shall communicate the same to the applicant, the concerned commissioner and the Board, within seven working days of the conclusion of the thirty or sixty days period, as the case may be.
(3) The recording of every such agreement shall provide for the terms of the agreement including any duty and tax payable or subject to refund, and such other matters as the facilitator may think fit to make the agreement effective.
(4) The agreement shall be signed by the applicant importer or exporter, commissioners representative and the facilitator.
(5) The agreement shall be void if it is subsequently found that it has been concluded by fraud or misrepresentation of facts.
(6) Where no agreement, whether wholly or in part, is reached, the facilitator shall communicate about such unsuccessful dispute resolution in writing to the applicant, the concerned commissioner and the Board within such period and in such manner as may be prescribed by rules.
(7) Upon an agreement being reached and communicated as provided herein, the usual process of recovery of dues, if any, payable to the Government or refund of money to the importer or exporter [or Pre-shipment Inspection Agency] or any other necessary action shall proceed in accordance with the normally applicable provisions of the applicable laws.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: This mechanism allows for the resolution of customs disputes through an agreement between parties, which may involve commitments to pay or refund duties and taxes within a specified timeframe.

An agreement can be reached in whole or in part based on the mutual acceptance of facts or legal interpretations, and must be documented and signed by the facilitator, the applicant, and the customs representative.
The agreement becomes void if it is later proven that it was reached through fraud or misrepresentation of facts.
If an agreement is reached, the subsequent recovery of dues or processing of refunds must follow the standard legal procedures provided under applicable laws.
Importer: An applicant importer may enter into a dispute resolution agreement with the customs commissioner's representative to settle tax or duty disputes.
Exporter: An applicant exporter is authorized to participate in the alternative dispute resolution process to reach a settlement on customs matters.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: Pre-shipment Inspection Agencies are recognized as parties that may participate in the alternative dispute resolution process alongside customs authorities.
National Board of Revenue: The Board must be formally communicated with in writing by the facilitator regarding the outcome of any dispute resolution attempt, whether successful or unsuccessful.
Commissioner of Customs: The concerned commissioner receives official communication from the facilitator regarding the conclusion of a dispute resolution agreement or the notification of an unsuccessful resolution.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Effects of Agreement or Resolution
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
192 I. Effects of Agreement or Resolution .- (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of this Act where an agreement is concluded for ADR under this chapter, it shall be binding for both the parties and cannot be challenged in any appellate forum or court either by the applicant or by the customs authorities.
(2) Every order of agreement, passed under this chapter shall be conclusive as to the matters stated therein and no matter covered by such order shall, save as otherwise provided in this chapter, be reopened in any proceeding under this Act or under any other law for the time being in force.
(3) If the dues, payable to either party as per agreement, are not paid and if the same including any penalty or interest for default in making payment of such sum, if not paid within one year, such sum may either be recovered or refunded with annually 10 percent interest, or as sums due to the Government under section 202 or the applicant under section 33 of this Act.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: Once an agreement is reached under this mechanism, it becomes legally binding on both the applicant and the customs authorities.

An agreement reached through this process cannot be challenged in any court or appellate forum, and matters covered by the agreement are considered conclusive and cannot be reopened in subsequent legal proceedings.
Duty Payment: If dues resulting from an agreement are not paid, they may be recovered or refunded with an annual interest rate, and such sums are treated as amounts due to the Government or the applicant under the relevant provisions of the Customs Act 1969.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the overarching legal framework for Alternative Dispute Resolution and establishes the procedures for recovering or refunding payments and interest due under such agreements.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Limitation for Appeal where Agreement is not concluded
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
192 J. Limitation for Appeal where Agreement is not concluded.- (1) Notwithstanding any thing contained in any other provisions of this Act, where an agreement is not concluded fully or in part, the concerned importer or exporter [or Pre-shipment Inspection Agency] may, after completion of adjudication process, if pending, prefer an appeal to the respective appellate authorities on the unresolved issue.
(2) Where a dispute under appeal, an application for ADR is made but agreement could not have been concluded within the period mentioned in section 192G or negotiation ended in disagreement, the ADR process shall automatically stand terminated and the original appeal shall be deemed to have been revived before the concerned appellate authority including any court from the day immediately after the date the ADR process stands terminated and provisions contained in respective sections of the respective law shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly.
(3) In computing the period of limitations for filing appeal, the time elapsed between the filing of the application and the communication of the decision or order of the ADR by the facilitators to all the parties shall be excluded.

Importer: In cases where an agreement is not reached during an alternative dispute resolution process, the importer is permitted to pursue an appeal before the relevant appellate authorities regarding unresolved issues once any pending adjudication process is completed.
Exporter: If an agreement is not concluded in full or in part, the exporter may prefer an appeal to the designated appellate authority for unresolved issues, following the conclusion of any pending adjudication process.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: The agency is entitled to pursue an appeal to the relevant appellate authorities on unresolved issues if a dispute remains after the conclusion of the adjudication process and failure to reach an agreement.
Alternative Dispute Resolution: If a dispute fails to reach a conclusion within the prescribed timeframe or ends in disagreement, the process is automatically terminated, reviving any original pending appeal.
Limitation of Legal Actions: When calculating the period allowed for filing an appeal, the time spent from the application for alternative dispute resolution until the communication of the final decision or order by the facilitators shall be excluded.
Adjudication of Customs Cases: The process of adjudication serves as a prerequisite that must be completed before an importer, exporter, or inspection agency can proceed with an appeal in instances where alternative dispute resolution has failed to resolve the matter.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Reservation of Rights
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 192 K. Reservation of Rights.- No person shall be issued a written order or notice, to attend the court as a witness to give evidence and no person shall be involved in the ADR proceedings in whatever capacity to compel disclosure of any representation made or document tendered in the course of the proceedings or the facilitator of the ADR proceedings to compel disclosure of any representation made or document tendered in the course of proceedings.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: No person involved in the proceedings shall be compelled to disclose any representations made or documents tendered during the process, and this protection extends to the facilitator of the proceedings.
The confidentiality of representations and documents submitted during the proceedings is preserved by prohibiting the compulsion of testimony or disclosure from those involved in any capacity.
Documentary Evidence: Documents tendered during the course of Alternative Dispute Resolution proceedings are protected from compulsory disclosure in court or other legal forums.
Person: No person shall be served a notice or order to testify as a witness regarding representations or documents related to Alternative Dispute Resolution proceedings.
Individuals involved in the proceedings, including facilitators, are protected from being compelled to disclose confidential information presented during the process.
Civil Court: Persons are exempt from being issued orders or notices to attend court as witnesses to reveal information or documents originating from Alternative Dispute Resolution proceedings.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER XIX
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER XIX
APPEALS AND REVISION

Customs Appeals and Applications: This chapter establishes the legal framework and procedures for filing appeals and seeking revisions regarding customs decisions and orders.
It provides the mechanisms for taxpayers or relevant parties to challenge rulings made by customs authorities before higher legal or administrative bodies.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Appeals to Commissioner (Appeal)
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[193. Appeals to Commissioner (Appeal).- (1) Any person aggrieved by any decision or order passed under this Act, not being a decision or order passed under section 82 or section 98, by an officer of customs lower in rank than a Commissioner of Customs, may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeal) within three months from the date of communication to him of such decision or order:
Provided that the Commissioner (Appeal) may, if he is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient causes from presenting the appeal within the aforesaid period of three months, allow it to be presented within a further period of two months.
(2) Every appeal under this section, shall be in such form and shall be verified in such manner as may be specified by rules made in this behalf.]

Person: Any person who is aggrieved by a customs decision or order may lodge an appeal against that decision, provided the order was not made under specific excluded sections of the Customs Act 1969.
Commissioner (Appeals): The Commissioner (Appeals) acts as the authority to hear appeals against decisions made by customs officers ranked lower than a Commissioner of Customs.

The Commissioner (Appeals) has the discretion to condone a delay in filing an appeal if the appellant provides sufficient evidence for why the appeal could not be filed within the standard statutory timeframe.
Customs Decision: Appeals may be filed against customs decisions or orders, with the exception of those specifically excluded by the Act.
Rules: The form and verification procedures for filing an appeal must comply with the requirements specified under the relevant rules.
Customs Act 1969: The Act establishes the appellate mechanism for addressing grievances arising from customs orders, excluding decisions issued under specific sections related to particular customs procedures.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Procedure in appeal
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
2[3[193A. Procedure in appeal.- (1) The Commissioner (Appeal) shall give an opportunity to the appellant to be heard if he so desires.
(2) The Commissioner (Appeal) may, at the hearing of an appeal, allow the appellant to go into any ground of appeal not specified in the grounds of appeal, if the Commissioner (Appeal) is satisfied that the omission of that ground from the grounds of appeal was not wilful or unreasonable.
(3) The Commissioner (Appeal) may, after making such further inquiry as may be necessary, pass such order as he thinks fit conforming, modifying or annulling the decision or order appealed against:
Provided that an order enhancing any penalty or fine in lieu of confiscation or confiscating goods of grater value or reducing the amount of refund shall not be passed unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed order:
Provided further that where the Commissioner (Appeal) is of opinion that any duty has not been levied or has been short levied or erroneously refunded, no order requiring the appellant to pay any duty not levied, short-levied or erroneously refunded shall be passed unless the appellant is given notice within the time-limit specified in section 168 to show cause against the proposed order.
(4) The order of the Commissioner (Appeal) disposing of the appeal shall be in writing and shall state the points for determination, the decision thereon and the reasons for the decision.
(5) On the disposal of the appeal, the Commissioner (Appeal) shall communicate the order passed by him to the appellant, the adjudicating authority and the Commissioner of Customs.]

Commissioner (Appeals): The Commissioner (Appeals) is empowered to hear appeals and may allow the appellant to raise additional grounds not previously specified if the omission was not deliberate.
The Commissioner (Appeals) may conduct further inquiries and pass orders to confirm, modify, or annul decisions, provided that parties are given opportunities to be heard.

When issuing an order that might increase penalties, increase the value of confiscated goods, or reduce a refund, the Commissioner (Appeals) must provide the appellant a reasonable opportunity to show cause.

If the Commissioner (Appeals) determines that duty was not levied, short-levied, or erroneously refunded, they may order payment only if a show-cause notice is issued within the time-limit prescribed by law.
The Commissioner (Appeals) must record orders in writing, detailing the points for determination, the decisions reached, and the underlying reasoning.
Upon disposing of an appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) is required to communicate the final order to the appellant, the original adjudicating authority, and the Commissioner of Customs.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs must be formally notified by the Commissioner (Appeals) regarding the outcome of any appeal.
Show Cause Notice: A show cause notice is a mandatory legal requirement before the Commissioner (Appeals) can issue orders that negatively impact the appellant regarding duties, penalties, or refunds.
Confiscated Goods: The Commissioner (Appeals) cannot increase the scope or value of confiscation in an order without first granting the appellant a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the proposal.
Refund of Customs Duty: An order reducing the amount of a refund cannot be passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power of the Board to rectify any mistake, error, etc.
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[193B]. Power of the Board to rectify any mistake, error, etc.- The Board may on its own motion or on an application made by any person within one year of the passing of an order, rectify any mistake or error which is apparent from the record in any order passed by it under any provision of this Act or the rules made thereunder:
Provided that no such rectification which has the effect of enhancing any penalty or fine or requiring the payment of a greater amount of duty shall be made unless the person affected by such rectification has been given an opportunity of being heard in person or through a counsel or other person duly authorized by him.]

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to rectify any mistake or error apparent from the record in any order passed by it under the Customs Act 1969 or its associated rules.
This rectification can be initiated by the Board on its own motion or upon an application submitted by an affected person within one year of the date of the original order.
Person: Any person may apply to the National Board of Revenue for the rectification of an error within one year of the passing of an order.
If a proposed rectification increases a penalty, fine, or duty amount, the affected person must be granted a reasonable opportunity to be heard in person or through an authorized representative.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal framework under which the National Board of Revenue exercises its authority to correct administrative errors or mistakes appearing in official records.
Rules: The power of the National Board of Revenue to rectify errors extends to orders passed under the rules made in accordance with the Customs Act 1969.
Authorized Representative: An affected person may utilize an authorized representative or counsel to present their case during proceedings where the National Board of Revenue contemplates a rectification that would increase a financial liability.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Review Committee
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
2[3[193C, Review Committee.- 4[(1) There shall be a Review Committee consisting of such number of members as the Board may determine for the purposes of reviewing any matter related to the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) issued by the pre-shipment inspection agencies appointed by the Government under section 25A.]
(2) Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Review Committee may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 196.
(3) The Appellate Tribunal may, after making such enquiry as it considers necessary and after giving the Commissioner or his authorised representative, the local representative of the concerned pre-shipment inspection agency, and the importer an opportunity of being heard, if they so desire, pass such order as it thinks fit, including fixing the price of the subject goods for the purpose of final assessment.
(4) No fee shall be payable for an appeal under this section.]

Review Committee: A Review Committee is established with a number of members determined by the National Board of Revenue to review matters concerning Clean Report of Findings issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies.
Any person who is aggrieved by a decision of this committee is entitled to file an appeal with the Appellate Tribunal.
National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is authorized to determine the number of members to serve on the Review Committee.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: These agencies are appointed by the Government under the Customs Act to issue Clean Report of Findings, which are subject to review by the Review Committee.
Local representatives of these agencies must be provided an opportunity to be heard by the Appellate Tribunal during appeal proceedings.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: The Appellate Tribunal is authorized to hear appeals against decisions made by the Review Committee.

The Tribunal is empowered to conduct inquiries and pass final orders, including determining the value of goods for final assessment, after providing a hearing to the Commissioner of Customs, the pre-shipment inspection agency, and the importer.
No fees are required to be paid for filing an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal under this section.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs or their authorized representative is entitled to be heard by the Appellate Tribunal during the appeal process regarding the Review Committee's decision.
Importer: The importer has the right to be heard by the Appellate Tribunal during proceedings related to the review of findings issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
194. Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied.- (1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 5[or section 196A] against any decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if he is so permitted by the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer 37[fifty per cent of the duty demanded or fifty per cent of the penalty imposed, or both, as the case may be]:
Provided that such person may, instead of depositing 38[the amount of the penalty as aforesaid] deposit only fifty per cent thereof and furnish a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the due payment of the balance:
Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or 39[penalty imposed] will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose.
(2) If, upon an appeal it is decided that the whole or any portion of the aforesaid duty or penalty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall return to the appellant such amount or portion as the case may be.

Customs Authority: The customs authority maintains control over goods, and certain appeal processes regarding duty or penalties apply when goods have ceased to be under their custody.
Duty Payment: A person appealing a decision regarding demanded duties is generally required to deposit a specified percentage of the demanded amount with the appropriate officer, unless otherwise permitted by the appellate authority.
If an appeal results in a decision that the duty was not leviable, the appropriate officer is required to refund the amount paid by the appellant.
Customs Penalty: A person appealing against a levied penalty must deposit a specified percentage of the penalty amount, or may alternatively provide a bank guarantee for the balance under specific conditions.
The appellate authority has the discretion to waive the deposit requirement for penalties if it determines that payment would cause undue hardship to the appellant.
Upon a successful appeal where it is decided the penalty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall refund the paid amount to the appellant.
Customs Appellate Tribunal: The appellate authority has the power to allow the deposit of duty or penalties at a later stage before the appeal is considered and may dispense with the deposit requirement entirely if deemed necessary to avoid undue hardship.
Scheduled Bank: An appellant may provide a guarantee from a scheduled bank to cover the balance of a penalty amount instead of depositing the full required sum.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is responsible for receiving the required deposits of duty or penalties from the appellant and for processing refunds if an appeal is successful.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power of the Board to call for and examine records, etc.
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
195. Power of the Board to call for and examine records, etc.- (1) The Board may of its own motion call for and examine the records of any proceedings under this Act for the purpose of satisfying itself as to the legality or propriety of any decision or order passed therein by an officer subordinate to it and may pass such orders as it thinks fit:
Provided that no order confiscating goods of greater value, or enhancing any fine in lieu of confiscation, or imposing or enhancing any penalty, or requiring payment of any duty not levied or short-levied shall be passed unless the person affected thereby has been given any opportunity of showing cause against it and of being heard in person or through a counsel or other person duly authorised by him.
(2) No record of any proceedings relating to any decision or order passed by an officer of customs shall be called for and examined under sub-section(1) after the expiry of two years from the date of such decision or order.

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to call for and examine the records of any customs proceedings to ensure the legality and propriety of decisions made by subordinate officers.
The National Board of Revenue has the authority to pass any orders it deems appropriate during its review of proceedings.
Officer of Customs: An officer of customs is subject to the review and oversight of the National Board of Revenue regarding their decisions and orders.

The power of the National Board of Revenue to call for and examine records relating to orders passed by an officer of customs is limited to a two-year period following the date of the original decision or order.
Customs Legal Proceedings: The records of any customs proceedings may be subject to review by the National Board of Revenue to verify the legal validity of the actions taken.
Person: Any person affected by an order involving confiscation, enhanced fines, penalties, or duty recovery has a legal right to be notified and given an opportunity to show cause and be heard, either personally or through an authorized representative, before the order is passed.
Confiscation of Goods: When reviewing proceedings, the National Board of Revenue cannot pass orders that increase the scope of confiscation or enhance associated fines without providing the affected party a formal opportunity to be heard.
Duty Payment: The National Board of Revenue must provide an opportunity for a hearing to any person before issuing an order that mandates the payment of previously unlevied or short-levied duties.
Customs Penalty: The National Board of Revenue is restricted from imposing or increasing any customs penalty without first allowing the affected party to present their case in a hearing.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Appellate Tribunal
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[196. Appellate Tribunal.- (1) The Government shall constitute an Appellate Tribunal to be called the Customs, Excise and Appellate Tribunal which shall consist of as many technical and judicial members as it thinks fit to exercise the powers and discharge the functions conferred on the Appellate Tribunal by this Act.
(2) A technical member shall be a person who has held 2[or is holding] the post of Member of the Board or has held 2[or is holding] the post of Commissioner of Customs and Excise or any equivalent post for 40[at least one year].
(3) A judicial member shall be a person who has for at least ten years held a judicial office in the capacity of a District and Sessions Judge in the territory of Bangladesh or who has been a member of Bangladesh Civil Service (Judicial) and has held a judicial post for at least three years having earned pay in the selection grade of the scale of pay, or who has been an advocate for at least ten years in a court, not lower than that of a Court of District and Sessions Judge.
(4) The Government shall appoint one of the members of the Appellate Tribunal to be the President thereof.

Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: The Government is empowered to establish this tribunal to exercise powers and discharge functions conferred under the Customs Act 1969.
The tribunal is composed of both technical and judicial members appointed by the Government, with one member designated as the President.
National Board of Revenue: The post of Member of this Board serves as a qualification criterion for the appointment of a technical member to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal.
Commissioner of Customs: Experience serving in the position of Commissioner of Customs or equivalent is a mandatory qualification for individuals to be appointed as technical members of the Appellate Tribunal.
President of the Appellate Tribunal: The Government is responsible for appointing one of the existing members of the Appellate Tribunal to serve as its President.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Appeals to the Appellate Tribunal
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1196A. Appeals to the Appellate Tribunal.- (1) Any person aggrieved by any of the following orders may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against such order:-
(a) a decision or order passed by the Commissioner of Customs as an adjudicating authority, not being decision or order passed under section 82 or section 98; or
(b) an order passed by the Commissioner (Appeal) under section 193 as it stood immediately before the appointed day or under section 193A.
(2) The Commissioner of Customs may, if he is of the opinion that an order passed by the Commissioner (Appeal) under section 193 as it stood immediately before the appointed day or under section 193A is not legal or proper, direct the proper officer to appeal on his behalf to the Appellate Tribunal against such order.
(3) Every appeal under this section shall be filed within three months from the date on which the order sought to be appealed against is communicated to the Commissioner of Customs or, as the case may be, the other party preferring appeal.
(4) On receipt of notice that an appeal has been preferred under this section, the party against whom the appeal has been preferred may, not withstanding that he may not have appealed against such order or any part thereof, file, within forty-five days of the receipt of the notice, a memorandum of cross-objections verified in such manner as may be specified by rules made on this behalf against any party of the order appeals against and such memorandum shall be disposed of by the Appellate Tribunal as if it were an appeal presented within the time specified in sub-section (3).
(5) The Appellate Tribunal may admit an appeal or permit the filing of a memorandum of cross-objections after the expiry of the relevant period referred to in sub-section (3) or sub-section (4), if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not presenting it within that period.
(6) An appeal to the Appellate Tribunal shall be in such form and shall be verified in such manner as may be specified by rules made in this behalf and shall, in the case of an appeal made on or after the appointed day, irrespective of the date of demand or duty and interest or of levy of penalty in relation to which the appeal is made, be accompanied by a fee of,-
(a) where the amount of duty and interest demanded and penalty levied by any officer of Customs in the case to which the appeal relates is one lakh taka or less, [three hundred taka;
(b) where the amount of duty and interest demanded and penalty levied by any officer of Customs in the case to which the appeal relates is more than one lakh taka, [one thousand two taka];
(7) The Appellate Tribunal shall dispose of the appeal [within four years] from the date of its receipt.
(8) If the appeal is not disposed of within the time specified in sub-section (7), the appeal shall be deemed to have been allowed by the Appellate Tribunal.
Provided that no such fee shall be payable in the case of an appeal referred to in sub-section (2) or a memorandum of cross-objections referred to in sub-section (4).

Customs Appellate Tribunal: This entity acts as the primary body for hearing appeals against specific adjudication orders or previous appellate orders under the customs law.
It holds the authority to admit late appeals if sufficient cause is shown and is mandated to dispose of appeals within a specified timeframe, failing which the appeal is deemed allowed.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs serves as an adjudicating authority whose decisions may be appealed to the Tribunal, excluding specific operational orders.
The Commissioner is also empowered to direct proper officers to file appeals to the Tribunal if they determine a previous order is legally improper.
Commissioner (Appeals): Orders passed by this official are subject to appeal before the Customs Appellate Tribunal.
Customs Appeals and Applications: Appeals must be filed within a set period after communication of the contested order, and they must be accompanied by a prescribed fee, with certain exemptions provided for specific types of appeals or cross-objections.
The process allows for cross-objections to be filed by the opposing party within a set timeframe after notice of an appeal is received, which are then processed similarly to regular appeals.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Orders of Appellate Tribunal
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1196B. Orders of Appellate Tribunal.- (1) The Appellate Tribunal may, after giving the parties to the appeal, an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit, confirming, modifying or annulling the decision or order 41[or may refer the case back to the authority which passed such decision or order with such directions as the Appellate Tribunal may think fit, for a fresh adjudication or decision, as the case may be, after taking additional evidence, if necessary]
(2) The Appellate Tribunal may, at any time within four years from the date of the order, with a view to rectifying any mistake apparent from the record, amend any order passed by it under sub-section (1) and shall make such amendments if the mistake is brought to its notice by the Commissioner of Customs or the other party to the appeal:
Provided that an amendment which has the effect of enhancing the assessment or reducing a refund or otherwise increasing the liability of the other party shall not be made under this sub-section, unless the Appellate Tribunal has given notice to him of its intention to do so and has allowed him a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
(3) The Appellate Tribunal shall send a copy of every orders passed under this section to the Commissioner of Customs and the other party to the appeal.
(4) Save as otherwise provided in section 196D, order passed by the Appellate Tribunal on appeal shall be final.

Customs Appellate Tribunal: The Customs Appellate Tribunal is empowered to pass orders confirming, modifying, or annulling original decisions after providing parties an opportunity to be heard.
The Tribunal may remand a case back to the original authority with specific directions for fresh adjudication, including the collection of additional evidence where necessary.
The Tribunal possesses the authority to rectify mistakes apparent from the record within a specified timeframe of four years from the date of the original order.
When amending an order that would increase a party's liability, reduce a refund, or enhance an assessment, the Tribunal must provide notice and a hearing to the affected party.
The Tribunal is required to distribute copies of its final orders to the Commissioner of Customs and the opposing party to the appeal.
Orders issued by the Tribunal are considered final, subject only to the provisions set forth in Section 196D of the Customs Act 1969.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is entitled to receive copies of all orders passed by the Customs Appellate Tribunal.
The Commissioner of Customs has the right to bring apparent mistakes in the Tribunal's orders to its attention for the purpose of rectification.
Customs Assessment: The Tribunal may amend its orders to rectify record-based mistakes, provided such amendments do not result in the unauthorized enhancement of a customs assessment.
Refund of Customs Duty: Amendments made by the Tribunal to its own orders are restricted if they would lead to a reduction in the refund of customs duty due to a party without following due process.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Procedure of Appellate Tribunal
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
2196C. Procedure of Appellate Tribunal.- (1) The powers and functions of the Appellate Tribunal may be exercised and discharged by Benches constituted by the President from amongst the members thereof.
(2) Subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (3) and (4), a Bench shall consist of one technical member and one judicial member.
(3) Every appeal against a decision or order relating, among other things, to the determination of any question having a relation to the rate of duty of customs or to the value of goods for purposes of assessment shall be heard by a special Bench constituted by the President for hearing such appeals and such Bench shall consist of not less than two members and shall include at least one technical member and one judicial member.
(4) The President or any other member of the Appellate Tribunal authorised in this behalf by the President may, sitting singly, dispose of any case which has been allotted to the Bench of which he is a member where-
(a) the value of the goods confiscated without option having been given to the owner of the goods to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation under section 181; or
(b) in any disputed case, other than a case where the determination of any question having a relation to the rate of duty of customs or to the value of goods for purpose of assessment is in issue or is one of the points in issue, the difference in duty involved or the duty involved; or
(c) the amount of fine or penalty involved;
does not exceed one lakh taka.
(5) If the members of a Bench differ in opinion on any point, the point shall be decided according to the opinion of the majority, if there is a majority; but if the members are equally divided, they shall state the point or points on which they differ and make a reference to the President who shall either hear the point or points by one or more of the other members of the Appellate Tribunal and such point or points shall be decided according to the opinion of the majority of these members of the Appellate Tribunal who have heard the case, including those who first heard it.
(6) Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Appellate Tribunal shall have power to regulate its own procedure and the procedure of the Benches thereof in all matters arising out of the exercise of its powers or of the discharge of its functions, including the places at which the Benches shall hold their sittings.
(7) The Appellate Tribunal shall, for the purposes of discharging its functions, have the same powers as are vested in a court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908), when trying a suit in respect of the following matters, namely-
(a) discovery and inspection;
(b) enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath;
(c) compelling the production of books of account and other documents; and
(d) issuing commissions.
(8) Any proceeding before the Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 and 228 and for the purposes of section 196 of the Penal Code (Act XLV of 1860) and the Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for all the purposes of section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898).

Customs Appellate Tribunal: The Appellate Tribunal is empowered to constitute Benches from its members to exercise its powers and discharge its functions.
The Tribunal has the authority to regulate its own procedures and the sittings of its Benches.

For specific legal purposes, proceedings before the Tribunal are deemed judicial proceedings, and the Tribunal itself is recognized as a Civil Court under specified sections of the Penal Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure.
President of the Appellate Tribunal: The President is responsible for constituting the Benches of the Appellate Tribunal and assigning cases to them.
The President possesses the authority to resolve cases where members of a Bench are equally divided in opinion by referring the matter to other members for a final decision.
Customs Assessment: Special Benches are required to hear appeals regarding the determination of customs duty rates or the valuation of goods for assessment purposes.
Code of Civil Procedure 1908: The Appellate Tribunal is vested with the same powers as a court under this Code regarding discovery, inspection, compelling attendance, production of documents, and issuing commissions.
Penal Code 1860: Proceedings before the Appellate Tribunal are classified as judicial proceedings under specific sections of this Code.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: The Appellate Tribunal is deemed a Civil Court for the purposes of specified sections and chapters of this Code.
Confiscated Goods: Single-member Benches of the Tribunal may dispose of cases where the value of goods confiscated without an option for a fine in lieu of confiscation does not exceed a specified monetary threshold.
Customs Penalty: A single-member Bench may hear and dispose of cases involving fines or penalties that do not exceed a prescribed financial limit, provided the case does not involve fundamental issues of duty rate or valuation.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Appeal to the High Court Division
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 1[2[196D. Appeal to the High Court Division.- The Commissioner of Customs or the other party may, within 3[ninety] days of the date upon which he is served with notice of an order under section 196B, by an application, prefer an appeal to the High Court Division against such order.]

Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is authorized to file an appeal against an order issued under the specified section of the Customs Act 1969. This appeal must be submitted to the High Court Division within a prescribed timeframe after being served with the notice of the order.
High Court Division: The High Court Division serves as the appellate authority for customs-related orders passed under the prescribed section. Parties aggrieved by such orders may file an application for an appeal within a fixed number of days from the date of receiving the notice.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Case before High Court Division to be heard by not less than two judges
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
5[196F. Case before High Court Division to be heard by not less than two judges.- (1) 6[Where an appeal has been preferred to the High Court Division under section 196D], it shall be heard by a Bench of not less than two judges of the High Court Division and shall be decided in accordance with the opinion of such judges or of the majority, if any, of such judges.
(2) Where there is no such majority, the judges shall state the point of law upon which they differ and the case shall then be heard upon that point only by one or more of the other judges of the High Court Division, and such point shall be decided according to the majority of the judges who have heard the case including those who first heard it.

High Court Division: Cases or appeals brought before the High Court Division under customs law must be heard by a bench consisting of at least two judges.
The decision of the court is reached based on the opinion of the presiding judges or by the majority opinion of such judges.

In the event of a split decision where no majority exists, the judges must identify the specific point of law in dispute for referral to additional judges of the High Court Division, ensuring the final ruling aligns with the majority opinion of the total pool of judges who reviewed the case.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Decision of the High Court Division on the appeal
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[2[196G. Decision of the High Court Division on the appeal.- (1) Where an appeal is preferred under section 196D, the High Court Division shall decide the points raised therein and such other points incidental thereto as are deemed necessary and shall deliver its judgement thereon,
(2) The High Court Division, in its judgement, may award any costs upon any party to the appeal.
(3) A copy of the judgement delivered under sub-section (1) shall, under the seal and signature of an officer of that Division, be sent to the Appellate Tribunal.]

High Court Division: The High Court Division is empowered to hear appeals and issue decisions on the legal points raised in the appeal, along with any incidental matters it deems necessary.
The court has the authority to award costs to any party involved in the appeal proceedings.
The High Court Division must issue its judgment and ensure that a certified copy, bearing the seal and signature of its officer, is transmitted to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: The Appellate Tribunal is the recipient of the formal judgment rendered by the High Court Division regarding customs appeal matters.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Sums due to be paid notwithstanding reference, etc.
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 3[196H. Sums due to be paid notwithstanding reference, etc.- Notwithstanding that a reference has been made to the High Court Division, sums due to the Government as a result of an order passed under sub-section (1) of section 196B shall be payable in accordance with the order so passed.]

Government: Sums payable to the Government following a specific legal order must be paid regardless of whether an appeal or reference has been filed with the High Court Division.
High Court Division: The initiation of a reference case before the High Court Division does not stay the requirement to pay sums due under an order issued by customs authorities.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Exclusion of the time taken for copy
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 4[196I. Exclusion of the time taken for copy.- In computing the period of limitation specified for an appeal or application under this Chapter, the day on which the notice of the order complained of was served, and if the party preferring the appeal or making the application was not furnished with a copy of the order when the notice of the order was served upon him, the time requisite for obtaining a copy of such order shall be excluded.]

Limitation of Legal Actions: In calculating the limitation period for filing an appeal or application under this Chapter of the Customs Act 1969, the day on which the notice of the order is served must be excluded.
If the party was not provided with a copy of the order at the time of service, the time required to obtain that copy is also excluded from the computation of the limitation period.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Transfer of certain pending proceedings and transitional provisions
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
5[196J. Transfer of certain pending proceedings and transitional provisions.- (1) Every appeal which is pending immediately before the appointed day before the Board under section 193 as it stood immediately before that day, and any matter arising out of or connected with such appeal and which is so pending shall stand transferred on that day to the Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal may proceed with such appeal or matter from the stage at which it was on that day:
Provided that the appellant may demand that before proceeding further with that appeal or matter, he may be re-heard.
(2) Every proceeding which is pending immediately before the appointed day before the Government under section 196 as it stood immediately before that day, and any matter arising out of or connected with such proceeding and which is so pending shall stand transferred on that day to the Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal may proceed with such proceeding or matter from the stage at which it was on that day as if such proceeding or matter were an appeal filed before it:
Provided that if any such proceeding or matter relates to an order where-
(a) the value of the goods confiscated without option having been given to the owner of the goods to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation under section 181(1); or
(b) in any disputed case, other than a case where the determination of any question having a relation to the rate of duty of customs or to the value of goods for purposes of assessment is in issue or is one of the points in issue, the difference in duty involved or the duty involved; or
(c) the amount of fine or penalty determined by such order;
does not exceed ten thousand taka such proceeding or matter shall continue to be dealt with by the Government as if the said section 196 had not been substituted:
Provided further that the applicant or the other party may make a demand to the Appellate Tribunal that before proceeding further with that proceeding or matter, he may be re-heard.
(3) Every proceeding which is pending immediately before the appointed day before the Board under section 193A or before the Government under section 196B as they stood immediately before that day, and any matter arising out of or connected with such proceeding and which is so pending shall continue to be dealt with by the Board or the Government, as the case may be, as if the said sections had not been substituted.
(4) Any person who immediately before the appointed day was authorised to appear in any appeal or proceeding transferred under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall, notwithstanding anything contained in section 196K, have the right to appear before the Appellate Tribunal in relation to such appeal or proceeding.]

Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: The Appellate Tribunal is designated as the successor body for the transfer of pending appeals and proceedings that were previously under the jurisdiction of the Board or the Government before the appointed day.
The Appellate Tribunal is empowered to continue proceedings from the stage they reached prior to the transfer and must allow for re-hearing upon the request of an appellant or party involved.
National Board of Revenue: Pending appeals previously filed before the Board under the former provisions are transferred to the Appellate Tribunal, while other specific pending proceedings continue to be handled by the Board as if the relevant sections had not been substituted.
Government: The Government retains jurisdiction over certain pending proceedings related to customs orders where the value of confiscated goods, the difference in duty, or the penalty amount does not exceed a specified threshold.
Proceedings not meeting the criteria for transfer to the Appellate Tribunal continue to be processed by the Government as if the original legal provisions remained in effect.
Confiscation of Goods: For cases involving goods confiscated without an option for a fine in lieu of confiscation, the value of the goods determines whether the legal proceeding is transferred to the Appellate Tribunal or remains under the authority of the Government.
Customs Duty Rate: Cases involving the determination of customs duty rates or the value of goods for assessment purposes are excluded from the threshold-based retention of jurisdiction by the Government.
Customs Legal Proceedings: The act provides transitional mechanisms for pending legal matters, establishing clear rules for the transfer of cases to the Appellate Tribunal while ensuring the right of parties to seek re-hearing.
Legal practitioners or authorized representatives who were active in proceedings prior to the transition retain their right to appear before the Appellate Tribunal for the transferred cases.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Appearance by the authorised representative
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[2[196K]. Appearance by the authorised representative.- Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, any person, who is entitled or required to attend before any officer of customs, an appellate authority, the Board or the Government in any proceedings under this Act or any, rules made thereunder, otherwise than when required under law to attend personally, may attend in such proceedings by a person authorised by him in writing in this behalf, being a relative of, or a person regularly employed by, the aggrieved person, or an advocate who is entitled to plead in any Court of Law, or a Customs Consultant as defined and licensed under rules prescribed in this behalf, and not being disqualified under sub-section (2).
(2) No person who has been dismissed from Government service shall be qualified to represent a person under sub-section (1); and if any advocate or Customs Consultant is found guilty of misconduct in connection with any customs proceedings by the authority empowered to take disciplinary action against members of the profession to which he belongs, or if any other person is found guilty of such misconduct by the 3[Commissioner of Customs], the 3[Commissioner of Customs] may direct that he shall be thence forward disqualified to represent a person under sub-section (1) :
Provided that-
(a) no such direction shall be issued in respect of any person unless he is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard;
(b) any person against whom such direction is issued may, within one month from the date of receipt of the direction, appeal to the Board to have the direction cancelled; and
(c) no such direction shall take effect until one month from the date of receipt thereof by the person concerned or, when an appeal is preferred; until the disposal of the appeal.]

Authorized Representative: An authorized representative may appear on behalf of a person in customs proceedings, except when personal attendance is legally required.
Eligible representatives include relatives, regular employees, advocates, or licensed Customs Consultants, provided they are not disqualified by law.
Customs Authority: This entity includes any officer of customs, an appellate authority, the National Board of Revenue, or the Government, before whom a person may be required to attend in proceedings under the Customs Act 1969.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to investigate and determine misconduct by a person acting as an authorized representative and may issue a direction disqualifying them from future representation.
Any disqualification order issued by the Commissioner of Customs is subject to an appeal process to the National Board of Revenue and requires a prior opportunity for the affected person to be heard.
National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue acts as the appellate body for any person seeking to cancel a disqualification order issued by the Commissioner of Customs.
Person: Any person involved in customs proceedings has the right to be represented by an authorized person, provided the requirements of the Customs Act 1969 are met.
Persons dismissed from Government service are expressly prohibited from acting as authorized representatives.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power of the Board to rectify any mistake, error, etc
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
1[196L]. Power of the Government to call for and examine records.- The Government may, on its own motion 3[* *], within one year of the passing of an order under this Act or the rules made thereunder, call for and examine the records of the proceedings relating to such order for the purpose of satisfying itself as to the legality or property of the order and may pass such orders as it thinks fit, rectifying any mistake or error which becomes apparent from such examination:

Provided that no such order which has the effect of confiscating goods of greater value or, enhancing any fine in lieu of confiscation or enhancing any penalty or requiring the payment of a greater amount of duty shall be made unless the person affected by such order has been given an opportunity of being heard in person or through a counsel or other person duly authorised by him.]

Government: The Government is empowered to call for and examine the records of proceedings of any order made under the Customs Act 1969 or its rules within one year to ensure legality or propriety.

The Government may pass orders to rectify any apparent mistakes or errors found during such examination, provided that it does not unilaterally increase penalties or duties without granting the affected person a right to be heard.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal authority for the Government to review and correct administrative orders made pursuant to its provisions or subordinate rules.
Confiscation of Goods: The Government may not issue an order that increases the confiscation value of goods or enhances fines or penalties without first providing the affected person an opportunity to be heard.
Duty Payment: Any order by the Government that would result in a requirement for a greater amount of duty payment cannot be made without providing the affected person an opportunity of being heard in person or through a representative.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Bar to the jurisdiction of the Courts
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 4196M. Bar to the jurisdiction of the Courts.- No appeal shall lie to any civil court by any person, aggrieved by any decision or order, passed by an officer of customs before appealing to and getting decision or order thereon from the Commissioner (Appeal) or the Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be.

Civil Court: No appeal may be filed in a civil court by an aggrieved person against a decision or order made by an officer of customs until the matter has first been adjudicated by the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal.
Officer of Customs: Decisions or orders passed by an officer of customs are subject to administrative review before they can be challenged in a civil court.
Commissioner (Appeals): This authority acts as a mandatory appellate body that must render a decision or order on an issue before the aggrieved party is permitted to seek further legal recourse in a civil court.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: This body serves as a mandatory appellate authority whose decision or order must be obtained before an aggrieved person can pursue an appeal in a civil court regarding customs matters.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Definitions

Appointed Day: The appointed day is defined as the first day of October in the year nineteen hundred and ninety-five for the purposes of this chapter.
President of the Appellate Tribunal: The term President refers to the individual holding the position of the President of the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal.

processed_clauses.metadata_title: CHAPTER XX - MISCELLANEOUS
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
CHAPTER XX

MISCELLANEOUS

processed_clauses.clause_title: Customs control over conveyances and goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text: 197. Customs control over conveyances and goods.- The appropriate officer shall, for the purposes of this Act, have control over all conveyances and goods in a customs-area.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is granted the legal authority to exercise control over all conveyances and goods located within a customs-area for the purposes of the Customs Act 1969.
Conveyance: Conveyances within a customs-area are subject to the official control and oversight of the appropriate officer of customs.
Goods: All goods located in a customs-area fall under the regulatory control of the appropriate officer of customs as mandated by the Act.
Customs-area: This area is defined as the jurisdiction where the appropriate officer of customs exercises control over all conveyances and goods present within it.

processed_clauses.clause_title: Power to open packages and examine, weight or measure goods
processed_clauses.resolved_text:
198. Power to open packages and examine, weight or measure goods.- 1[(1)] The appropriate officer may open any package or container and examine, weight or measure any goods brought to the customs-station for importation or exportation and may for that purpose unload any such goods from the conveyance on which they have been imported or are to be exported.

1[(2)] The owner of such goods or his authorized representative may be allowed to inspect such goods before the presentation or transmission of the bill of entry or the bill of export thereof, as the case may be, subject to the conditions laid down by an officer of customs not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner.]

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to open any package or container to examine, weigh, or measure goods brought to a customs station for import or export.
The officer has the authority to unload goods from a conveyance as part of the examination, weighing, or measurement process.
Goods: Goods brought to a customs station for importation or exportation are subject to inspection, weighing, and measurement by customs authorities.
Conveyance: Goods may be unloaded from a conveyance by the appropriate officer of customs for the purpose of examination, weighing, or measurement.
Owner of Warehoused Goods: The owner or their authorized representative is permitted to inspect goods prior to the formal presentation or transmission of the bill of entry or bill of export, provided they meet specific conditions set by an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs.
Authorized Representative: An authorized representative may inspect goods on behalf of the owner before the submission of the bill of entry or bill of export, subject to conditions imposed by customs officials.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: An officer of customs not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs is authorized to lay down the conditions under which an owner or their representative may inspect goods.
Bill of Entry: The inspection of imported goods by the owner or their representative must occur before the presentation or transmission of the bill of entry.
